lessons.title: What Multimedia Is and Why Raw Media Is Huge
lessons.content:
Think about the last time you opened YouTube on your phone to watch a cricket highlight. In a few seconds your screen showed moving pictures, the commentator's voice, the crowd noise, the score written at the top, and a small animated logo in the corner. Your phone was juggling five kinds of information at once and keeping all of them in step. That juggling act is what this course is about. Multimedia Systems asks a simple question with a deep answer: how do we turn pictures, sounds and words into bits, squeeze those bits small enough to store and send, and then play them back so that a human being enjoys them?

What multimedia is: The word is just "multi" (many) plus "media" (ways of carrying information). A multimedia system is a computer system that captures, stores, processes, sends and presents information that uses more than one medium, usually including at least one time-based medium such as audio or video. A Word document with only text is not really multimedia. A Bangla news portal page with text, photos and an embedded video report is. A Zoom class with your teacher's face, voice and shared slides is multimedia at its most demanding, because it all has to happen live.

The main media types: Most textbooks list six. Text is letters, digits and symbols, stored as character codes. Images are photos made of pixels. Graphics are drawings described by shapes, such as lines, circles and curves, like a logo in SVG form. Audio is sound, stored as a long list of samples. Video is a sequence of images shown quickly, usually with audio attached. Animation is movement created from drawings or models, such as a cartoon or a moving infographic. Each type has its own way of being represented as numbers, and that is why a multimedia engineer needs a small toolbox for each one.

Static versus continuous media: A key split is time. Text, images and graphics are static, also called discrete media. A photo has no clock inside it; you can look at it for one second or one hour and it is the same photo. Audio, video and animation are continuous, or time-based, media. A song only makes sense if its samples are played at the right speed, in the right order, without gaps. If a photo arrives two seconds late, nobody notices. If one second of a song arrives two seconds late, you hear a stall. This one difference creates most of the hard problems in the second half of this course: buffering, jitter, synchronisation and quality of service.

Linear versus interactive: A film in a cinema hall is linear multimedia. It starts, it runs, it ends, and you cannot change its path. A website, a game, an e-learning module or a museum kiosk is interactive (non-linear) multimedia: the user clicks, chooses and controls what comes next. When the content is linked together so that you can jump from one piece to another, we call it hypermedia, the multimedia version of hypertext. Web pages with links to images, sound and video are hypermedia.

The parts of a multimedia system: Picture the whole journey of one video lecture. First comes capture: a camera sensor and a microphone turn light and sound into electrical signals, and analog-to-digital converters turn those into numbers. Second, storage: the numbers are saved on a phone, a hard disk, or a server. Third, processing: they are edited, compressed and converted between formats. Fourth, transmission: they travel over Wi-Fi, mobile data or fibre. Fifth, presentation: a screen and a speaker turn the numbers back into light and sound for a human. Every lesson of this course zooms into one of these five boxes.

How media becomes bits, in one picture: From Digital Signal Processing you already know the recipe for turning a smooth signal into numbers. Sample it, meaning measure it at regular points in time or space. Quantize each measurement to one of a fixed set of levels. Encode each level as a binary code. An image is sampled in space (pixels), a sound is sampled in time (samples per second), and a video is sampled in space and in time (pixels per frame and frames per second). We will not redo the theory of aliasing and SQNR here; we will use the results and focus on what happens to all those numbers next.

The file size formula: For any uncompressed medium the size is just "how many samples" times "how many bits per sample". For an image: bits = width x height x bit depth. For audio: bits = sample rate x bit depth x channels x seconds. For video: bits per second = width x height x bits per pixel x frames per second. Divide bits by 8 to get bytes. That is all the maths you need to understand why compression exists.

Worked example, one photo: A Full HD screen is 1920 x 1080 pixels. If each pixel stores red, green and blue with 8 bits each, that is 24 bits per pixel. Size = 1920 x 1080 x 24 / 8 = 6,220,800 bytes, about 6.2 MB. One single still frame, not even a video yet. Your phone gallery has thousands of photos; if each were stored raw, a 64 GB phone would fill up with roughly ten thousand of them, with no room for apps.

Worked example, one minute of music: CD-quality audio uses 44,100 samples per second, 16 bits per sample and 2 channels. Bit rate = 44,100 x 16 x 2 = 1,411,200 bits per second. One minute is 1,411,200 x 60 / 8 = 10,584,000 bytes, about 10.6 MB. A three-minute song is about 31.75 MB. Compare that with the 3 to 5 MB MP3 files people share, and you can already feel the power of compression.

Worked example, one second of video: Take 1080p video at 30 frames per second. If every pixel kept full 24-bit colour, the bit rate would be 1920 x 1080 x 24 x 30 = 1,492,992,000 bits per second, almost 1.5 gigabits every second. Real video systems first store colour more cleverly (a trick called 4:2:0 chroma subsampling, lesson 4) which brings it to 12 bits per pixel: 1920 x 1080 x 12 x 30 = 746,496,000 bits per second, about 746 Mbps. One minute of that is about 5.6 GB. A typical home broadband line in Bangladesh might give you 20 to 50 Mbps. Raw HD video simply cannot travel on it. Yet Netflix or YouTube send you good-looking 1080p at a few megabits per second. The gap between 746 Mbps and a few Mbps is the story of compression, and it is roughly a factor of one hundred or more.

KB versus KiB, a small trap: Storage people and memory people count differently. In the SI system, 1 kilobyte (kB) = 1000 bytes, 1 megabyte (MB) = 1,000,000 bytes, and 1 gigabyte (GB) = 1,000,000,000 bytes. In the binary system, 1 kibibyte (KiB) = 1024 bytes, 1 mebibyte (MiB) = 1,048,576 bytes and 1 gibibyte (GiB) = 1024 x 1024 x 1024 bytes. Our photo of 6,220,800 bytes is 6.22 MB but only 5.93 MiB. Many operating systems show binary units while writing "MB", which is why a "64 GB" memory card shows up as about 59.6 GB on a computer. Network speeds are almost always in decimal bits per second: 1 Mbps = 1,000,000 bits per second. Mixing bits and bytes is the most common mistake: 8 Mbps internet downloads about 1 MB per second, not 8.

Why compression and networking dominate: Put the three worked examples together. Raw media is large, continuous media must arrive on time, and networks are shared and imperfect. So the course splits naturally. First we learn how each medium is represented (text, images, colour, audio). Then we learn the theory and tools of compression, both lossless (nothing lost, like ZIP) and lossy (throw away what humans will not notice, like JPEG and MP3). Then we look at video compression, the heaviest hitter. Finally we look at how media is packaged, streamed, given quality of service, stored in databases, authored, protected by DRM, and used ethically.

Quality versus size, the eternal trade-off: Every design decision in multimedia is a trade between three things: quality, size (or bit rate), and computing cost. Higher resolution and more bits look better but cost more storage and bandwidth. Stronger compression saves bandwidth but needs more processing and may lose quality. A designer for a rural Bangladeshi user on a slow 3G or crowded 4G connection makes very different choices from a designer for a cinema projector. Learning to reason about this trade with numbers is the main skill you will take away.

Real-life example 1, a bKash tutorial video: Suppose a company wants a 5-minute video explaining how to send money with bKash, aimed at shopkeepers in small towns. The script (text), screen recordings (video), a voice-over in Bangla (audio), arrows and highlights (graphics) and a small animated logo (animation) are all combined. The raw recording might be several gigabytes. After compression for mobile it might be a few tens of megabytes. Captions in Bangla make it usable in a noisy bazar. Every box of the system diagram appears: capture, storage, processing, transmission, presentation.

Real-life example 2, a voice message on WhatsApp or Messenger: When you hold the mic button and say "Ammu, ami 10 minute e ashchi", your phone samples your voice, compresses it with a speech codec designed for low bit rates, wraps it in a file, sends it over the network, and your mother's phone plays it back. It is a continuous medium, but because it is not a live call it can be stored and forwarded, so a little delay does not hurt. Compare that with a live video call, where every few hundred milliseconds of delay make conversation awkward. Same media types, very different requirements.

Where multimedia lives today: Streaming services, social media, online classes, video calls, telemedicine, digital TV, games, digital signage at shopping malls, security cameras, voice assistants, e-books, museum guides and virtual reality all depend on the ideas in this course. Game Development (a separate course) focuses on real-time interaction and engines; here we focus on the media themselves and how they move.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Students mix up graphics and images (graphics are shape descriptions, images are pixel grids). They forget to divide by 8 when converting bits to bytes. They confuse MB with MiB, and Mbps with MBps. They call any web page "multimedia" even when it is only text. Exams typically ask you to define multimedia, list media types, classify media as static or continuous, explain linear versus interactive, draw the components of a multimedia system, and compute the raw size of an image, an audio clip or a second of video. Practise the three formulas until you can do them on paper.

Recap: Multimedia combines several media types, at least one of which is usually time-based. Media are turned into bits by sampling, quantizing and encoding. Raw sizes are enormous: about 6.2 MB for one Full HD photo, about 10.6 MB per minute of CD audio, and about 746 Mbps for 1080p30 video even with clever colour storage. That is why the rest of this course is about representing media wisely, compressing it hard, and delivering it on time.
key_points: Multimedia = information using several media (text, image, graphics, audio, video, animation), usually including a time-based one.
Static (discrete) media have no timing; continuous media (audio, video, animation) must be played at the right rate and order.
Linear media run in one fixed order; interactive and hypermedia let the user choose and jump via links.
A multimedia system has five stages: capture, storage, processing, transmission, presentation.
Raw size = number of samples x bits per sample; divide by 8 for bytes.
Worked: 1920x1080x24-bit photo = 6,220,800 bytes; CD audio = 1,411,200 bps; 1080p30 at 12 bits/pixel = 746,496,000 bps.
1 MB = 1,000,000 bytes but 1 MiB = 1,048,576 bytes; network speeds are in bits, so 8 Mbps is about 1 MB/s.
Every multimedia design trades quality against size/bit rate and computing cost.
lessons.tip: Keep three formulas on one index card: image = W x H x depth, audio = rate x depth x channels x time, video = W x H x bits per pixel x fps. Half of the numerical exam questions in this course start from one of them.
lessons.task: Pick one photo, one song and one short video on your phone. Note the resolution, duration and file size from the file info. Compute what each would weigh uncompressed with the formulas from this lesson, then divide raw size by actual size to find the compression ratio of each.

quiz.q: Which of these is a continuous (time-based) medium?
quiz.explain: Audio only makes sense when its samples are played at the right rate and in order, so it is time-based. Photos, text and logos are static.

quiz.q: What is the raw size of a 1920 x 1080 image with 24 bits per pixel?
CD audio uses 44,100 samples/s, 16 bits and 2 channels. What is its bit rate?
quiz.explain: 44,100 x 16 x 2 = 1,411,200 bits per second.

quiz.q: A website where you click links to jump between text, photos and videos is best described as:
quiz.explain: Linked, non-linear multimedia is called hypermedia.

quiz.q: Your internet plan is 8 Mbps. Roughly how fast can you download in megabytes per second?
quiz.explain: Network speeds are in bits. 8 Mbps / 8 bits per byte = 1 MB per second, ignoring overhead.

lessons.title: Text, Fonts and Unicode (with Bangla Script Shaping)
lessons.content:
Have you ever received a Bangla message that showed up as a row of empty boxes, or as strange Latin letters like "Avwg evsjv"? That is not the phone being rude. It is a text representation problem: the sender's computer and the receiver's computer did not agree on which number means which letter, or the receiver had no font that could draw the letters. Text looks like the simplest medium, but getting it right for every language on Earth, Bangla included, took decades of engineering. In this lesson we start from zero: what a character is, how it becomes bytes, how a font turns bytes back into shapes, and why Bangla needs extra care.

Characters versus glyphs: A character is an abstract unit of meaning, like "the letter ka" or "the digit 5". A glyph is a particular drawn shape of a character in a particular font. The letter "a" in Times New Roman and in Arial is the same character but two different glyphs. In Bangla the difference is even bigger: one visible shape, such as the conjunct ক্ষ, may be built from several characters, and one character, such as the vowel sign o, may be drawn as two pieces on two sides of a consonant. Computers store characters; fonts and shaping engines produce glyphs.

ASCII, the starting point: In the 1960s the American Standard Code for Information Interchange gave each English letter, digit, punctuation mark and some control codes a number from 0 to 127. That needs 7 bits. Capital A is 65 (hex 41), small a is 97 (hex 61), the digit 0 is 48 (hex 30), and space is 32. ASCII was perfect for English teleprinters and useless for almost everyone else.

Code pages, the messy middle: Since a byte has 8 bits, vendors used the extra 128 values (128 to 255) for local letters. Western Europe got one table (for example ISO-8859-1), Russian got another, Greek another. These tables are called code pages. The trouble is that byte 233 might be é in one code page and a Cyrillic letter in another. A file carried no label saying which table it used, so text written in one country turned to garbage in another. Worse, 256 slots are nowhere near enough for Chinese, and scripts like Bangla were often handled by fonts that simply drew Bangla shapes on top of Latin code numbers.

The Bijoy-era problem in Bangladesh: For years, much Bangla typing in Bangladesh used legacy ANSI-based fonts, where the byte for an English letter was drawn as a Bangla glyph by a special font. On a computer with that font, the text looked fine. Without it, you saw meaningless Latin letters, which is where messages like "Avwg evsjv" come from. Such text cannot be searched properly on the web, cannot be sorted alphabetically, and breaks when the font changes. The fix is to store real Bangla characters, which is what Unicode provides. Today phones, Google, Facebook and government websites use Unicode Bangla, typed with keyboards such as Avro or the phone's built-in Bangla keyboard.

Unicode, one number for every character: Unicode gives every character in every writing system a unique number called a code point, written U+ followed by hex digits. A is U+0041. The Bangla letter অ is U+0985, ক is U+0995, and the taka sign ৳ is U+09F3. The Bengali block runs from U+0980 to U+09FF. The full code space goes from U+0000 to U+10FFFF, which is 1,114,112 possible code points, enough for all modern scripts, many historic ones, maths symbols and emoji. Unicode itself is just the numbering. How those numbers are stored as bytes is a separate decision called an encoding.

UTF-32 and UTF-16: The simplest encoding, UTF-32, stores every code point in 4 bytes. It is easy but wasteful: English text becomes four times larger than ASCII. UTF-16 stores most common characters (those up to U+FFFF, the Basic Multilingual Plane) in 2 bytes and the rest, such as most emoji, in 4 bytes using a pair of 16-bit units called a surrogate pair. Windows internals, Java and JavaScript strings use UTF-16 internally.

UTF-8, the web's choice: UTF-8 uses 1 to 4 bytes per code point. Code points up to U+007F take 1 byte and are identical to ASCII, so old English files are already valid UTF-8. Code points up to U+07FF take 2 bytes, up to U+FFFF take 3 bytes, and the rest take 4. The first byte tells you the length: 0xxxxxxx means 1 byte, 110xxxxx means 2, 1110xxxx means 3, 11110xxx means 4, and every following byte looks like 10xxxxxx. The vast majority of web pages today are served as UTF-8.

Worked example, encoding অ: অ is U+0985. In binary, hex 0985 is 0000 1001 1000 0101. It is between U+0800 and U+FFFF, so it needs 3 bytes with the pattern 1110xxxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx, which has room for 4 + 6 + 6 = 16 bits. Split our 16 bits as 0000, 100110, 000101. Fill them in: 11100000, 10100110, 10000101. In hex that is E0 A6 85. So one Bangla letter costs 3 bytes in UTF-8, while A costs 1 byte (41).

Worked example, a word and a conjunct: The word বাংলা is five code points: ব, the vowel sign া, the anusvara ং, ল and া again. In UTF-8 that is 5 x 3 = 15 bytes; in UTF-16 it is 5 x 2 = 10 bytes. The conjunct ক্ষ is three code points: ক (U+0995), the hasanta or virama ্ (U+09CD), and ষ (U+09B7). That is 9 bytes in UTF-8 and 6 in UTF-16, even though it looks like a single letter. So for mostly-Bangla text UTF-16 is smaller, while for mostly-English or mixed web text with HTML tags UTF-8 usually wins, and UTF-8's ASCII compatibility made it the standard on the internet.

Normalization, two spellings of one letter: Sometimes Unicode allows the same visible text to be stored two ways. The letter ড় has its own code point U+09DC, but it can also be written as ড (U+09A1) followed by the nukta sign (U+09BC). A search engine that compares raw code points would think these are different words. Unicode defines normalization forms (such as NFC and NFD) that convert text into one agreed form before comparing or storing. Good multimedia databases normalize Bangla text before indexing it.

Fonts, from bitmaps to outlines: A font is a collection of glyphs plus rules for using them. Early fonts were bitmap fonts: each glyph was a small grid of pixels, stored separately for each size. They are fast but look blocky when scaled. Modern fonts are outline fonts: each glyph is described by curves (TrueType uses quadratic Bezier curves, PostScript-style CFF outlines use cubic ones), so the same glyph scales smoothly from a phone screen to a billboard. A rasterizer converts the outline into pixels at the needed size, and hinting instructions nudge the outline so small text stays crisp on low-resolution screens.

OpenType and typographic terms: OpenType is a font format that can hold either TrueType or CFF outlines and, importantly, layout tables. The substitution table tells the renderer which glyph to use when certain characters appear together (for example, swap three characters for one conjunct glyph). The positioning table tells it how to shift glyphs (for example, where to put a vowel sign). Other terms you will meet: font size in points (1 point = 1/72 inch), kerning (adjusting the space between particular pairs like "AV"), tracking (spacing a whole word evenly), leading (line spacing), serif versus sans-serif, and proportional versus monospaced fonts.

Bangla script shaping: Bangla is a complex script, meaning that the order of stored characters is not simply the left-to-right order of shapes on screen. Take কি. It is stored as ক followed by the vowel sign ি (U+09BF), because that is the order you pronounce it. But the vowel sign is drawn to the left of ক. The vowel sign ো (U+09CB) wraps around the consonant, with one part before and one after it. A hasanta between two consonants, as in ক + ্ + ষ, asks the font to form a conjunct glyph if it has one, or to show ক with a visible hasanta if it does not. The software that applies these rules is called a shaping engine. HarfBuzz is a widely used open-source one, used by Android, Chrome and Firefox among others. Without proper shaping you see ি floating on the wrong side, broken conjuncts, or dotted circles.

How a Bangla line is rendered, step by step: First the app stores Unicode code points in logical (spoken) order. Second, the text is split into runs of the same script and font. Third, the shaping engine reads the font's OpenType tables and turns the code point sequence into a sequence of glyph IDs, reordering vowel signs and choosing conjunct glyphs. Fourth, it computes the position of each glyph. Fifth, the rasterizer draws the outlines into pixels with anti-aliasing. Only the first step is stored; the rest happens every time the text is shown.

Text inside multimedia: Text appears as titles, captions, subtitles, menus and labels. A golden rule is to keep text as real text, not baked into an image, whenever possible. Real text can be searched, translated, read aloud by screen readers for blind users, resized, and stored in a few bytes. A screenshot of a paragraph might be 200 KB while the text itself is a couple of kilobytes. Subtitles for videos are stored as small text files with timestamps and drawn by the player on top of the video.

Real-life example 1, a Bangla news portal: A Dhaka news site stores its articles as UTF-8 in a database, serves HTML that declares charset UTF-8, and ships a web font such as a Unicode Bangla font so readers on any device see the same shapes. Because the text is real Unicode, Google can index the headline, and a reader searching for "বাজেট" finds it. If the site had used a legacy ANSI font, searches would fail and copied text would turn into gibberish.

Real-life example 2, an SMS and a form: Many phone systems count SMS length in units. A message using only basic Latin characters fits about 160 characters in one SMS, but a message with Bangla characters must use a 16-bit encoding (UCS-2), which cuts it to about 70 characters per SMS. That is why bank OTP messages in Bangla may split into several parts. Similarly, a university admission form that only accepts ASCII names will break for students who want to write their names in Bangla; the database column must be Unicode.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students mix up Unicode (the numbering) with UTF-8 (one way to store the numbers). They assume one visible letter equals one character, which is false for conjuncts. They forget that UTF-8 is variable-length, so string length in bytes differs from length in characters. Exams commonly ask: compare ASCII and Unicode, encode a code point in UTF-8 by hand, explain glyph versus character, compare bitmap and outline fonts, define kerning and leading, and explain why complex scripts need shaping.

Recap: Characters are abstract; glyphs are shapes. ASCII covers 128 English characters; code pages caused chaos; Unicode gives every character one code point up to U+10FFFF. UTF-8 stores them in 1 to 4 bytes (অ = E0 A6 85, 3 bytes) and dominates the web. Fonts store outlines plus OpenType rules, and a shaping engine reorders and combines Bangla characters into the right glyphs. Keep text as real Unicode text and your multimedia will be searchable, accessible and tiny.
key_points: A character is an abstract unit; a glyph is its drawn shape in a font.
ASCII uses 7 bits for 128 characters (A = 65 = 0x41); 8-bit code pages conflicted with each other.
Unicode assigns every character a code point from U+0000 to U+10FFFF; Bangla lives in U+0980-U+09FF.
UTF-8 uses 1-4 bytes and is ASCII-compatible; অ (U+0985) = E0 A6 85; UTF-16 uses 2 or 4 bytes, UTF-32 always 4.
ক্ষ is three code points (ক + ্ + ষ) = 9 bytes in UTF-8; বাংলা = 5 code points = 15 bytes.
Outline fonts (TrueType/CFF in OpenType) scale smoothly; OpenType layout tables drive substitution and positioning.
Bangla is a complex script: ি is stored after the consonant but drawn before it; a shaping engine such as HarfBuzz handles this.
Legacy ANSI-based Bangla fonts look fine only with that font; Unicode text is searchable, sortable and portable.
lessons.tip: Whenever text breaks, ask two questions in order: did both sides agree on the encoding (bytes to code points), and does the device have a font plus shaping for the script (code points to glyphs)? Almost every text bug is one of these two.
lessons.task: Open any online "Unicode code point" or character inspector tool in your browser (or Python: [hex(ord(c)) for c in 'আমার নাম']). Type your own name in Bangla, list each code point, count how many code points it has, and compute its size in UTF-8 and UTF-16 by hand.

quiz.q: What is the UTF-8 encoding of অ (U+0985)?
How many Unicode code points make up the conjunct ক্ষ?
quiz.explain: ক (U+0995) + hasanta (U+09CD) + ষ (U+09B7) = 3 code points, shown as one conjunct glyph.

quiz.q: Why is কি drawn with ি on the left even though ি is stored after ক?
options: A shaping engine reorders vowel signs using the font's rules
quiz.explain: Characters are stored in spoken (logical) order; the shaping engine places the glyph of ি before ক.

quiz.q: Which statement about Unicode and UTF-8 is correct?
options: UTF-8 always uses 2 bytes per character
Unicode is the numbering; UTF-8 is one way to store those numbers as bytes
quiz.explain: Unicode assigns code points; UTF-8, UTF-16 and UTF-32 are encodings of those code points.

quiz.q: Why does text made with a legacy ANSI-based Bangla font show as "Avwg evsjv" on another phone?
options: The bytes are Latin code numbers that only that special font draws as Bangla
The phone's screen is too small
quiz.explain: Legacy fonts mapped Bangla glyphs onto Latin code positions; without that font, the bytes show as ordinary Latin letters.

lessons.title: Digital Images: Pixels, Resolution and Bit Depth
lessons.content:
Look very closely at your phone screen with a magnifying glass, or put a drop of water on it, and the smooth photo of your friend breaks into a grid of tiny coloured squares. Each square shows only one colour. Your brain blends thousands of them into a face. That grid is a digital image, and every photo you take, send on Messenger or post on Facebook is, at its heart, a big table of numbers. This lesson builds that table from scratch: what a pixel is, what resolution and bit depth mean, how the different image types store colour, and how to calculate the size of an image before any compression.

What a digital image is: A digital image is a two-dimensional grid of picture elements, called pixels. Each pixel stores a number (or a few numbers) describing the brightness or colour at that spot. We write a pixel's position as (x, y), usually with (0, 0) at the top-left corner, x growing to the right and y growing downward. So a digital image is simply a function f(x, y) whose input is a position and whose output is a colour value. Graphics people call this a raster image, in contrast to vector graphics, which you met in Computer Graphics.

How a camera makes the grid: A camera lens focuses light onto a sensor covered with millions of tiny light-sensitive sites. Each site measures how much light fell on it during the exposure. That is sampling in space: the smooth scene is measured only at grid points. Each measurement is then quantized into one of a fixed number of levels and stored as bits. Most sensors put a colour filter (usually red, green or blue in a pattern called a Bayer filter) over each site, so each site sees only one colour, and software fills in the missing two colours for every pixel by looking at neighbours. This process is called demosaicing.

Spatial resolution: Resolution is how many pixels the image has, written width x height. A Full HD image is 1920 x 1080 = 2,073,600 pixels, about 2 megapixels. A 12-megapixel phone photo is about 4000 x 3000. More pixels capture finer detail, the same way a map with more grid squares shows smaller streets. If you sample too coarsely, thin lines disappear or turn into jagged staircases and fine patterns like a striped shirt can produce strange wavy patterns called moire, which is aliasing in space.

Bit depth: Bit depth is the number of bits used for each pixel, and it decides how many different values a pixel can take. With b bits there are 2^b values. A 1-bit pixel has 2 values (black or white). An 8-bit pixel has 256 values. A 24-bit pixel (8 bits each for red, green and blue) has 2^24 = 16,777,216 possible colours, often called true colour. Too few levels cause banding: a smooth sky turns into visible stripes because neighbouring shades are forced into the same level. This is quantization error in the brightness direction.

Binary images: A binary (bilevel) image uses 1 bit per pixel: 0 for black, 1 for white (or the other way round). Fax pages, scanned signatures, QR codes and simple line art are binary. They are very compact. A 640 x 480 binary image needs 640 x 480 / 8 = 38,400 bytes, under 38 KB.

Grayscale images: A grayscale image stores one brightness value per pixel, usually 8 bits, where 0 is black, 255 is white, and 128 is middle grey. X-ray images, old newspaper photos and many computer vision inputs are grayscale. A 640 x 480 grayscale image takes 640 x 480 x 1 = 307,200 bytes. Medical images often use 12 or 16 bits per pixel because doctors need very fine brightness steps.

True colour images: A true colour image stores three values per pixel, one each for red, green and blue, each typically 8 bits, giving 24 bits per pixel. A 640 x 480 true colour image takes 640 x 480 x 3 = 921,600 bytes. If we add an alpha channel for transparency (how see-through each pixel is), we get 32 bits per pixel, RGBA. Alpha is what lets a sticker or a logo sit on any background with smooth edges.

Indexed colour and palettes: An indexed (palette) image stores, for each pixel, not the colour itself but an index into a small table of colours called the palette or colour lookup table. With 8-bit indices you can pick any 256 colours out of the 16.7 million, and each pixel costs only 1 byte. The palette itself costs 256 x 3 = 768 bytes. So a 640 x 480 indexed image is 307,200 + 768 = 307,968 bytes, about one third of the true colour version. This works beautifully for logos, cartoons and charts with few colours, and badly for photos with smooth gradients. GIF images are always indexed with at most 256 colours, which is why GIF photos look blotchy.

Worked example, file sizes at a glance: The general formula is size in bytes = width x height x bits per pixel / 8, plus a small header. For 1920 x 1080: binary is 259,200 bytes, grayscale is 2,073,600 bytes, true colour is 6,220,800 bytes (about 6.22 MB or 5.93 MiB), and RGBA is 8,294,400 bytes. A 4000 x 3000 phone photo at 24 bits is 36,000,000 bytes raw. The JPEG your phone actually saves is usually a few megabytes, which tells you compression is doing a lot of quiet work.

Resolution for print, PPI and DPI: On a screen, size is in pixels. On paper, we need pixels per inch (PPI), and printers talk about dots per inch (DPI), the number of ink dots they place per inch. People often use the two terms loosely. A common rule for sharp photo prints is 300 PPI. An A4 page is 210 x 297 mm, which is 8.27 x 11.69 inches. At 300 PPI that needs 2480 x 3508 pixels. In 24-bit colour that is 2480 x 3508 x 3 = 26,099,520 bytes, about 26.1 MB before compression. Going the other way, a 4000-pixel-wide photo printed at 300 PPI is 4000 / 300 = 13.3 inches wide, about 34 cm. Changing the PPI number in a file's settings without changing the pixels does not add any detail; it only changes the printed size.

Raster versus vector, a quick recap: A raster image is a pixel grid. A vector graphic is a list of shapes, like "circle at (50, 50), radius 20, filled red". Vectors scale to any size without blur and are tiny for simple drawings, so logos, icons, maps and fonts are often vectors. Photos have too much irregular detail for shapes, so they are raster. When a vector is shown on a screen, it is rasterized into pixels at that moment. Computer Graphics covered the drawing algorithms; for multimedia the key point is choosing the right representation for the content.

The image histogram: A histogram counts how many pixels have each value. For an 8-bit grayscale image it is a bar chart with 256 bars, one for each brightness from 0 to 255. A dark photo has most of its bars on the left, a bright one on the right, a low-contrast foggy photo has all bars bunched in the middle. Phone camera apps often show a histogram so you can see if parts of the photo are clipped to pure black or pure white. Histograms also power simple editing like contrast stretching and histogram equalization, and they reappear later in this course as a feature for image search.

Simple point operations: Many basic image edits change each pixel on its own. Brightness adds a constant: new = old + 30, clipped at 255. Contrast multiplies around the middle. Inversion gives a negative: new = 255 - old. Thresholding turns grayscale into binary: new = 1 if old > 128 else 0, which is how a scanned page becomes clean black text. These are the building blocks for filters in photo apps.

Image file structure: An image file is not only pixels. It usually begins with a header that says the format, width, height, bit depth and colour type. It may contain a palette, metadata such as camera model, date and GPS location (EXIF data), and finally the pixel data, often compressed. A plain BMP file stores pixels almost raw, which is why a BMP screenshot is huge. Formats such as PNG, JPEG, GIF and WebP compress the pixel data in different ways, which we compare in a later lesson.

Resizing an image: When you shrink a 4000 x 3000 photo to 800 x 600 for WhatsApp, the software must decide each new pixel's value from many old ones, usually by averaging neighbours, which also smooths away detail that the smaller grid cannot hold. When you enlarge an image, it must invent pixels that were never captured. Nearest-neighbour copies the closest old pixel and looks blocky; bilinear interpolation blends the four nearest pixels and looks smoother but softer. No interpolation can recover detail that was never sampled, which is why "enhance" in crime dramas is fiction.

High dynamic range in one paragraph: Real scenes, such as a room with a bright window, can have a huge range between the darkest shadow and the brightest highlight. An 8-bit channel offers only 256 steps, so either shadows go pure black or the window goes pure white. HDR photography takes several exposures or uses a sensor with more bits and then maps the result into a displayable range, and HDR video formats use 10 or more bits per channel (1024 levels or more) to reduce banding in bright displays.

Real-life example 1, a national ID photo: Many online application forms in Bangladesh ask for a photo with a fixed pixel size and a maximum file size, for example a small passport-style image under a few hundred kilobytes. If your phone photo is 4000 x 3000, you must crop and resize it, which reduces resolution, and then save as JPEG at a suitable quality so the file fits. Understanding resolution and file size lets you do this correctly instead of guessing.

Real-life example 2, scanning exam scripts: Suppose a university wants to scan answer scripts. A grayscale scan of an A4 page at 300 PPI is 2480 x 3508 = 8,699,840 pixels, so about 8.7 MB per page raw at 8 bits. A binary scan is one eighth of that, about 1.09 MB raw, and compresses even better, but loses pencil shading. For handwriting in blue ink, the scanning team must decide if grayscale's extra detail is worth eight times more data. Thousands of scripts make this choice very real.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students confuse resolution (number of pixels) with print size (which also depends on PPI). They forget to divide bits by 8. They think 24-bit colour means 24 colours, when it means 2^24 colours. They mix up DPI of a printer with PPI of an image. Exams ask you to define pixel, resolution and bit depth; compare binary, grayscale, indexed and true colour images; calculate image size in bytes; explain palettes and why GIF photos look poor; and draw or interpret a histogram.

Recap: A digital image is a grid of pixels, each a quantized sample of light. Resolution is the number of pixels; bit depth is bits per pixel, giving 2^b values. Binary uses 1 bit, grayscale usually 8, true colour 24, RGBA 32, and indexed colour stores small indices into a palette. Raw size = width x height x bits per pixel / 8, for example 6,220,800 bytes for a Full HD true colour image. These raw numbers are the starting point for every compression method that follows.
key_points: A digital image is a grid of pixels f(x, y); a camera samples light in space and quantizes each value.
Resolution = width x height in pixels; bit depth b gives 2^b possible values per pixel.
Binary = 1 bit, grayscale usually 8 bits, true colour 24 bits (16,777,216 colours), RGBA 32 bits.
Indexed colour stores 1-byte indices into a palette of up to 256 colours (palette = 768 bytes).
Raw size = W x H x bits per pixel / 8: 1920x1080x24 = 6,220,800 bytes; 640x480 binary = 38,400 bytes.
Print needs PPI: A4 at 300 PPI = 2480 x 3508 pixels, about 26.1 MB raw in 24-bit colour.
A histogram counts pixels per value and reveals dark, bright or low-contrast images.
Image files hold a header, optional palette and metadata (EXIF), then pixel data, usually compressed.
lessons.tip: When you meet an image size question, write the formula W x H x bits / 8 first, then plug numbers. Writing the unit at each step (pixels, bits, bytes) stops the classic divide-by-8 mistake.
lessons.task: Take one photo with your phone. Find its resolution in the photo details, calculate its raw 24-bit size, and compare with the real file size. Then work out how large (in cm) it would print at 300 PPI and at 150 PPI.

quiz.q: How many different colours can a 24-bit true colour pixel represent?
What is the raw size of a 640 x 480 binary (1-bit) image?
How many pixels are needed to print an A4 page (8.27 x 11.69 in) at 300 PPI?
quiz.explain: 8.27 x 300 is about 2480 and 11.69 x 300 is about 3508.

quiz.q: In an 8-bit indexed colour image, what does each pixel store?
options: An index into a palette of up to 256 colours
Its red, green and blue values directly
quiz.explain: Indexed images store a small index; the palette holds the actual RGB colours.

quiz.q: A photo's histogram has almost all bars bunched in the middle. What does that suggest?
options: The photo has an alpha channel
quiz.explain: Values crowded in the middle mean few darks and few brights, i.e. low contrast.

lessons.title: Colour in Images and Video: YCbCr and Chroma Subsampling
lessons.content:
Take a colourful photo of a Pohela Boishakh rally and turn it into black and white on your phone. You can still recognise every face, every banner, every letter on the posters. Now imagine the opposite: keep only the colour but remove all brightness detail. You would get blurry blobs of red and white with no faces at all. This little experiment reveals a fact about human eyes that every image and video codec in the world exploits: we see brightness detail very sharply, and colour detail much more loosely. This lesson shows how engineers separate brightness from colour with the YCbCr colour space, and how they then store colour at lower resolution, a trick called chroma subsampling, that cuts video data in half before any real compression starts.

RGB, a quick recap: From Computer Graphics you know RGB, the additive colour model used by screens. Each pixel has a red, a green and a blue value, typically 0 to 255 each. (255, 0, 0) is pure red, (255, 255, 255) is white, (0, 0, 0) is black, and equal values like (128, 128, 128) are greys. RGB is natural for cameras and displays, because sensors and screen sub-pixels really are red, green and blue. But for compression RGB is awkward: all three channels carry a copy of the brightness information, so they are strongly correlated, and changing any channel changes both brightness and colour at once.

Why separate brightness from colour: The retina has about 120 million rod cells and only about 6 million cone cells, and the cones that sense colour are packed tightly only in a small central area. In practice, our visual system resolves fine detail mostly through brightness, while colour is perceived at a coarser scale. So a representation that puts brightness in one channel and colour in two others lets us treat them differently: keep brightness sharp, and make colour cheaper. This idea is older than digital media. Colour television in the 1950s had to stay compatible with black and white TV sets, so it sent a brightness signal that old sets could show, plus extra colour-difference signals that new sets could add.

Luma, the brightness channel: Luma, written Y' (or simply Y), is a weighted sum of the red, green and blue values. In the classic standard-definition recommendation BT.601, Y = 0.299R + 0.587G + 0.114B. The weights add up to 1 and reflect how bright each primary looks to us: green looks brightest, blue darkest. Pure white (255, 255, 255) gives Y = 255, black gives 0, pure red gives about 76, pure green about 150. HD video uses the BT.709 recommendation, which has slightly different weights (about 0.2126, 0.7152 and 0.0722), so always check which standard a system uses.

Chroma, the colour channels: The two chroma channels store how far the colour is from grey. Cb is a scaled version of blue minus luma (B - Y), and Cr is a scaled version of red minus luma (R - Y). For a grey pixel, R = G = B = Y, so both differences are zero. To store them as unsigned 8-bit numbers we add an offset of 128, so neutral grey has Cb = Cr = 128. The full-range version used by JPEG files (JFIF) is: Cb = 128 - 0.168736R - 0.331264G + 0.5B and Cr = 128 + 0.5R - 0.418688G - 0.081312B.

Worked example, converting one pixel: Take an orange-brown pixel with R = 200, G = 100, B = 50. Luma: Y = 0.299 x 200 + 0.587 x 100 + 0.114 x 50 = 59.8 + 58.7 + 5.7 = 124.2, about 124. Blue difference: Cb = 128 - 33.75 - 33.13 + 25 = about 86.1, below 128 because the pixel has less blue than grey of the same brightness. Red difference: Cr = 128 + 100 - 41.87 - 4.07 = about 182.1, well above 128 because the pixel is reddish. So (200, 100, 50) becomes about (124, 86, 182).

Going back to RGB: The conversion is reversible. For JFIF: R = Y + 1.402(Cr - 128), G = Y - 0.344136(Cb - 128) - 0.714136(Cr - 128), and B = Y + 1.772(Cb - 128). Plug in Y = 124.2, Cb = 86.13, Cr = 182.07 and you get back R = 200, G = 100, B = 50 (to rounding). So converting to YCbCr loses almost nothing by itself; only rounding to integers causes tiny errors. The saving comes from what we do next.

Studio range versus full range: In broadcast and most video files, 8-bit luma does not use 0 to 255. It uses 16 to 235, and chroma uses 16 to 240, leaving headroom and footroom for filter overshoots. This is called limited or studio range. JPEG photos use full range 0 to 255. If a player assumes the wrong range, blacks look grey and washed out, or shadows get crushed. That is a common real-world bug when video is converted by careless software.

Chroma subsampling, the idea: Since the eye cares less about colour detail, we can store Cb and Cr at fewer samples than Y. The notation J:a:b describes it using a reference block J pixels wide and 2 rows tall, usually J = 4. The number a is how many chroma samples are in the first row of 4 pixels, and b is how many new chroma samples are in the second row. So 4:4:4 means no subsampling: every pixel has its own Cb and Cr. 4:2:2 means chroma is halved horizontally: two chroma samples per row of four, and the second row also has two. 4:2:0 means chroma is halved both horizontally and vertically: two chroma samples in the first row and zero new ones in the second, so one Cb and one Cr serve each 2 x 2 group of pixels.

Worked example, bits per pixel: Count samples in a 2 x 2 block of four pixels with 8 bits per sample. In 4:4:4 there are 4 Y + 4 Cb + 4 Cr = 12 samples = 96 bits, or 24 bits per pixel, the same as RGB. In 4:2:2 there are 4 Y + 2 Cb + 2 Cr = 8 samples = 64 bits, or 16 bits per pixel. In 4:2:0 there are 4 Y + 1 Cb + 1 Cr = 6 samples = 48 bits, or 12 bits per pixel. So 4:2:0 halves the raw data compared with RGB, and viewers usually cannot tell the difference in natural video.

Worked example, one Full HD frame: In RGB or 4:4:4, a 1920 x 1080 frame is 1920 x 1080 x 3 = 6,220,800 bytes. In 4:2:2 it is 1920 x 1080 x 2 = 4,147,200 bytes. In 4:2:0 the Y plane is 1920 x 1080 = 2,073,600 bytes, and each chroma plane is 960 x 540 = 518,400 bytes, for a total of 2,073,600 + 2 x 518,400 = 3,110,400 bytes, exactly half of RGB. This is where the 12 bits per pixel and the 746 Mbps raw 1080p30 figure in lesson 1 come from.

How subsampling is done and undone: The encoder produces each 4:2:0 chroma sample from its 2 x 2 group, usually by filtering or simply averaging. If the four Cr values in a group are 180, 184, 176 and 180, the stored value is their average, 180. The decoder then upsamples: it spreads each chroma sample back over four pixels, often with interpolation so edges are smoother. Every pixel gets its own full luma back, but the four pixels share almost the same colour. The detail lost in chroma never returns, which is why subsampling is the first lossy step of the pipeline.

Who uses which: 4:2:0 is the workhorse for delivery: JPEG photos (commonly), DVDs, Blu-ray, digital TV, YouTube, Netflix and video calls almost all use 4:2:0. 4:2:2 is common in professional cameras and broadcast production, where footage will be edited and colour-graded and needs extra colour precision. 4:4:4 is used for computer screen content, graphics and high-end post-production, because thin coloured text and lines suffer badly from subsampling. There is also 4:1:1, which keeps one chroma sample per four pixels in each row, used by some older DV formats; it also averages 12 bits per pixel.

Where subsampling shows: Subsampling is nearly invisible on faces, landscapes and cricket fields, but visible on sharp coloured edges. Red text on a blue background, a thin coloured line in a chart, or a screen recording of a coding editor with coloured syntax can look smudged or fringed in 4:2:0. That is why screen-sharing tools and some codecs offer 4:4:4 modes for desktop content.

Gamma in one paragraph: Cameras and displays do not store light linearly. Our eyes are more sensitive to differences in dark tones than in bright ones, so encoding uses a non-linear curve, called gamma encoding, that spends more code values on dark shades. Displays then apply the inverse curve. The common sRGB standard behaves roughly like a power of 2.2. The prime in Y' reminds us that luma is computed from gamma-encoded R'G'B' values, not from linear light. You do not need the formula here; just remember that pixel values are not proportional to physical light.

Other colour spaces you may meet: HSV and HSL (hue, saturation, value or lightness) are friendly for colour pickers and editing. CMYK is for printing. YUV is an older name, often used loosely for YCbCr in software. Lab is designed so that equal numerical distances look roughly equally different to humans, useful in colour matching and image search. For multimedia compression, though, YCbCr is king.

Real-life example 1, a video call on a slow connection: When you join an online class from a village with weak 4G, the app converts your camera frames to YCbCr 4:2:0 before encoding. That single step halves the data the encoder has to deal with, at no visible cost to your face. If you then share a colourful slide with thin red text, it may look slightly blurry, which is the subsampling showing.

Real-life example 2, a designer's logo on a TV ad: A Dhaka agency designs a logo with thin red lines on navy blue. It looks perfect in the design software, which works in RGB at full resolution. After the TV channel broadcasts it in 4:2:0 video, the red lines bleed. Experienced designers test their graphics after conversion to 4:2:0, or thicken coloured details, because they know chroma will be halved in each direction.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students think 4:2:0 means "no Cr", but it means chroma is halved horizontally and vertically, with both Cb and Cr kept. They forget the 128 offset and get negative chroma values. They assume luma weights are equal; green dominates. Exams ask you to explain why YCbCr is used, convert an RGB pixel to YCbCr, explain J:a:b notation, compute bits per pixel for 4:4:4, 4:2:2 and 4:2:0, and calculate frame sizes.

Recap: Human vision is sharper for brightness than for colour. YCbCr separates luma Y = 0.299R + 0.587G + 0.114B (BT.601) from two chroma differences Cb and Cr centred at 128. The conversion is reversible. Chroma subsampling then stores colour at lower resolution: 4:4:4 is 24 bits per pixel, 4:2:2 is 16, and 4:2:0 is 12, halving a Full HD frame from 6,220,800 to 3,110,400 bytes. That free factor of two is the first step of almost every image and video codec.
key_points: Eyes resolve brightness detail much better than colour detail; codecs exploit this.
YCbCr separates luma Y from chroma Cb (blue difference) and Cr (red difference), offset to 128 for grey.
Worked: (200, 100, 50) -> Y about 124, Cb about 86, Cr about 182; the conversion is reversible.
J:a:b notation: 4:4:4 = 24 bits/pixel, 4:2:2 = 16, 4:2:0 = 12 (one Cb and one Cr per 2x2 block).
A 1080p frame is 6,220,800 bytes in 4:4:4 and 3,110,400 bytes in 4:2:0.
Video usually uses limited range (Y 16-235); JPEG uses full range 0-255.
4:2:0 suits natural video; 4:4:4 suits screen content with thin coloured text.
lessons.tip: For subsampling questions, always draw a 4 x 2 grid of pixels and mark where Y, Cb and Cr samples are. Counting samples on the drawing gives the bits per pixel without memorising anything.
lessons.task: Use any photo editor or the Python Pillow library (img.convert('YCbCr').split()) on a colourful photo. Save the Y, Cb and Cr channels as separate grayscale images and compare them. Notice how much detail is in Y and how blurry Cb and Cr look even before subsampling.

quiz.q: In BT.601, which colour contributes most to luma Y?
quiz.explain: Y = 0.299R + 0.587G + 0.114B; green has the largest weight.

quiz.q: A neutral grey pixel in 8-bit full-range YCbCr has Cb and Cr equal to:
quiz.explain: Chroma is a difference from grey, offset by 128, so grey gives Cb = Cr = 128.

quiz.q: How many bits per pixel does 8-bit 4:2:2 use?
quiz.explain: In a 2x2 block: 4 Y + 2 Cb + 2 Cr = 8 samples = 64 bits, so 16 bits per pixel.

quiz.q: What is the size of one 1920 x 1080 frame in 8-bit 4:2:0?
quiz.explain: Y = 2,073,600 bytes plus two 960 x 540 chroma planes of 518,400 bytes each = 3,110,400 bytes.

quiz.q: Why might thin red text on a blue slide look smudged in a video call?
options: Luma is stored at half resolution
4:2:0 stores colour at half resolution horizontally and vertically
quiz.explain: Chroma subsampling blurs sharp colour edges; luma stays full resolution.

lessons.title: Digital Audio: PCM, Sample Rates, Bit Rates and Channels
lessons.content:
Stand near a tabla player and you can almost feel the sound on your chest. That feeling is real: the drum skin pushes the air back and forth, the air molecules bump into their neighbours, and a wave of tiny pressure changes travels to your ears and your body. Your eardrum vibrates with the same pattern, and your brain hears "dha" or "tin". Digital audio is the art of measuring that pressure pattern as numbers, storing the numbers, and later pushing a speaker cone back and forth so the air moves the same way again. This lesson explains sound from zero, recaps the PCM recipe from DSP in the language of multimedia, and teaches you to calculate audio bit rates and file sizes with confidence.

Sound as a pressure wave: Sound is a mechanical wave: a travelling pattern of compressions and rarefactions in a medium such as air. It needs a medium; there is no sound in a vacuum. In air at room temperature sound travels at about 343 metres per second. A microphone turns the pressure changes into a matching electrical voltage, so the waveform you see in an audio editor is a graph of pressure (or voltage) against time.

Frequency and pitch: Frequency is how many cycles the wave completes per second, measured in hertz (Hz). We hear frequency as pitch: a low frequency sounds deep like a bass drum, a high frequency sounds shrill like a whistle. The wavelength is speed divided by frequency, so a 1000 Hz tone has a wavelength of 343 / 1000 = 0.343 m, while a 20 Hz rumble is about 17 m long. Young people hear roughly from 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz (20 kHz); the upper limit drops with age and with noise exposure. Real sounds are mixtures of many frequencies: a note has a fundamental frequency that sets its pitch plus harmonics that give it its colour, or timbre, which is why a flute and a harmonium playing the same note sound different.

Amplitude, loudness and decibels: Amplitude is how big the pressure swings are; we hear it as loudness. Because the ear handles an enormous range, from a whisper to a jet engine, we use a logarithmic scale, the decibel. Sound pressure level in dB SPL is 20 log10(p / p0), where p0 = 20 micropascals is roughly the quietest sound a healthy ear can detect (0 dB SPL). Normal conversation is around 60 dB SPL, busy Dhaka traffic can easily reach 80 to 90 dB, and around 120 to 130 dB sound becomes painful. Doubling the amplitude adds about 6 dB. As a rough rule, a 10 dB increase sounds about twice as loud to a listener.

From DSP, the PCM recipe: Pulse code modulation is the standard way to store uncompressed audio. You already studied it in DSP: sample the voltage at a fixed rate fs, quantize each sample to one of 2^N levels, and store the level as an N-bit number. The sampling theorem says fs must be more than twice the highest frequency you want to keep, and an anti-aliasing filter removes anything above fs / 2 before sampling. Each extra bit adds about 6 dB of signal-to-quantization-noise ratio, so 16 bits give about 98 dB for a full-scale sine. Here we take those results as tools.

Common sample rates and why: 8 kHz is classic telephone speech: it can carry frequencies up to 4 kHz, and phone systems keep roughly 300 to 3400 Hz, which is enough to understand words but makes voices sound thin. 16 kHz is "wideband" speech used by many modern voice apps; it sounds noticeably more natural. 44.1 kHz is the audio CD rate, covering everything up to 22.05 kHz, just above human hearing. 48 kHz is the standard for video, films and professional audio. 96 kHz and higher are used in studios and so-called hi-res audio, mainly to give filters and editing more room; most listeners cannot hear the difference in playback.

Bit depth and dynamic range: Bit depth sets the quietest detail you can record relative to the loudest. 8-bit audio has audible hiss and graininess. 16 bits, the CD standard, is enough for finished music played at normal volume. 24 bits is used during recording because it gives lots of headroom: the engineer can record at a safe low level to avoid clipping and still keep the noise floor far below the music. Remember clipping from DSP: if the signal exceeds the largest level, the peaks are cut flat and you hear harsh distortion. In multimedia apps, a voice recorded too loud on a phone mic is a very common example.

Channels: Each independent audio signal is a channel. Mono has one channel, fine for speech, voice notes and phone calls. Stereo has two, left and right, which lets our brain place instruments in space by comparing the two ears. Surround sound uses more: 5.1 means five full-range channels (front left, centre, front right, surround left, surround right) plus one low-frequency effects channel for deep bass, the ".1". Cinemas and home theatres use 5.1 or 7.1, and newer object-based systems place sounds as objects in 3D space rather than fixed channels. More channels mean more data, in direct proportion.

The bit rate formula: For uncompressed PCM, bit rate = sample rate x bit depth x number of channels. File size in bytes = bit rate x duration in seconds / 8. That is the whole story for raw audio, and it is the same formula you met in lesson 1.

Worked example, CD audio: fs = 44,100 Hz, 16 bits, 2 channels. Bit rate = 44,100 x 16 x 2 = 1,411,200 bits per second, often written 1411.2 kbps. A 3-minute song lasts 180 seconds, so its size is 1,411,200 x 180 / 8 = 31,752,000 bytes, about 31.75 MB (30.28 MiB). A 74-minute CD therefore holds roughly 780 MB of audio data.

Worked example, telephone speech: fs = 8000 Hz, 8 bits per sample (with logarithmic companding, as DSP explained), 1 channel. Bit rate = 8000 x 8 x 1 = 64,000 bps, the famous 64 kbps of a digital telephone channel. Wideband speech at 16 kHz with 16 bits mono is 16,000 x 16 = 256,000 bps, four times more, which is why voice apps compress speech heavily with special speech codecs.

Worked example, film audio: A 5.1 soundtrack at 48 kHz and 24 bits has 6 channels. Bit rate = 48,000 x 24 x 6 = 6,912,000 bps, almost 7 Mbps of raw audio, more than many compressed HD videos. A 2-hour film would need about 6.2 GB for the soundtrack alone, uncompressed. This is why film sound is always compressed for streaming.

The WAV file: The most common container for raw PCM on computers is WAV, which uses the RIFF structure. A WAV file begins with a header holding the format code (PCM or something else), number of channels, sample rate, byte rate, block alignment and bits per sample, followed by a data chunk with the samples. For 16-bit stereo, samples are interleaved: left, right, left, right, each 2 bytes, in little-endian order. A simple PCM WAV header is typically 44 bytes, so the file is essentially "header plus raw samples". WAV files are large but perfect for editing, because nothing has been thrown away.

MIDI versus sampled audio: Sampled audio records the actual sound wave. MIDI (Musical Instrument Digital Interface) records instructions instead: "note on, middle C, this velocity", "note off", "change instrument to piano". A note-on message is just 3 bytes. A whole song in MIDI form may be a few tens of kilobytes, because it is like a music score, not a recording. The catch is that MIDI has no sound of its own: a synthesizer, either a hardware keyboard or software with sampled instrument sounds, turns the instructions into audio, so the same MIDI file can sound cheap on one phone and rich on a professional keyboard. MIDI is widely used in music production, ringtones on old phones, and controlling instruments and lights. It cannot store a human voice singing.

Speech versus music: Speech has most of its useful energy between a few hundred hertz and a few kilohertz, and it is produced by a fairly predictable system (vocal cords plus the shape of the mouth and throat). Music covers the full hearing range and comes from endlessly varied sources. That is why speech codecs can work at a few kilobits per second by modelling the voice, while music codecs need much higher rates and rely on models of the ear rather than the source. We will meet both in the psychoacoustics lesson.

Simple audio operations: Many editing operations are plain arithmetic on samples. Changing volume multiplies every sample by a gain: x 2 is about +6 dB. Mixing two tracks adds their samples, which can push the sum beyond the maximum and clip, so mixers scale down first. A fade-in multiplies by a gain that rises from 0 to 1. Reversing a clip just reads samples backwards. Changing the sample rate needs proper filtering (the multirate ideas from DSP); simply dropping samples causes aliasing.

Real-life example 1, a Bangla podcast: A student in Rajshahi records a podcast on a phone. The app records at 48 kHz, 16 bits, mono, which is 768,000 bps, about 5.76 MB per minute. A 40-minute episode would be about 230 MB as WAV. Mono is a good choice for a single voice, halving the data with no loss of meaning. Before publishing, the file is compressed with a perceptual codec to a fraction of that size, which we will learn later.

Real-life example 2, a mosque or school PA system: An old public address system is analog, but many new ones use digital audio over the network. The engineer chooses 16 kHz or 48 kHz sampling and mono channels for each speaker zone, and calculates bandwidth per zone with the same formula, making sure the network switch can carry all zones at once without dropouts.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students confuse sample rate with bit rate; sample rate is samples per second, bit rate is bits per second. They forget to multiply by the number of channels. They think a higher sample rate always means better sound, even above what ears can hear. They mix up MIDI and recorded audio. Exams ask: define frequency, amplitude and the decibel; state the human hearing range; explain sample rate and bit depth choices; compute bit rate and file size for given settings; describe WAV structure; compare MIDI with sampled audio.

Recap: Sound is a pressure wave; frequency gives pitch, amplitude gives loudness, measured in decibels. PCM samples it at a fixed rate and quantizes each sample. Typical rates are 8, 16, 44.1 and 48 kHz; typical depths 16 and 24 bits; channels range from mono to 5.1 and beyond. Bit rate = sample rate x bit depth x channels: 1,411,200 bps for CD, 64 kbps for telephone, about 6.9 Mbps for 5.1 film sound. MIDI stores instructions, not sound. These raw numbers are why audio compression matters.
key_points: Sound is a pressure wave; frequency is heard as pitch, amplitude as loudness.
Human hearing spans roughly 20 Hz to 20 kHz; dB SPL = 20 log10(p / 20 micropascals), and doubling amplitude adds about 6 dB.
PCM samples at fs (> 2 x highest frequency) and quantizes to N bits; each bit adds about 6 dB of SQNR.
Common rates: 8 kHz phone, 16 kHz wideband speech, 44.1 kHz CD, 48 kHz video/pro audio.
Bit rate = sample rate x bit depth x channels: CD 1,411,200 bps; phone 64,000 bps; 5.1 at 48 kHz/24-bit 6,912,000 bps.
A 3-minute CD-quality song is 31,752,000 bytes as raw PCM (WAV = small header + samples).
5.1 surround = 5 full-range channels + 1 low-frequency effects channel.
MIDI stores note instructions (a note-on is 3 bytes), not sound; a synthesizer creates the audio.
lessons.tip: For every audio question, write the three numbers (rate, bits, channels) in a row before multiplying. Most wrong answers in exams come from a forgotten channel count or a forgotten divide-by-8.
lessons.task: Record the same 10-second sentence with your phone's voice recorder at two quality settings (if available). Check the file sizes and compute the bit rate of each (size x 8 / 10). Compare with what raw 44.1 kHz 16-bit stereo would need for 10 seconds.

quiz.q: What is the bit rate of 16 kHz, 16-bit mono PCM speech?
quiz.explain: 16,000 x 16 x 1 = 256,000 bits per second.

quiz.q: How large is a 3-minute CD-quality (44.1 kHz, 16-bit, stereo) WAV, ignoring the header?
What does the '.1' in 5.1 surround sound mean?
options: A low-frequency effects channel for deep bass
A tenth of a second delay
quiz.explain: 5.1 = five full-range channels plus one limited-bandwidth LFE channel.

quiz.q: Why is a MIDI file so much smaller than a recording of the same song?
options: It stores note instructions, not sound samples
It is always compressed with MP3
quiz.explain: MIDI lists events like note on/off; a synthesizer generates the sound when played.

quiz.q: Telephone audio samples at 8 kHz. What is the highest frequency it can represent?
quiz.explain: By the sampling theorem the limit is fs / 2 = 4 kHz; phone systems keep about 300-3400 Hz.

lessons.title: Information Theory Basics: Redundancy and Entropy
lessons.content:
During the monsoon in Dhaka, if your friend texts "it's raining", you are not surprised at all. You almost knew it already. But if the same friend texts "it's snowing in Dhaka", that message carries a shock, and you would remember it for years. Claude Shannon, the engineer who founded information theory in 1948, turned this everyday feeling into mathematics: the less likely a message, the more information it carries. That single idea tells us exactly how small any lossless file can be, and it is the foundation of every compression method in this course. In this lesson we learn why media can be compressed at all, how to measure information in bits, and how to compute entropy by hand.

Why compression is possible, redundancy: Data can be compressed only if it contains redundancy, meaning parts that are predictable from other parts or not needed by the user. Multimedia is full of redundancy, and it comes in four flavours. Each flavour is attacked by a different tool, so learning to name them is the first step in understanding any codec.

Spatial redundancy: Neighbouring pixels in an image are usually similar. In a photo of a blue sky, if one pixel is light blue, the next one is almost certainly light blue too. Storing every pixel independently wastes bits. Techniques like run-length coding, prediction and transforms such as the DCT exploit this.

Temporal redundancy: Consecutive video frames are usually almost identical. In a news broadcast, the studio background does not change from one frame to the next; only the presenter's lips and eyes move. Sending each frame as a fresh image would be wasteful. Video codecs send the differences, using motion compensation, which we study later.

Coding or statistical redundancy: Some symbols are more common than others. In English text, e and space are frequent while z and q are rare. In a medical X-ray, mid-grey values are frequent and some values never appear at all. If every symbol gets a code of the same length, frequent symbols are paying more bits than they need. Variable-length codes such as Huffman and arithmetic coding remove this.

Perceptual (psychovisual or psychoacoustic) redundancy: Some information is real but humans cannot see or hear it. Very fine colour detail, very high frequencies, or a quiet sound right next to a loud one are examples. Removing such information is lossy, because the original cannot be rebuilt exactly, but the result looks or sounds the same. The first three kinds can be removed losslessly; this fourth kind is where lossy compression lives.

Lossless versus lossy: A lossless method lets the decoder rebuild the original data bit for bit. ZIP, PNG and FLAC are lossless. They are required when every bit matters: text, program files, medical images in some settings, legal documents. A lossy method gives an approximation that is close enough for human use, and in return reaches much higher compression. JPEG, MP3, AAC and almost all video codecs are lossy. Real systems often combine both: a lossy step that throws away what is not needed, followed by lossless coding of what remains.

Measuring information, self-information: Shannon defined the information content, or self-information, of an event with probability p as I = -log2 p bits (equivalently log2 of 1/p). Try a few. A fair coin toss result has p = 1/2, so I = 1 bit. One face of a fair 8-sided die has p = 1/8, so I = 3 bits. An event with p = 0.9, like rain on a monsoon afternoon, carries only about 0.152 bits: hardly any news. An event with p = 0.1 carries about 3.32 bits. A certain event, p = 1, carries 0 bits, because you learn nothing. The logarithm is base 2 so the unit is bits; it also makes information add up when independent events combine.

Entropy, the average information: A source is something that emits symbols, like a camera emitting pixel values or a keyboard emitting letters. If symbol i has probability pi, the average information per symbol is the entropy: H = - sum of pi log2 pi, measured in bits per symbol. Entropy measures how unpredictable the source is. It is highest when all symbols are equally likely and lowest when one symbol dominates.

Worked example 1, a nicely skewed source: Four symbols A, B, C, D with probabilities 0.5, 0.25, 0.125 and 0.125. Their self-information is 1, 2, 3 and 3 bits. Entropy H = 0.5 x 1 + 0.25 x 2 + 0.125 x 3 + 0.125 x 3 = 0.5 + 0.5 + 0.375 + 0.375 = 1.75 bits per symbol. A fixed-length code for four symbols needs 2 bits each. So in principle we can save 0.25 bits per symbol, 12.5 percent, and in this special case a simple code (A = 0, B = 10, C = 110, D = 111) achieves exactly 1.75 bits on average.

Worked example 2, a less tidy source: Suppose we count the letters in the string AAAABBBCCD. A appears 4 times, B 3, C 2 and D 1 out of 10, so the probabilities are 0.4, 0.3, 0.2 and 0.1. The terms are: 0.4 x 1.322 = 0.529, 0.3 x 1.737 = 0.521, 0.2 x 2.322 = 0.464, 0.1 x 3.322 = 0.332. Adding them gives H = about 1.846 bits per symbol. For 10 symbols, that means no lossless code (with this simple model) can use fewer than about 18.46 bits on average, while a fixed 2-bit code uses 20 bits. In the next lesson Huffman coding will reach 19 bits for this exact string.

Worked example 3, extremes: If all four symbols have probability 0.25, H = 4 x 0.25 x 2 = 2 bits, exactly the fixed-length cost, so this source cannot be compressed symbol by symbol. For a binary source with probabilities 0.9 and 0.1, H = 0.9 x 0.152 + 0.1 x 3.322 = about 0.469 bits per symbol. That means a black-and-white fax page that is 90 percent white could in theory be stored in less than half a bit per pixel. Note that the maximum possible entropy for n equally likely symbols is log2 n: 2 bits for 4 symbols, 8 bits for 256 symbols, about 4.7 bits for the 26 English letters.

Shannon's source coding theorem: The theorem says that for a source with entropy H, no lossless code can have an average length less than H bits per symbol, and there exist codes whose average length L satisfies H <= L < H + 1. So entropy is a hard floor, a speed limit for lossless compression. It also hints at a trick: if we code blocks of several symbols together, the "+1" overhead is shared among them, and the average per symbol gets closer to H. Arithmetic coding, later, pushes this idea to the limit.

Worked example 4, coding pairs to beat 1 bit: Go back to the binary source with probabilities 0.9 and 0.1. Any code that gives each single symbol its own codeword needs at least 1 bit per symbol, far above the entropy of 0.469. Now group symbols in pairs. The four pairs have probabilities 0.81 (00), 0.09 (01), 0.09 (10) and 0.01 (11). A good code gives them lengths 1, 2, 3 and 3 bits. The average is 0.81 x 1 + 0.09 x 2 + 0.09 x 3 + 0.01 x 3 = 1.29 bits per pair, which is 0.645 bits per symbol. Longer groups get closer still to 0.469. This is the "+1 overhead shared among symbols" idea in action.

A tiny bit of history, Morse code: Long before Shannon, Samuel Morse's telegraph code already used the idea. The most common English letter, E, is a single dot, and T is a single dash, while rare letters such as Q and Z get four symbols. Operators sent messages faster because frequent letters were cheap. Information theory explained, a century later, why this works and how far it can go.

Information is not meaning: Shannon's information measures surprise, not importance or truth. A file of pure random noise has the maximum possible entropy, yet it means nothing to anyone. A poem may have lower entropy than noise but enormous meaning. Compression engineers only care about the statistical side, which is exactly what makes the theory so general: the same mathematics works for Bangla text, X-ray pixels, cricket scores and music.

Entropy depends on the model: The entropy you compute depends on what you assume about the source. Treating each English letter independently gives one number, but letters are not independent: after "q" comes "u" almost always, and after "th" comes "e" very often. A model that uses context sees less surprise, so it measures lower entropy and allows better compression. In images, a model that predicts each pixel from its neighbours and codes only the prediction error sees much lower entropy than a model that treats pixels independently. Much of the cleverness in real codecs is building a better model, then coding with near-entropy efficiency.

Measuring compression: The compression ratio is original size divided by compressed size. A Full HD photo of 6,220,800 raw bytes saved as a 600,000-byte JPEG has a ratio of about 10.4 to 1. Another common measure for images is bits per pixel (bpp): 600,000 x 8 / 2,073,600 pixels = about 2.31 bpp, compared with 24 bpp raw. For audio and video we usually quote bit rate, such as 128 kbps or 5 Mbps. Some books also use space savings = 1 - compressed / original, which here is about 90 percent.

Real-life example 1, a cricket scoreboard feed: A sports app sends ball-by-ball events. Dot balls and singles are very common, sixes and wickets are rare. Giving a short code to a dot ball and a longer code to a wicket reduces the data, exactly as entropy suggests. During a tense last over, though, the probabilities change, which is why adaptive models that update their statistics on the fly are popular.

Real-life example 2, why your ZIP of photos barely shrinks: Students are often surprised that zipping a folder of JPEG photos saves almost nothing, while zipping a folder of text files or CSV data saves a lot. The reason is entropy: JPEG data has already been compressed close to its entropy, so it looks almost random to ZIP. Text still has plenty of statistical redundancy. Encrypted files also look random, so they do not compress either; a good rule is to compress first and encrypt afterwards.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students use log base 10 or natural log and forget to convert to base 2. They think entropy is a property of a file alone, when it depends on the probability model. They believe compression can always shrink any file; but a counting argument shows no lossless method can shrink every possible input, since there are fewer short files than long ones. Exams ask: list and explain types of redundancy, define lossless versus lossy, compute self-information and entropy for a given set of probabilities, compare entropy with fixed-length coding, and state the source coding theorem.

Recap: Compression works by removing redundancy: spatial, temporal, statistical and perceptual. The first three can be removed losslessly; perceptual removal is lossy. Self-information is -log2 p, and entropy H = - sum p log2 p is the average information per symbol and the floor for lossless coding. Worked results: 1.75 bits for 0.5/0.25/0.125/0.125, about 1.846 bits for 0.4/0.3/0.2/0.1, about 0.469 bits for 0.9/0.1. Compression ratio and bits per pixel let us compare methods. The next three lessons build codes that approach the entropy.
key_points: Compression removes redundancy: spatial, temporal, statistical (coding) and perceptual.
Lossless coding rebuilds the data exactly (ZIP, PNG, FLAC); lossy coding keeps a close approximation (JPEG, MP3, video codecs).
Self-information I = -log2 p: p = 1/2 gives 1 bit, p = 1/8 gives 3 bits, p = 0.9 gives about 0.152 bits.
Entropy H = - sum p log2 p is the average information per symbol and the lower bound for lossless coding.
Maximum entropy for n equally likely symbols is log2 n; a uniform source cannot be compressed symbol by symbol.
Source coding theorem: H <= L < H + 1 for the best prefix code; better models lower the entropy.
Compression ratio = original / compressed; a 6,220,800-byte photo stored in 600,000 bytes is about 10.4:1 or 2.31 bpp.
lessons.tip: Memorise the log2 values of 1/2, 1/4, 1/8 and 1/16 (1, 2, 3, 4) and of 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4 (3.32, 2.32, 1.74, 1.32). With those eight numbers you can do most entropy questions without a calculator.
lessons.task: Write any Bangla or English sentence of about 30 letters. Count how often each letter appears, turn counts into probabilities, and compute the entropy. Compare it with log2 of the number of different letters you used to see how much statistical redundancy your sentence has.

quiz.q: What is the self-information of an event with probability 1/8?
quiz.explain: I = -log2(1/8) = 3 bits.

quiz.q: Which redundancy do video codecs remove when they send only the differences between consecutive frames?
quiz.explain: Similarity between successive frames in time is temporal redundancy.

quiz.q: What is the entropy of a source with four equally likely symbols?
quiz.explain: H = 4 x 0.25 x log2 4 = 2 bits per symbol, the same as a fixed 2-bit code.

quiz.q: A source has probabilities 0.5, 0.25, 0.125, 0.125. Its entropy is:
Why does zipping a folder of JPEG photos save almost no space?
options: JPEG data is already compressed close to its entropy and looks nearly random
quiz.explain: Already-compressed data has little statistical redundancy left for ZIP to remove.

lessons.title: Run-Length Coding and Huffman Coding
lessons.content:
Imagine dictating a long row of a chessboard-free floor tile pattern over the phone: "white, white, white, white, white, white, white, white, white, white, white, white, black". Your friend would beg you to just say "twelve white, one black". That is run-length coding. Now imagine you send many text messages and notice that you type "ok" far more often than "congratulations". If you could make your common words shorter and your rare words longer, your total typing would drop. That is the idea behind Huffman coding. These two methods are the oldest and simplest lossless compressors, and they are still inside JPEG, PNG, ZIP, fax machines and MP3 files today. In this lesson we build both by hand.

Run-length encoding, the idea: Run-length encoding (RLE) replaces a run of identical symbols with a pair: (count, symbol). It attacks spatial redundancy in its simplest form, long stretches of the same value. It is lossless: the decoder simply writes the symbol count times.

RLE worked example: Take a line of a black-and-white scanned page with 28 pixels: WWWWWWWWWWWWBWWWWWWWWWWWWBBB. There are four runs: 12 W, 1 B, 12 W and 3 B. Written as RLE that is 12W 1B 12W 3B, just 4 pairs instead of 28 symbols. If each count fits in one byte and each symbol in one byte, the line goes from 28 bytes to 8 bytes. For binary images we can do even better: since colours must alternate, we only store the counts, agreeing that each line starts with white (a zero-length white run is used if the line begins with black). The line becomes 12, 1, 12, 3.

When RLE makes things worse: RLE only helps when runs are long. Apply it to ABCD and you get 1A 1B 1C 1D, which is twice as large. Photographs with noise and gradients rarely have long runs of exactly equal values, so plain RLE on a photo often expands it.
