Practical formats fix this with a flag that switches between "run" packets and "literal" packets that copy unrepeated bytes as they are. Some old image formats such as BMP and TIFF offer RLE options of this kind, and simple icons and cartoons compress well with it.

RLE in the real world: Fax machines are the classic user. A typical printed page is mostly white with short black runs where letters are. The ITU-T fax standards code the run lengths of each line, and they go one step further: they give short codes to common run lengths and longer codes to rare ones. That second step is exactly the idea of variable-length coding, which leads us to Huffman. JPEG also uses run-length coding, of a special kind, to describe the long runs of zeros after quantization, as we will see in the JPEG lesson.

Fixed-length versus variable-length codes: A fixed-length code gives every symbol the same number of bits. For 4 symbols that is 2 bits each: A = 00, B = 01, C = 10, D = 11. It is simple, and the decoder can find symbol boundaries by counting. But from the entropy lesson we know a skewed source has entropy below 2 bits, so a variable-length code, short codes for frequent symbols, can do better on average.

The prefix-free rule: Variable-length codes bring a danger. Suppose A = 0, B = 01 and C = 1. When the decoder receives 01, is it AC or B? It cannot tell. The fix is to use a prefix-free code (often just called a prefix code): no codeword may be the beginning of another codeword. Then the decoder can read bits one at a time and the moment it matches a codeword, it knows that symbol is complete. Prefix codes can be drawn as binary trees: each left branch is a 0, each right branch a 1, and every symbol sits on a leaf, never on an inner node. Codeword lengths of any prefix code satisfy the Kraft inequality: the sum of 2 to the power minus length over all codewords is at most 1.

Huffman's algorithm: In 1952 David Huffman, then a student, found a simple method that always produces an optimal prefix code for given symbol probabilities, meaning no other symbol-by-symbol prefix code has a smaller average length. The steps are: list every symbol with its count or probability; repeatedly take the two smallest, merge them into a new node whose weight is their sum, and put the new node back in the list; stop when one node remains, the root. Then label the two branches of each merge 0 and 1, and read each symbol's code from the root down to its leaf.

Why merging the two smallest works, the intuition: In any optimal prefix tree, the two least likely symbols should sit at the deepest level, side by side as siblings, because if a rare symbol were higher up than a common one, swapping them would shorten the average. So the two rarest symbols differ only in their last bit. Merge them into one combined symbol, solve the smaller problem the same way, then split them again at the end. Repeating this argument at every step is exactly Huffman's algorithm, and it is why the result is optimal and not just "pretty good".

Huffman worked example, building the tree: Let us code the string AAAABBBCCD. The counts are A = 4, B = 3, C = 2, D = 1. Step 1: the two smallest are D (1) and C (2). Merge them into a node CD with weight 3. The list is now A 4, B 3, CD 3. Step 2: the two smallest are B (3) and CD (3). Merge into a node with weight 6. The list is A 4 and the node 6. Step 3: merge A (4) and the node 6 into the root with weight 10. Done.

Huffman worked example, reading codes: Label A's branch 0 and the weight-6 node's branch 1. Inside the weight-6 node, label B 0 and CD 1. Inside CD, label C 0 and D 1. Reading from the root: A = 0, B = 10, C = 110, D = 111. Check it is prefix-free: 0 does not start any other code, 10 does not start 110 or 111, and so on. The frequent A got 1 bit, the rare D got 3 bits.

Huffman worked example, counting bits: Encode the whole string: AAAA becomes 0000, BBB becomes 101010, CC becomes 110110, and D becomes 111. Joined: 0000101010110110111, which is 19 bits. A fixed 2-bit code would need 20 bits. The average length is 19 / 10 = 1.9 bits per symbol, compared with the entropy of about 1.846 bits. The efficiency is 1.846 / 1.9, about 97 percent, and the redundancy left is only about 0.054 bits per symbol. The saving here is small because the string is tiny, but on real data with very skewed statistics, Huffman savings are large.

Decoding Huffman: The decoder starts at the root, follows 0 or 1 for each bit, and outputs a symbol whenever it reaches a leaf, then jumps back to the root. Decode 1100111100 with our code: 110 is C, 0 is A, 111 is D, 10 is B, 0 is A. So the message is CADBA. Notice that the decoder never needs separators between codes; that is the beauty of the prefix property. In practice decoders use lookup tables instead of walking a tree bit by bit, for speed.

When Huffman is perfect, and when it is not: For the source with probabilities 0.5, 0.25, 0.125 and 0.125, Huffman gives lengths 1, 2, 3 and 3 and an average of exactly 1.75 bits, equal to the entropy. That happens whenever all probabilities are powers of 1/2. Otherwise there is a small gap, because each codeword must be a whole number of bits. The worst case is a very skewed source: for probabilities 0.9 and 0.1 Huffman must still give each symbol at least 1 bit, while the entropy is only about 0.469 bits. Grouping symbols into blocks helps, and arithmetic coding, two lessons from now, solves this more elegantly.

Practical details: The decoder must know the code. Sending the full tree costs bits, so real formats send only the code length of each symbol, and both sides rebuild the same codes with a fixed rule; this is called canonical Huffman coding and is used in DEFLATE (ZIP, gzip, PNG). Ties during merging can produce different trees, but all have the same optimal average length, so the agreed rule matters only for matching encoder and decoder. If statistics are not known in advance or change over time, adaptive Huffman coding updates the tree as symbols arrive, so no table needs to be sent. Some formats, like JPEG, also allow fixed example tables from the standard to avoid sending a table at all.

Where you will meet Huffman: JPEG codes its run-length pairs with Huffman tables. DEFLATE, used in ZIP, gzip and PNG, codes the output of its dictionary stage with Huffman. MP3 uses Huffman tables for quantized spectral values. Fax uses fixed Huffman-style tables for run lengths. In all these systems Huffman is the last step, the entropy coder, after a model or transform has made the data more predictable.

Real-life example 1, SMS lingo as compression: Bangladeshi teenagers texting in Banglish often write "k" for "ok", "tmi" for "tumi", "ksm" for "kemon". The most frequent words get the shortest forms, rare words are written in full. Without knowing it, they are building a rough Huffman code: frequent symbols short, rare symbols long. The difference is that Huffman makes this optimal and unambiguous.

Real-life example 2, an attendance register: A school stores daily attendance as P (present), A (absent), L (late) and E (excused leave). In a good school P might be 85 percent of entries. A fixed code needs 2 bits per entry. A Huffman code gives P a 1-bit code and the others 2 or 3 bits, cutting storage noticeably over a whole year of records for thousands of students. And because most students are present day after day, running RLE on each student's row first (for example "P x 20") shrinks it even more.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students forget to re-sort after each merge and merge the wrong pair. They put symbols on inner nodes, breaking the prefix rule. They compute the average length with counts but forget to divide by the total. They claim Huffman always reaches the entropy. Exams ask: run-length encode a given string or binary image row; explain when RLE expands data; define prefix codes; build a Huffman tree and codes for given frequencies; compute total bits, average length, entropy and efficiency; decode a bit string; state limitations of Huffman.

Recap: RLE replaces runs with (count, symbol) pairs, great for long runs and bad for busy data; 12W 1B 12W 3B shrinks 28 symbols to 4 pairs. Huffman coding builds an optimal prefix code by repeatedly merging the two least frequent nodes. For AAAABBBCCD it gives A = 0, B = 10, C = 110, D = 111, 19 bits versus 20 fixed, average 1.9 versus entropy 1.846. Huffman is exact when probabilities are powers of 1/2 and cannot go below 1 bit per symbol. It is the entropy-coding workhorse inside JPEG, DEFLATE, MP3 and fax.
key_points: RLE stores runs as (count, symbol): 28-symbol row WWWWWWWWWWWWBWWWWWWWWWWWWBBB -> 12W 1B 12W 3B.
RLE expands data without long runs (ABCD -> 1A1B1C1D); practical formats mix run and literal packets.
Prefix-free codes: no codeword starts another, so decoding needs no separators; they form a binary tree with symbols on leaves.
Huffman: repeatedly merge the two smallest weights, then read 0/1 labels from root to leaf; the result is an optimal prefix code.
Worked: A4 B3 C2 D1 -> A=0, B=10, C=110, D=111; 19 bits vs 20 fixed; average 1.9 vs entropy about 1.846 (about 97% efficient).
Huffman equals the entropy only when probabilities are powers of 1/2 and cannot go below 1 bit per symbol.
Canonical Huffman sends only code lengths; adaptive Huffman updates codes on the fly.
Huffman is the final entropy coder in JPEG, DEFLATE (ZIP/gzip/PNG), MP3 and fax.
lessons.tip: When building a Huffman tree on paper, rewrite the full sorted list after every merge. It costs ten seconds and prevents the most common exam error, merging nodes that are not the two smallest.
lessons.task: Count the letters in your full name (ignore spaces). Build a Huffman tree for those counts on paper, write each letter's code, encode your name, and compare the total bits with a fixed-length code using ceil(log2(number of distinct letters)) bits per letter.

quiz.q: What is the RLE of WWWWWBBBWW?
quiz.explain: Five W, then three B, then two W.

quiz.q: Which set of codewords is NOT prefix-free?
quiz.explain: 0 is the beginning of 01, so a decoder cannot tell where a codeword ends.

quiz.q: For counts A4 B3 C2 D1 with codes A=0, B=10, C=110, D=111, how many bits encode AAAABBBCCD?
With codes A=0, B=10, C=110, D=111, what does 1100111100 decode to?
Why can't Huffman reach the entropy of 0.469 bits for a source with probabilities 0.9 and 0.1?
options: The entropy formula does not apply
Every codeword needs at least 1 whole bit
quiz.explain: Coding single symbols, each gets an integer number of bits, at least 1; grouping or arithmetic coding is needed to go lower.

lessons.title: Dictionary Coding: LZ77, LZW and DEFLATE
lessons.content:
Imagine your class teacher writing the same long phrase on the board again and again: "Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology". After the third time she gets tired and writes "BUET" instead, trusting everyone remembers what it means. She has built a tiny dictionary in the students' heads and now sends short references instead of long phrases. That is exactly the idea behind dictionary coding, the family of compression methods behind ZIP files, gzip on web servers, GIF images and PNG images. Instead of giving short codes to frequent single symbols, as Huffman does, dictionary coders find whole repeated strings and replace each repeat with a short pointer to an earlier copy or a dictionary entry.

Where we are in the course: In lesson 06 we saw that redundancy makes compression possible, and in lesson 07 we built Huffman codes, which exploit statistical redundancy symbol by symbol. Huffman has a weakness: it looks at symbols one at a time and needs to know their probabilities. Real data, like text, program code or a screenshot, is full of repeated phrases and patterns that are longer than one symbol. Dictionary coding attacks exactly that, and it does not need a probability table in advance. It adapts as it reads.

Two big families: Almost all practical dictionary coders come from two papers by Abraham Lempel and Jacob Ziv, published in 1977 and 1978. The 1977 method, LZ77, uses the recent past of the data itself as the dictionary: "copy what you saw a little while ago". The 1978 method, LZ78, builds an explicit table of phrases as it goes. In 1984 Terry Welch published an improved, simpler version of LZ78, which became known as LZW. Keep this map in mind: LZ77 means back-references into a sliding window, LZ78 and LZW mean growing a numbered dictionary.

LZ77, the sliding window: The encoder keeps a window of the most recently processed characters, called the search buffer, and looks ahead at the characters still to be encoded, called the look-ahead buffer. At each step it searches the window for the longest match with the start of the look-ahead buffer. If it finds a match, it outputs a pointer: how far back the match starts (the offset) and how long it is (the length). In the classic textbook version the output is a triple (offset, length, next character), where the next character is the first symbol after the match. If there is no match it outputs (0, 0, character), which is just the literal character.

A small LZ77 worked example: Take the string ABCABCABC, nine characters. At the start the window is empty, so the encoder emits (0, 0, A), then (0, 0, B), then (0, 0, C). Now the look-ahead buffer holds ABCABC. Searching back, the encoder finds ABC starting 3 characters ago. Here is the clever part: the match is allowed to run past the current position into the text being produced, so it can copy 6 characters from offset 3, because each copied character becomes available just in time to be copied again. In the pure (offset, length) style used by DEFLATE, the whole tail is one pointer: offset 3, length 6. Nine characters became three literals and one pointer.

How the decoder copies an overlapping match: The decoder holds ABC. It reads "go back 3, copy 6". It copies position by position: it goes back 3 to A and writes A, then copies B, then C, and now the text is ABCABC. The fourth copy goes back 3 from the new end and finds the A it just wrote, and so on. This overlapping copy is how LZ77 encodes long runs cheaply: a run of 100 spaces becomes one literal space followed by a pointer with offset 1 and length 99. So LZ77 includes run-length coding from lesson 07 as a special case.

Why the window has a size: Searching the entire history would be slow and the offsets would need many bits. So implementations limit the window. DEFLATE, for example, uses a window of 32 KB and match lengths from 3 to 258 bytes. A bigger window can find older repeats and compress more, but needs more memory and searching time. Encoders use hash tables of recent three-byte sequences to find candidate matches quickly. The important asymmetry: encoding (searching) is slow, decoding (just copying) is very fast. That is why web servers can compress a page once and millions of phones decode it cheaply.

LZ78 and LZW, the growing dictionary: Instead of pointing back into raw text, LZ78-style coders build a table of phrases, each with a number. Both encoder and decoder build the same table by following the same rules, so the table itself is never transmitted. LZW, the popular variant, starts with a dictionary that already contains every single symbol. For bytes that means entries 0 to 255. Then it repeats one simple rule: keep reading while the current string w plus the next character is still in the dictionary; when it is not, output the code for w, add w plus that character as a new entry, and restart w from that character.

LZW worked example, encoding: Let us use a tiny alphabet with A = 1 and B = 2, and encode ABABABA. Start with w empty. Read A: w = A. Read B: AB is not in the table, so output 1 (for A), add AB = 3, and set w = B. Read A: BA is not in the table, so output 2 (for B), add BA = 4, set w = A. Read B: AB is in the table now, so w = AB. Read A: ABA is not in the table, so output 3 (for AB), add ABA = 5, set w = A. Read B: w = AB. Read A: ABA is in the table, so w = ABA. The input ends, so output 5 (for ABA). The output is 1 2 3 5: seven symbols in four codes, and the dictionary grew to AB = 3, BA = 4, ABA = 5.

LZW worked example, decoding: The decoder starts with only A = 1 and B = 2. Read 1: output A, remember previous = A. Read 2: output B, and add previous plus the first character of the current string, A + B = AB as code 3. Previous = B. Read 3: it is in the table, AB, so output AB and add B + A = BA as code 4. Previous = AB. Read 5: but the table only goes up to 4. This is the famous special case.

The tricky case, a code not yet in the table: The decoder is always one step behind the encoder, because the encoder adds an entry and may use it immediately. When the decoder receives a code it does not know yet, there is only one possibility: the new string must be previous plus the first character of previous. Here that is AB + A = ABA. So the decoder outputs ABA and adds ABA = 5. The full decoded text is A, B, AB, ABA, which is ABABABA. Exams love this case. If your decoder forgets it, it crashes on inputs like ABABABA or long runs such as AAAAAA.

Pseudo-code for LZW encoding: dict = all single symbols; w = ""; for each c in input: if w + c in dict then w = w + c else output dict[w]; dict[w + c] = next_code; next_code++; w = c. At the end, if w is not empty output dict[w]. It is short enough to write from memory in an exam, which is one reason LZW appears so often in syllabi.

Code width and a full dictionary: Codes are written with a fixed number of bits that grows as the table grows. Practical LZW starts with 9-bit codes for byte data (because 256 symbols plus a few control codes need more than 8 bits) and raises the width as entries are added, up to a limit such as 12 bits, which allows 4,096 entries. When the table fills, the coder either freezes it or sends a special clear code and starts afresh. A dictionary that only fills with phrases from the start of a file would serve the rest poorly if the content changes, so resetting matters.

LZW in GIF: The GIF image format, from 1987, stores its palette-index pixels with LZW. Rows of the same colour, such as a flat logo background, turn into long dictionary phrases and compress very well, while noisy photos compress poorly, and the 256-colour limit hurts them anyway. LZW was covered by a patent held by Unisys, and in the 1990s its licensing demands upset many developers. That pressure helped motivate the creation of PNG, which uses DEFLATE instead. The LZW patents have since expired, but by then PNG was established. We compare these formats properly in lesson 13.

DEFLATE, LZ77 plus Huffman: DEFLATE is the most widely used lossless compressor in the world. It works in two stages. First, LZ77 turns the data into a stream of literals and (length, distance) pairs. Second, Huffman coding (lesson 07) compresses that stream, using one Huffman code for literals and lengths and another for distances. The two ideas fit together beautifully: LZ77 removes repeated strings, Huffman removes the remaining statistical bias. DEFLATE is inside ZIP archives, gzip files, the HTTP Content-Encoding gzip used by web servers, and PNG images.

Real-life example 1, a news site in Dhaka: When you open a Bangla news website on a phone, the HTML, CSS and JavaScript files contain the same tags again and again: div, class, span, the same Unicode Bangla words in headlines. The server sends them gzip-compressed (or with Brotli, a newer LZ77-family compressor that also uses a built-in dictionary of common web strings). Text files like these often shrink to a fraction of their original size, which means faster loading and less mobile data spent on a slow 4G connection in a village.

Real-life example 2, office documents and APK files: A .docx Word file or an Android .apk app package is actually a ZIP archive. Rename a .docx to .zip and you can open it and see XML files inside. Those XML files are extremely repetitive, so DEFLATE squeezes them very well. When a government office in Bangladesh emails a 40-page report as a .docx, it is much smaller than the raw XML would be, thanks to LZ77 plus Huffman working quietly inside.

When dictionary coding does not help: Already-compressed data such as JPEG photos, MP3 audio, H.264 video or an existing ZIP file has almost no repeated strings left; it looks random. Zipping a folder of JPEGs barely changes its size and may even add a few bytes of overhead. Random data cannot be compressed by any lossless method, as lesson 06 showed with entropy. So zip your text, logs and spreadsheets, not your photos and videos.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Students often mix up LZ77 and LZ78: remember LZ77 points back into the text (offset, length), while LZ78/LZW sends dictionary index numbers. Another mistake is thinking the dictionary must be sent; it is not, because the decoder rebuilds it. A third is forgetting the special case in LZW decoding. Typical exam questions: encode a short string with LZW and show the dictionary, decode a given code sequence, explain the KwKwK case, encode a string with LZ77 triples for a given window size, and explain why DEFLATE combines LZ77 with Huffman.

Recap: Dictionary coders replace repeated strings with short references. LZ77 uses a sliding window and (offset, length) pointers, with overlapping copies handling runs. LZW grows a numbered dictionary that both sides build identically, so ABABABA becomes 1 2 3 5. Decoding is fast and simple, with one special case when a code arrives before the decoder has added it. GIF uses LZW; ZIP, gzip and PNG use DEFLATE, which is LZ77 followed by Huffman. Next lesson we meet arithmetic coding, which breaks Huffman's whole-bit limit, and predictive coding, which prepares data so these coders work even better.
key_points: Dictionary coders replace repeated strings with short references instead of coding symbols one by one.
LZ77 uses a sliding window and (offset, length) pointers; overlapping copies encode long runs cheaply.
LZ78/LZW build a numbered phrase dictionary that encoder and decoder grow identically, so it is never sent.
Worked LZW: ABABABA with A=1, B=2 gives 1 2 3 5, adding AB=3, BA=4, ABA=5.
Special decoding case: an unknown code must be previous + first character of previous.
GIF uses LZW; DEFLATE (ZIP, gzip, PNG) is LZ77 followed by Huffman coding.
Encoding is slow (searching), decoding is fast (copying); already-compressed data does not shrink.
lessons.tip: Practise LZW on two or three tiny strings until the encode loop is automatic, and always run your output back through the decoder. The decoder check catches almost every mistake, including the special case.
lessons.task: Encode AAAAAAA (seven A) with LZW using A = 1, B = 2. Write the dictionary as it grows and the output codes, then decode them back and note where the special case happens. Then rename a copy of any .docx file to .zip and open it to see the compressed XML inside.

quiz.q: What does an LZ77 pointer (offset, length) tell the decoder?
options: Which dictionary entry number to output
The Huffman code length of the next symbol
How far back to go in already decoded text and how many characters to copy
How many times to repeat the next literal byte
quiz.explain: LZ77 points back into the recent output: go back offset positions and copy length characters, even overlapping the new text.

quiz.q: LZW encodes ABABABA with A = 1 and B = 2. What is the output?
quiz.explain: Outputs: A(1), B(2), AB(3), ABA(5), while adding AB=3, BA=4, ABA=5.

quiz.q: Why does an LZW decoder never need the dictionary to be transmitted?
options: The dictionary is fixed by the standard
It is stored in the file header
It is guessed from symbol probabilities
The decoder rebuilds it with the same rules from the codes it receives
quiz.explain: Both sides start with the single symbols and add the same new phrase at each step.

quiz.q: DEFLATE, used in ZIP, gzip and PNG, combines which two techniques?
options: LZ77 back-references followed by Huffman coding
quiz.explain: DEFLATE first finds matches with LZ77, then Huffman-codes the literals, lengths and distances.

quiz.q: An LZW decoder receives a code that is not yet in its table. What string does it stand for?
options: The previous string plus the first character of the previous string
The single character with that number
An error; the file is corrupt
quiz.explain: The encoder used an entry it had just created, which must be previous + its own first character (the KwKwK case).

lessons.title: Arithmetic Coding and Predictive Coding
lessons.content:
Think of a cricket score bar that has room for only one number. Instead of writing every run, ball and wicket separately, imagine you could squeeze the whole innings into a single long decimal like 0.5871394, and anyone with the same rulebook could unpack the full innings from it. It sounds like magic, but that is exactly what arithmetic coding does: it turns an entire message into one number between 0 and 1. In the same lesson we will meet a second, much simpler trick, predictive coding, which says: do not send the value, send how wrong your guess was. Both ideas show up inside modern image and video codecs.

Why we need something beyond Huffman: In lesson 07 Huffman gave each symbol a whole number of bits. That works perfectly when probabilities are powers of one half (0.5, 0.25, 0.125), as in our entropy example of 1.75 bits. But look at a very skewed source, such as a black-and-white document where 90 percent of pixels are white. Its entropy, from lesson 06, is only about 0.469 bits per symbol. Huffman cannot give any symbol less than 1 bit, so with two symbols it spends 1 bit per pixel, more than double the entropy. Tricks like grouping symbols into pairs help, but the clean fix is to stop giving each symbol its own codeword at all.

The core idea of arithmetic coding: Start with the interval from 0 to 1. Split it into pieces whose widths equal the symbol probabilities. To encode the first symbol, zoom into its piece. Then split that smaller interval again in the same proportions and zoom into the piece of the second symbol, and so on. After the whole message, you have a narrow interval. Any number inside it identifies the message. The width of the final interval equals the product of the probabilities of all the symbols, so a likely message leaves a wide interval and an unlikely one a tiny interval.

How many bits the final number needs: To point to a spot inside an interval of width w, you need about -log2(w) bits. Since w is the product of the probabilities, -log2(w) is the sum of -log2 p for each symbol, which is exactly the total self-information from lesson 06. So arithmetic coding gets within a couple of bits of the entropy for the whole message, not within one bit per symbol. That is the big win.

Worked example, encoding AAB: Let P(A) = 0.8 and P(B) = 0.2. The rule: A takes the lower 80 percent of the current interval, B takes the upper 20 percent. Start with [0, 1). First symbol A: the new interval is [0, 0.8). Second symbol A: the width is 0.8, and the lower 80 percent of it is [0, 0.64). Third symbol B: the width is 0.64; B takes the top 20 percent, which starts at 0 + 0.8 x 0.64 = 0.512, so the final interval is [0.512, 0.64). Its width is 0.128, which is 0.8 x 0.8 x 0.2, as promised.

Choosing the code number: The information in AAB is -log2(0.128), about 2.97 bits. We need a short binary fraction inside [0.512, 0.64). Binary 0.1 is 0.5, just below. Binary 0.101 is 0.5 + 0.125 = 0.625, which is inside. So the bits 101 can represent the message, assuming the decoder knows the message has three symbols (in practice the length is sent or a special end symbol is used, and real encoders add a bit or two of safety margin).

The general update rule: Write the cumulative probability of a symbol, C(s), as the total probability of all symbols listed before it. Here C(A) = 0 and C(B) = 0.8. With the current interval [low, high) and width = high - low, the new interval for symbol s is low_new = low + width x C(s) and high_new = low + width x (C(s) + p(s)). For the B step above: low_new = 0 + 0.64 x 0.8 = 0.512 and high_new = 0 + 0.64 x 1.0 = 0.64. With three or more symbols the rule is identical; only the table of C values grows. Writing these two lines in an exam before you start number crunching saves many careless mistakes.

Worked example, decoding 0.625: The decoder uses the same probabilities. Is 0.625 in A's range [0, 0.8)? Yes, so the first symbol is A. Rescale: 0.625 / 0.8 = 0.78125. Is that below 0.8? Yes, so A again. Rescale: 0.78125 / 0.8 = 0.9765625. That is in B's range [0.8, 1), so B. Three symbols decoded: AAB. The decoder simply repeats "which piece am I in, then zoom".

Where arithmetic coding beats Huffman: For three symbols our example used 3 bits, the same as Huffman would. The gain appears on longer messages. Take 100 symbols with 90 A and 10 B. The total information is 90 x (-log2 0.9) + 10 x (-log2 0.1), about 46.9 bits, so arithmetic coding needs roughly 47 to 49 bits. Huffman needs 1 bit per symbol, 100 bits. More than twice as good. This is why skewed data such as binary decisions in a video codec is a perfect match for arithmetic coding.

Practical details without the maths: A real coder cannot keep infinitely precise fractions, so it works with integers of fixed size. Whenever the top bits of the low and high ends of the interval agree, those bits are final, so the coder outputs them and shifts them away. This renormalisation keeps the numbers small and lets the coder stream bits as it goes. Probabilities can also be updated as the message is read; this adaptive version needs no table in advance, because the decoder updates its counts the same way.

Arithmetic coding in real standards: In H.264 and H.265 video, the entropy coder called CABAC, context-adaptive binary arithmetic coding, turns every syntax element into a series of binary decisions and codes each with an adaptive probability chosen by its context. It is a major reason those codecs compress better than earlier ones that used only variable-length codes. JPEG also defined an arithmetic-coding option, but for years it was rarely used, partly due to patents and partly because the Huffman option was everywhere. Arithmetic coding is slower than Huffman because each symbol needs multiplication-like work and the steps are serial.

Range coding and ANS: You may meet two relatives. Range coding is essentially arithmetic coding done with integers and bytes. Asymmetric numeral systems (ANS) is a newer family that achieves similar compression with speed closer to Huffman, and it is used in some modern compressors such as Zstandard. You do not need their details here; just know they solve the same problem: coding near the entropy without whole-bit codewords.

Predictive coding, the second idea: Many signals change slowly. In a photo, a pixel is usually close to its left neighbour; in audio, the next sample is close to the previous one; a temperature sensor reads 31.2, 31.2, 31.3. Predictive coding guesses each value from values already sent, then transmits only the prediction error, also called the residual. If the guesses are good, the residuals are small numbers clustered around zero, and small numbers have low entropy, so Huffman or arithmetic coding packs them tightly.

Worked example, simple differences: Samples 100, 102, 105, 104, 108. The simplest predictor says "the next value equals the previous one". Send the first value, then the differences: 100, 2, 3, -1, 4. The receiver rebuilds them by adding: 100, then 100 + 2 = 102, then 102 + 3 = 105, then 105 - 1 = 104, then 104 + 4 = 108. Exact. The originals needed 7 bits each to cover up to 108, while the differences fit in 4 signed bits. This is delta encoding, also used for timestamps in log files and for version control diffs in spirit.

DPCM, the general form: Differential pulse code modulation (DPCM) uses a predictor, often a weighted sum of a few previous samples, and codes the difference. If the difference is coded exactly, DPCM is lossless. If the difference is quantized, it becomes lossy, and then a key rule applies: the encoder must predict from the reconstructed values the decoder will have, not from the originals, otherwise errors pile up step after step. Early speech codecs and the ADPCM family (adaptive DPCM) use this idea, and the DC coefficients in JPEG use a simple form of it, as we will see in lesson 12.

PNG filters, prediction for images: Before DEFLATE compresses a PNG, each row of pixels goes through a filter that replaces values with prediction errors. PNG defines five filter types: None, Sub (predict from the pixel to the left), Up (from the pixel above), Average (the mean of left and above) and Paeth (picks whichever of left, above or upper-left is closest to a simple estimate). The encoder can choose a different filter for each row. On a smooth gradient, Sub turns 96, 104, 112, 120 into 96, 8, 8, 8, which LZ77 and Huffman love.

Lossless JPEG and JPEG-LS: The original JPEG standard also had a lossless mode that uses a choice of predictors from neighbouring pixels plus entropy coding, not the DCT. A later standard, JPEG-LS, uses a smarter context-based predictor. Medical imaging, where every pixel matters for diagnosis, is a typical user of lossless image coding. These modes are less famous than baseline JPEG, but they show that prediction plus entropy coding is the recipe for lossless images.

Real-life example 1, a scanned land record: Land offices in Bangladesh have been digitising huge numbers of old mouza maps and khatian pages. A black-and-white scan of a document is mostly white paper. Fax-style and document coders exploit exactly this skew; the JBIG2 standard, for example, uses an adaptive arithmetic coder with context modelling for bi-level images. Because the white probability is so high, arithmetic coding can spend well under one bit on most pixels, something Huffman on single pixels cannot do.

Real-life example 2, a smart electricity meter: Prepaid smart meters in Dhaka report readings that rise slowly: 5321.4, 5321.6, 5321.9 kWh. Sending each full reading wastes bits. Sending the first reading and then small differences (2, 3 in tenths of a kWh) and entropy coding them can save a lot of data across millions of meters. The same idea compresses GPS tracks from ride-sharing apps, where consecutive positions are close.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Students sometimes think arithmetic coding outputs one codeword per symbol; it outputs one number for the whole message. Another mistake is updating the interval with the wrong base: always compute the new limits as low + width x cumulative probability. In DPCM, students forget that a lossy encoder must predict from reconstructed values. Typical questions: encode a short string with given probabilities and give the final interval, decode a given number, compare with Huffman, compute differences for a list of samples and reconstruct, and name the PNG filters.

Recap: Arithmetic coding narrows an interval for every symbol and sends one number for the whole message, reaching close to the entropy even for skewed sources. Our AAB example ended at [0.512, 0.64), width 0.128, about 2.97 bits, and 0.625 (binary 0.101) decodes back to AAB. CABAC brings this power to H.264 and H.265. Predictive coding sends residuals instead of values: 100, 102, 105, 104, 108 becomes 100, 2, 3, -1, 4. PNG filters and DPCM use this. Together with Huffman and LZ, these complete the lossless toolbox. Next lesson we cross the line into lossy compression.
key_points: Huffman spends at least 1 bit per symbol; a skewed source with 0.9/0.1 has entropy of only about 0.469 bits.
Arithmetic coding narrows an interval per symbol and sends one number for the whole message.
Final interval width = product of probabilities; bits needed are about -log2(width).
Worked: P(A)=0.8, P(B)=0.2, AAB gives [0.512, 0.64), width 0.128, about 2.97 bits; 0.625 = binary 0.101 decodes to AAB.
For 90 A and 10 B, arithmetic needs about 47 bits versus 100 for Huffman; CABAC uses this in H.264/H.265.
Predictive coding sends residuals: 100, 102, 105, 104, 108 becomes 100, 2, 3, -1, 4.
Lossy DPCM must predict from reconstructed values; PNG uses five filters (None, Sub, Up, Average, Paeth).
lessons.tip: For arithmetic coding exams, draw a vertical number line for every step and label low, high and each symbol's slice. Most marks are lost by arithmetic slips, not by misunderstanding the idea.
lessons.task: With P(A) = 0.8 and P(B) = 0.2, encode the string ABA by hand and write the final interval. Check that its width equals 0.8 x 0.2 x 0.8. Then write today's hourly temperatures from a weather app as first value plus differences and see how small the numbers get.

quiz.q: Why can Huffman coding not reach the entropy of a source with P = 0.9 and 0.1?
options: Huffman needs the data to be text
Every Huffman codeword is at least 1 bit, but the entropy is about 0.469 bits per symbol
Huffman only works for four symbols
quiz.explain: Whole-bit codewords cannot go below 1 bit per symbol, so Huffman spends more than twice the entropy here.

quiz.q: With P(A)=0.8 and P(B)=0.2, what is the final arithmetic-coding interval for AAB?
quiz.explain: A gives [0,0.8), A gives [0,0.64), B takes the top 20 percent: from 0.512 to 0.64.

quiz.q: In arithmetic coding, the width of the final interval equals what?
options: The product of the probabilities of the encoded symbols
The number of symbols divided by the alphabet size
quiz.explain: Each symbol shrinks the interval by its own probability, so the final width is the product.

quiz.q: Samples 100, 102, 105, 104, 108 are delta-encoded with "predict the previous value". What is sent?
quiz.explain: Send the first value, then each difference: 102-100 = 2, 105-102 = 3, 104-105 = -1, 108-104 = 4.

quiz.q: In lossy DPCM, why must the encoder predict from reconstructed values?
options: So encoder and decoder use the same predictions and quantization errors do not pile up
Because original values are deleted after reading
The standard forbids using originals for patent reasons
quiz.explain: The decoder only has reconstructed values; predicting from originals would make the two sides drift apart.

lessons.title: Lossy Compression Principles: Rate, Distortion, MSE and PSNR
lessons.content:
When your aunt in Sylhet sends a family photo on WhatsApp, the picture you receive is not the picture her camera captured. Some detail was thrown away on purpose, and yet everyone still recognises every face and smiles. Compare that with a bank statement: if a single digit changed, it would be a disaster. That difference is the dividing line of this lesson. Lossless compression, which we finished in lessons 07 to 09, must bring back every bit. Lossy compression is allowed to change the data, as long as the result looks or sounds good enough to a human. Almost every photo, song, voice call and video you meet is lossy.

Why lossless is not enough for media: Lossless coders are limited by entropy, and natural images, audio and video are full of fine noise that has high entropy. A camera photo often shrinks only about two times with lossless coding, which is not nearly enough. Lesson 01 showed raw 1080p30 video needs about 746 Mbps; a home broadband line might give 10 or 20 Mbps. To close a gap of more than 30 times, we must give up perfect reconstruction. The good news is that human eyes and ears ignore a great deal of the information in a raw signal, so we can drop exactly what they will not miss.

What lossy compression is: A lossy method produces a reconstruction that is close to the original but not identical. We measure two things: the rate, which is how many bits we spend (bits per pixel, bits per second), and the distortion, which is how different the reconstruction is. The central fact is a trade-off: fewer bits means more distortion. Every lossy codec gives you a knob, called quality, bitrate or quantization parameter, that moves you along this trade-off.

Rate in numbers: A raw true-colour image costs 24 bits per pixel. Suppose a lossy coder brings a 1920 x 1080 photo down to 2 bits per pixel. The file becomes 1920 x 1080 x 2 / 8 = 518,400 bytes instead of 6,220,800 bytes, a compression ratio of 24 / 2 = 12 to 1. At 1 bit per pixel the ratio is 24 to 1 and the file is about 259 KB, but now the distortion is clearly higher. Bits per pixel for images and bits per second for audio and video are the "rate" in rate-distortion, and they are the numbers you should quote when comparing codecs, because they do not depend on how large the picture is.

The rate-distortion curve: Imagine a graph with rate on the horizontal axis and distortion on the vertical axis. At very high rate, distortion is near zero. As the rate falls, distortion rises slowly at first, then quickly. Rate-distortion theory, also founded by Shannon, says that for a given source and distortion measure there is a best possible curve, the rate-distortion function R(D), that no codec can beat. Real codecs sit above it. A better codec is one whose curve is lower: the same quality for fewer bits, or better quality for the same bits. When people say a new video codec "saves 30 to 50 percent bitrate", they mean its curve sits that much to the left at equal quality.

The basic structure of a lossy coder: Almost every lossy media coder has three stages. First, a transform or prediction rearranges the data so that its information is concentrated in a few values (DCT in JPEG, filter banks in MP3, motion-compensated prediction in video). Second, quantization rounds those values coarsely. Third, lossless entropy coding (Huffman, arithmetic) packs the rounded values. Only the second stage loses information. The transform is reversible and entropy coding is lossless. This is the most important structural fact about lossy compression, and exams ask it constantly.

Quantization, the only lossy step: Quantization maps a value to an integer index by dividing by a step size and rounding: index = round(x / step). The decoder multiplies back: x_hat = index x step. Worked example with step 10: the values 37, 42 and 18 give indices round(3.7) = 4, round(4.2) = 4 and round(1.8) = 2. The decoder rebuilds 40, 40 and 20. The errors are 3, -2 and 2, never more than half a step, which is 5. Two different inputs, 37 and 42, became the same output, which is why this step cannot be undone. Lesson 04 of DSP already showed the same rounding in an ADC; here we apply it on purpose, with a step size we choose.

Why bigger steps save bits: With step 10, values from 0 to 255 need about 27 different indices (0 to 26); with step 40 only about 7. Fewer distinct indices, and many of them zero, means lower entropy and fewer bits after entropy coding. The price is a bigger error, up to half the step. So the step size is the knob on the rate-distortion curve. In JPEG and video codecs, different coefficients get different steps, fine for the ones the eye notices and coarse for the ones it does not.

Measuring distortion with MSE: The simplest distortion measure is the mean squared error. For N samples, MSE = (1/N) x sum of (original - reconstructed)^2. Worked example: the original pixels 52, 55, 61, 66 are reconstructed as 50, 56, 61, 70. The errors are -2, 1, 0 and 4; their squares are 4, 1, 0 and 16; the sum is 21; so MSE = 21 / 4 = 5.25. Squaring makes big errors count much more than small ones and removes the sign.

PSNR, the decibel version: Because MSE depends on the scale of the signal, we usually report peak signal-to-noise ratio: PSNR = 10 log10(MAX^2 / MSE), where MAX is the largest possible sample value, 255 for 8-bit images. For our example, PSNR = 10 log10(65025 / 5.25), about 40.93 dB. Other worked values: MSE 10 gives about 38.13 dB, MSE 100 gives about 28.13 dB, and MSE 1 gives about 48.13 dB. Notice the pattern: every ten times more MSE costs exactly 10 dB. Higher PSNR means closer to the original. As a rough rule of thumb, many lossy images at decent quality land somewhere in the 30s to low 40s of dB, but the number is only meaningful when comparing the same image or video coded different ways.

Where PSNR fails: PSNR treats every pixel error equally, but the eye does not. Blurring a face and adding faint noise to a busy grass texture can give the same MSE, yet the blurred face looks far worse. Shifting a whole image one pixel to the side gives a terrible PSNR though it looks identical. So researchers built perceptual metrics. SSIM (structural similarity) compares local patterns of brightness, contrast and structure. VMAF, developed by Netflix with academic partners, combines several measures using machine learning trained on human ratings. Codec engineers still report PSNR because it is simple, but they back it up with these.

Subjective quality and MOS: The final judge is people. In a subjective test, viewers or listeners rate clips on a scale, commonly 1 (bad) to 5 (excellent), and the average is the mean opinion score, MOS. Telephone and voice codecs are traditionally rated this way under ITU-T recommendations. Testing needs controlled rooms, many participants and careful methods, so it is expensive, but it is the ground truth that objective metrics try to predict.

Transform coding and energy compaction: Why transform before quantizing? In the pixel domain, every value matters roughly equally, so quantizing them all coarsely blurs everything. A good transform packs most of the signal's energy into a few coefficients and leaves many coefficients near zero. Preview from the next lesson: for an 8-pixel ramp 96, 104, ..., 152, the DCT puts about 98.9 percent of the energy into just two of the eight coefficients. Quantization then turns the small coefficients into zeros, which cost almost nothing to code, and spends bits only where the energy is.

Perceptual coding: The second big idea is to spend errors where humans do not notice them. The eye is less sensitive to fine detail in colour than in brightness, which is why we subsample chroma (lesson 04). It is also less sensitive to very high spatial frequencies and to noise hidden in busy textures. The ear cannot hear quiet sounds right next to loud ones in frequency or time, which is masking (lesson 14). A perceptual coder uses a model of human perception to decide where to put the quantization noise, so the noise is large in measurement but small in experience.

Generation loss: Every lossy encode adds a bit of damage. If you decode a JPEG, edit it and save it as JPEG again, you lose a little more, and repeating this many times eventually produces visible blocks and colour smears. Memes that have been screenshotted and reposted dozens of times show this beautifully. The rule for creators: keep a lossless master (RAW, PNG, or a high-quality intermediate), do all edits on it, and encode to a lossy format once at the end.

Real-life example 1, Facebook and WhatsApp photos: When you upload a photo from your phone, the app usually resizes it and re-encodes it with a lossy codec at a quality chosen by the service. A 12-megapixel camera image of a few megabytes can come out at a few hundred kilobytes. On a phone screen it looks fine, because the display is small and the codec spent its bits on the parts your eye checks. Zoom in on the sky or on text in the photo and you start to see blocking and ringing.

Real-life example 2, a mobile call from Rajshahi: Your voice is sampled, then a speech codec throws away much of the information and keeps only what matters for intelligibility and voice character, sending a small fraction of the raw PCM rate. Lesson 05 showed classic telephone PCM is 64 kbps; modern mobile voice codecs run at far lower rates while sounding as good or better, precisely because they model speech and hearing. On a weak signal the network may switch the codec to an even lower rate, trading quality for reliability: the rate-distortion knob, live.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Students often say the DCT is lossy; it is not, the quantization after it is. Another mistake is computing PSNR with the wrong MAX (use 255 for 8-bit, 1 for normalised images) or forgetting to divide by N in MSE. Some think higher MSE means higher PSNR; it is the opposite. Typical questions: define lossy versus lossless with examples, draw and explain the three-stage lossy coder, compute MSE and PSNR for a small block, quantize given values with a step size, explain rate-distortion trade-off, and explain why PSNR does not always match perceived quality.

Recap: Lossy compression accepts small, controlled errors to gain huge size savings. Its trade-off is rate versus distortion, and better codecs push the curve down. A lossy coder transforms or predicts, quantizes, then entropy-codes; only quantization loses information. Step 10 turned 37, 42, 18 into 40, 40, 20. MSE averages squared errors, and PSNR = 10 log10(255^2 / MSE): MSE 5.25 gives about 40.93 dB and each 10 times more MSE costs 10 dB. Perceptual metrics and MOS tell us what humans actually notice, and generation loss warns us to encode lossy only once. Next we open the most famous transform of all: the DCT.
key_points: Lossless coding is limited by entropy; natural media needs far more compression, so we accept controlled errors.
Rate versus distortion is the core trade-off; a better codec has a lower rate-distortion curve.
Lossy coder = transform/prediction, then quantization, then entropy coding; only quantization loses information.
Quantization: index = round(x/step); step 10 turns 37, 42, 18 into 40, 40, 20 (error at most step/2).
MSE = average squared error; worked 52,55,61,66 vs 50,56,61,70 gives MSE 5.25.
PSNR = 10 log10(255^2/MSE): 5.25 gives about 40.93 dB, 10 gives 38.13 dB, 100 gives 28.13 dB.
PSNR misses perception; SSIM, VMAF and MOS (1 to 5) try to capture what people see and hear.
Generation loss: keep a lossless master and encode to a lossy format only once.
lessons.tip: Learn the anchors "MSE 10 is about 38 dB, and each 10 times MSE costs 10 dB". With them you can check any PSNR answer in your head before the exam clock runs out.
lessons.task: Take any photo on your phone, save or share copies at low and high quality (for example via a messaging app versus the original), then zoom into the sky or some text and list the artefacts you see. Also compute the MSE and PSNR for the four pixels 100, 120, 140, 160 reconstructed as 102, 118, 141, 165.

quiz.q: In a typical lossy coder (transform, quantization, entropy coding), which stage actually loses information?
quiz.explain: The transform is reversible and entropy coding is lossless; rounding in quantization cannot be undone.

quiz.q: Original pixels 52, 55, 61, 66 become 50, 56, 61, 70. What is the MSE?
quiz.explain: Errors -2, 1, 0, 4; squares 4, 1, 0, 16; sum 21; divided by 4 pixels gives 5.25.

quiz.q: For an 8-bit image, an MSE of 100 gives a PSNR of about:
quiz.explain: 10 log10(65025/100) = about 28.13 dB, 10 dB below the MSE-10 value of 38.13 dB.

quiz.q: With step size 10, which values are reconstructed from 37, 42 and 18?
quiz.explain: round(3.7)=4, round(4.2)=4, round(1.8)=2, times 10 gives 40, 40, 20.

quiz.q: What is generation loss?
options: Loss of data when a cable is too long
Losing frames when a phone overheats
Quality dropping further each time media is decoded and re-encoded with a lossy codec
The difference between lossless and lossy file sizes
quiz.explain: Every lossy encode adds new errors, so repeated re-saving piles up artefacts.

lessons.title: The Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT)
lessons.content:
Think of a glass of borhani or a cup of tea. You could describe it molecule by molecule, or you could give its recipe: mostly milk, some tea, a little sugar, a pinch of masala. The recipe is far shorter, and if you skip the pinch of masala, most people will barely notice. The discrete cosine transform, the DCT, does this for a block of pixels. Instead of listing 64 brightness values, it says how much of each of 64 standard patterns, from "completely flat" to "very fine checkerboard", you need to mix to rebuild the block. For natural images, a few patterns carry almost all of the recipe. That is why the DCT sits at the heart of JPEG, of most video codecs, and in a modified form of MP3 and AAC.

Where we stand: Lesson 10 said a lossy coder first transforms, then quantizes, then entropy-codes, and that a good transform packs energy into a few values. The DSP course (deep-cse-5-7) taught the DFT and FFT and named the 8x8 DCT in JPEG. Here we open the DCT itself: the formula, what its coefficients mean, two worked blocks, and why it is preferred over the DFT for compression. It was published by Nasir Ahmed, T. Natarajan and K. R. Rao in 1974, and it became one of the most used transforms in history.

The idea of a transform as a change of view: Any list of 8 numbers can be written as a weighted sum of 8 fixed basis patterns. In the normal "pixel view" the basis is trivial: pattern 0 is (1,0,0,0,0,0,0,0), pattern 1 is (0,1,0,...), and the weights are the pixel values themselves. The DCT uses a different set of 8 patterns: smooth cosine waves of increasing frequency. The weights in that set are the DCT coefficients. No information is lost; it is the same block seen through different glasses. The inverse DCT switches back exactly, apart from tiny rounding.

The 1D DCT formula: For 8 samples x[0] to x[7], the DCT used in JPEG (called DCT-II) is X[k] = (C(k) / 2) x sum over n of x[n] cos((2n + 1) k pi / 16), for k = 0 to 7, where C(0) = 1 / sqrt(2) and C(k) = 1 for k > 0. The inverse is x[n] = sum over k of (C(k) / 2) X[k] cos((2n + 1) k pi / 16). With these scale factors the transform is orthonormal, which means it keeps energy: the sum of squares of the samples equals the sum of squares of the coefficients.

What each coefficient means: X[0] uses cos(0) = 1 for every sample, so it is just the sum of the samples divided by sqrt(8): it measures the average, and it is called the DC coefficient (a name borrowed from direct current in electronics). X[1] uses half a cosine cycle across the 8 samples, so it measures a slow change from one end to the other. X[2] is one full cycle, X[3] one and a half, and so on up to X[7], which flips sign almost every sample and measures the finest detail. All coefficients other than X[0] are called AC coefficients.

Worked example 1, a smooth ramp: Take the pixel row 96, 104, 112, 120, 128, 136, 144, 152, a gentle left-to-right brightening. First subtract 128 (the level shift used by JPEG to centre 8-bit values on zero): -32, -24, -16, -8, 0, 8, 16, 24. The DCT gives, rounded to two decimals: X = (-11.31, -51.54, 0, -5.39, 0, -1.61, 0, -0.41). Check X[0]: the sum is -32, and -32 / sqrt(8) is -11.31. X[1] is large and negative because the row rises from left to right while the first cosine falls. The even AC terms are exactly zero, and the odd ones shrink fast.

Energy compaction in numbers: The sum of squares of the shifted samples is 1,024 + 576 + 256 + 64 + 0 + 64 + 256 + 576 = 2,816. The sum of squares of the coefficients is also 2,816, as orthonormality promises. But X[0] and X[1] alone hold about 98.9 percent of it. If we keep only those two and set the other six to zero, the inverse DCT gives about 98.7, 102.6, 109.7, 119.0, 129.0, 138.3, 145.4, 149.3. Every pixel is within about 3 of the original, from just two numbers. That is energy compaction, and it is exactly what makes quantization cheap.

Worked example 2, the busiest possible row: Now take an alternating row, +100, -100, +100, -100, and so on. The DCT puts no energy in X[0], since the average is zero, and puts the largest coefficient in X[7], about 256.29, with smaller amounts in X[5], X[3] and X[1]. X[7] alone holds about 82 percent of the energy. So the DCT really does sort content by frequency: smooth rows land in the low coefficients, rapidly changing rows in the high ones. Natural photos are mostly smooth, which is why their energy gathers at the low end.

From 1D to 2D: Images are two-dimensional, so JPEG uses the 2D DCT on 8x8 blocks: F(u, v) = (1/4) C(u) C(v) x sum over x and y of f(x, y) cos((2x + 1) u pi / 16) cos((2y + 1) v pi / 16), for u and v from 0 to 7. Here u counts vertical frequency (down the rows) and v counts horizontal frequency (across the columns), in the indexing we use in this course. The 64 coefficients correspond to 64 basis images: F(0,0) is a flat grey square, F(0,1) a soft left-to-right shade, F(1,0) a top-to-bottom shade, and F(7,7) a fine checkerboard. Any 8x8 block is a weighted mix of these 64 tiles.

The DC term in 2D: With this scaling, F(0,0) = (1/4) x (1/2) x sum of all 64 values = sum / 8, which is 8 times the block average. Worked: a flat block where every pixel is 100. After the level shift every value is -28. The DC coefficient is 8 x (-28) = -224, and all 63 AC coefficients are exactly zero, because a flat block contains no change at all. One number describes the entire block. Exam tip: "DC = 8 x mean of the shifted block" is a quick check for any 8x8 problem.

Worked 2D block, the ramp in every row: Fill an 8x8 block so every row is our ramp 96 to 152. Nothing changes vertically, so every coefficient with u > 0 is zero. The first row of coefficients is: F(0,0) = -32, F(0,1) = -145.77, F(0,3) = -15.24, F(0,5) = -4.55, F(0,7) = -1.15, and the even ones are zero. Each is the 1D value times sqrt(8), because the eight identical rows add up coherently. Again about 98.9 percent of the energy sits in two of the 64 coefficients. We will push this exact block through JPEG quantization in the next lesson.

Separability, a big speed-up: The 2D DCT can be computed as 1D DCTs on each of the 8 rows, followed by 1D DCTs on each of the 8 columns of the result. Computed directly, each of the 64 outputs needs 64 multiply-adds, which is 4,096. Done separably, the rows cost 8 x 8 x 8 = 512 and the columns another 512, so 1,024 in total, four times fewer. Fast DCT algorithms, related to the FFT you met in DSP, cut the cost much further. That is why even cheap phone chips can run DCTs on millions of blocks per second.

Why the DCT and not the DFT: The DFT treats a block as one period of a repeating signal. For our ramp, the repeated version jumps from 152 straight back to 96 at the block edge, and that artificial jump needs many high-frequency coefficients to describe, which wastes bits (the leakage you saw in DSP). The DCT implicitly mirrors the block instead, so the extended signal goes 96 up to 152 and then back down to 96, with no jump. Smooth extension means faster-decaying coefficients. Bonus: DCT coefficients are real numbers, not complex, so there is half as much to store. For highly correlated data like images, the DCT comes very close to the theoretically best energy-compacting transform (the Karhunen-Loeve transform), without needing the data's statistics.

Why 8x8 blocks: A whole-image transform would mix distant, unrelated regions and be slower. Tiny blocks would not capture enough correlation. 8x8 was a practical compromise for the hardware and images of the 1980s and 1990s, and it gives 64 coefficients, a convenient size for one quantization table that a person can still read and tune by hand. Modern video codecs use a range of block sizes, from 4x4 up to 32x32 and beyond, often with integer approximations of the DCT so that encoder and decoder get bit-identical results; H.264, for example, uses a small integer transform derived from the DCT. Audio codecs such as MP3 and AAC use the MDCT, a modified DCT on overlapping windows that avoids clicks at block edges.

Real-life example 1, a Padma Bridge photo: In a photo of the bridge at sunset, the sky blocks are smooth gradients: a big DC term, a couple of low-frequency AC terms, and almost nothing else. The cable and railing blocks are full of sharp edges, so their energy spreads into higher frequencies. JPEG at the same quality will therefore spend very few bits on the sky and many on the bridge structure, which matches what your eye cares about. When quality is set too low, the high coefficients in the edge blocks vanish first, and you see ringing around the cables.

Real-life example 2, a scanned exam answer sheet: A scanned handwritten answer script has large white areas (flat blocks: DC only) and dark pen strokes (blocks with sharp edges: many AC terms). DCT-based JPEG blurs the strokes slightly at low quality, while a lossless method like PNG or a bi-level coder keeps them sharp. This is why documents with text are often better saved as PNG or PDF with appropriate compression, while photos suit JPEG. Knowing what the DCT does to edges lets you choose correctly.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: The DCT is not lossy; quantization is. The DC coefficient is not the average itself but a scaled average (8 times the mean in the 2D orthonormal form). Do not forget the level shift of 128 in JPEG problems, and do not mix up u and v. Typical questions: write the 1D or 2D DCT formula, compute DC for a given block, explain energy compaction, explain why DCT beats DFT for images, explain separability and its saving, and sketch a few basis images.

Recap: The DCT rewrites a block as a mix of cosine patterns. X[0] or F(0,0) measures the average; higher indices measure finer detail. The ramp row -32 ... 24 gives (-11.31, -51.54, 0, -5.39, 0, -1.61, 0, -0.41) with 98.9 percent of the energy in two coefficients; a flat block of 100 gives DC = -224 and nothing else. The 2D DCT is separable (1,024 versus 4,096 operations), real-valued, and avoids the DFT's edge jump. Next lesson we feed these coefficients into the full JPEG pipeline: quantization, zigzag and entropy coding.
key_points: The DCT rewrites a block as weights of fixed cosine patterns; it is reversible and keeps energy (orthonormal).
1D DCT-II: X[k] = (C(k)/2) sum x[n] cos((2n+1)k pi/16), with C(0) = 1/sqrt(2).
X[0] (DC) measures the average; higher-index AC coefficients measure finer detail.
Worked ramp -32..24 gives (-11.31, -51.54, 0, -5.39, 0, -1.61, 0, -0.41); two coefficients hold about 98.9 percent of the energy.
2D DC = 8 x mean of the shifted block: a flat block of 100 gives -28 x 8 = -224 and all AC zero.
Separable: rows then columns cost 1,024 multiply-adds instead of 4,096 for an 8x8 block.
DCT beats DFT for images: mirrored extension avoids edge jumps and coefficients are real.
lessons.tip: Do not memorise 64 cosine values. Remember three things instead: DC is a scaled average, smooth blocks put energy in the top-left corner, and edges spread energy to higher frequencies. Then check every answer against them.
lessons.task: Take four numbers, for example 10, 20, 30, 40. Compute their average and their "slope" by hand, then rebuild an approximation using only those two numbers (average plus slope times position). Compare with the original: this is energy compaction in miniature. If you have a laptop, try scipy.fft.dct with norm="ortho" on the ramp from this lesson.

quiz.q: What does the DC coefficient of a DCT block measure?
options: A scaled version of the block average
The sharpest edge in the block
quiz.explain: X[0] uses cos(0) = 1 for every sample, so it is the sum (average) times a scale factor.

quiz.q: An 8x8 block has every pixel equal to 100. After the JPEG level shift, what is F(0,0)?
quiz.explain: Shifted value is -28 and in the orthonormal 2D DCT, DC = 8 x mean = 8 x (-28) = -224. All AC terms are zero.

quiz.q: Why is the DCT preferred over the DFT for image compression?
options: The DCT is lossy so it compresses more
Its mirrored extension avoids an artificial jump at block edges, so coefficients decay faster
The DFT cannot be computed for 8 samples
The DCT uses complex numbers which hold more information
quiz.explain: The DFT assumes periodic repetition, causing a jump; the DCT implicitly mirrors the block, giving a smooth extension and real coefficients.

quiz.q: How many multiply-adds does a separable 8x8 DCT (rows then columns, no fast algorithm) need?
quiz.explain: 8 rows x 8 outputs x 8 terms = 512, plus the same for columns, gives 1,024 instead of 4,096.

quiz.q: For the ramp row 96, 104, ..., 152, roughly what share of the energy sits in X[0] and X[1]?
quiz.explain: (11.31^2 + 51.54^2) / 2,816 is about 0.989; the remaining coefficients are small.

lessons.title: The JPEG Pipeline Step by Step
lessons.content:
Picture a garment factory in Gazipur. Cloth goes in at one end and passes station after station: cutting, stitching, checking, ironing, packing. Each station does one simple job, and together they turn a roll of fabric into a packed shirt. JPEG works exactly like that assembly line. A photo goes in, passes through colour conversion, block splitting, the DCT, quantization, zigzag ordering and entropy coding, and comes out as a small .jpg file. In this lesson we walk one real 8x8 block through every station with actual numbers, so you can see where the bits go and where the quality goes.

What JPEG is: JPEG is named after the Joint Photographic Experts Group, the committee that created the standard; it was published in the early 1990s (as ITU-T T.81 and ISO/IEC 10918-1). The most common form, called baseline sequential JPEG, is lossy, works on 8-bit samples and uses Huffman coding. More than thirty years later it is still the most common photo format on the web and in cameras. What we usually call a "JPEG file" is technically the JPEG bitstream inside a small wrapper format, such as JFIF or Exif, that holds extra information.

The whole pipeline in one breath: Encoder: convert RGB to Y'CbCr, subsample chroma (often 4:2:0), split each channel into 8x8 blocks, subtract 128, apply the 2D DCT, divide by a quantization table and round, reorder in zigzag, code the DC difference and the AC run-lengths, Huffman-code everything, write headers. Decoder: undo each step in reverse. Only the rounding in quantization (and the chroma subsampling) throws information away.

Station 1, colour conversion and subsampling: Lesson 04 showed why we turn RGB into luma Y and two chroma channels Cb and Cr: the eye sees detail mainly in brightness. With 4:2:0, Cb and Cr keep one sample per 2x2 pixels, which already halves the raw data from 24 to 12 bits per pixel before any DCT. Each channel is then processed separately; from here on we follow a luma block.

Station 2, blocks and level shift: The image is cut into 8x8 blocks, left to right, top to bottom. If the width or height is not a multiple of 8 (or 16 with 4:2:0), the encoder pads the edge. Each sample, from 0 to 255, has 128 subtracted, so values run from -128 to 127 and a mid-grey block sits near zero. For our example we use the block from lesson 11: every row is 96, 104, 112, 120, 128, 136, 144, 152, which after the shift is -32 up to 24.

Station 3, the DCT: Lesson 11 computed this block's coefficients. Because nothing changes vertically, only the top row is non-zero: F(0,0) = -32, F(0,1) = -145.77, F(0,3) = -15.24, F(0,5) = -4.55, F(0,7) = -1.15, and the rest are zero. Remember, this step is reversible; we still have all the information.

Station 4, quantization, where quality is decided: Each coefficient is divided by its own step from a quantization table and rounded: Fq(u,v) = round(F(u,v) / Q(u,v)). The example luminance table printed in the JPEG standard has, in its top row, 16, 11, 10, 16, 24, 40, 51, 61, and its values grow towards the bottom-right corner, up to around 100 and more, because the eye is less sensitive to high-frequency detail. Encoders may use other tables; this one is the classic textbook choice.

Quantizing our block: DC: -32 / 16 = -2. F(0,1): -145.77 / 11 = -13.25, rounded to -13. F(0,3): -15.24 / 16 = -0.95, rounded to -1. F(0,5): -4.55 / 40 = -0.11, rounded to 0. F(0,7): -1.15 / 61 = -0.02, rounded to 0. Everything else was already 0. So 64 real numbers have become just three non-zero integers: -2, -13 and -1. That is where most of the compression comes from.

Station 5, zigzag ordering: The 8x8 grid of quantized values is read along anti-diagonals in a zigzag: (0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (2,0), (1,1), (0,2), (0,3), (1,2), (2,1), (3,0) and so on to (7,7). This puts low frequencies first and high frequencies last, so the zeros, which mostly live at high frequencies, bunch together at the end. For our block the zigzag list starts -2, -13, 0, 0, 0, 0, -1, and then 57 zeros. Note that (0,3) is at position 6 in the zigzag order.

Station 6a, coding the DC term: Neighbouring blocks usually have similar averages, so JPEG codes the DC value as the difference from the previous block's DC in the same channel. This is the predictive coding of lesson 09. If the previous block's DC was -5, we send -2 - (-5) = 3. Each difference is sent as a size category (how many bits the value needs) that is Huffman-coded, followed by that many raw bits giving the exact value.

Station 6b, coding the AC terms with run-lengths: The 63 AC values are turned into pairs (run, value), where run is the number of zeros before a non-zero value. Our AC list is -13, 0, 0, 0, 0, -1, then zeros. That gives (0, -13), meaning no zeros then -13, and (4, -1), meaning four zeros then -1. After the last non-zero value, a special end-of-block symbol, EOB, says "everything else is zero". So the entire block is: DC difference, (0, -13), (4, -1), EOB. If 16 or more zeros appear before a non-zero value, a special zero-run-length symbol (ZRL) covers each 16 zeros.

Station 7, Huffman coding: Each AC pair is turned into a symbol (run, size), where size is the number of bits needed for the value: -13 needs size 4 (magnitudes 8 to 15), -1 needs size 1. The (run, size) symbol is Huffman-coded, then the size-many raw bits for the value follow. JPEG provides example Huffman tables, and an encoder can also build optimised tables from the image's own statistics. Our 64-pixel block, which was 512 bits raw, now needs only a few dozen bits. Arithmetic coding is allowed by the standard as an alternative, but Huffman is what nearly every JPEG uses.

The decoder, step by step back: The decoder reads the Huffman codes, rebuilds the DC from the difference and the AC values from the run-lengths, undoes the zigzag, and multiplies by the table: -2 x 16 = -32, -13 x 11 = -143, -1 x 16 = -16. Then it runs the inverse DCT, adds 128 and clips to 0 to 255. For our block the first row comes back as 97, 104, 113, 121, 127, 135, 144, 151, against the original 96, 104, 112, 120, 128, 136, 144, 152. No pixel is off by more than 1, from three integers. Then chroma is upsampled and Y'CbCr is converted back to RGB for display.

Inside the file: A JPEG file is a sequence of segments, each starting with a two-byte marker. It begins with SOI (start of image, bytes FF D8) and ends with EOI (end of image, FF D9). In between come DQT segments carrying the quantization tables, a SOF segment giving the image size and the components, DHT segments carrying the Huffman tables, and then SOS (start of scan) followed by the entropy-coded data. Because the tables travel inside the file, any decoder can rebuild the image without knowing which encoder settings were used. Usually there is one quantization table for luma and a second, coarser one shared by Cb and Cr, since the eye forgives chroma errors more readily. Open any .jpg in a hex viewer and the first two bytes will be FF D8.

The quality setting: The familiar "quality 0 to 100" slider in image editors is not part of the JPEG standard itself; it is a convention of encoders such as the widely used Independent JPEG Group library. In that library, quality 50 uses the example table as is, and other qualities scale it: below 50 the scale is 5000 / quality percent, above 50 it is 200 - 2 x quality percent. So at quality 75 the DC step 16 becomes 8 and the first AC step 11 becomes 6; at quality 90 they become 3 and 2; at quality 10 they become 80 and 55. Smaller steps mean more non-zero coefficients, more bits and better quality.

Artefacts you can now explain: Blocking appears at low quality because each 8x8 block is quantized on its own, so neighbouring blocks no longer join smoothly; you see a grid, especially in smooth skies. Ringing, faint ripples next to sharp edges and text, comes from discarding the high-frequency coefficients that edges need. Colour bleeding comes from chroma subsampling. Mosquito noise around moving edges in videos has the same root cause as ringing.

Progressive JPEG: Baseline JPEG sends blocks in order from top to bottom. Progressive mode sends the image in several scans: first the DC and lowest frequencies of all blocks, giving a blurry full picture quickly, then more coefficients or more precision in later scans. On a slow connection the viewer sees the whole picture early and watches it sharpen. Progressive files are often a little smaller too. JPEG 2000, a later standard, uses wavelets instead of the DCT, which avoids blocking, but it never replaced classic JPEG on the web; newer formats are compared in lesson 13.

Real-life example 1, an online admission form: Many Bangladeshi university and job application portals ask for a passport photo under a size limit such as a few hundred kilobytes, often at a fixed pixel size. When you lower the JPEG quality in an editor until the file fits, you are scaling the quantization table up. Done sensibly, the face still looks fine, because the coarse steps hit high frequencies first. Done too aggressively, the background shows blocks, and the portal might reject a blurry photo.

Real-life example 2, a newspaper photo desk: A Dhaka newspaper receives photos from reporters, crops and corrects them, and publishes them on the web. A good desk keeps the camera originals and exports a JPEG once at the right size, instead of opening and re-saving the same JPEG after every edit. Each re-save quantizes again and adds new errors, the generation loss from lesson 10, which matters even more when the image is also resized between saves.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Students often forget the level shift, quantize with the wrong table entry, or read the zigzag in row order. Another error is coding DC values directly instead of as differences. Some think a higher quality number means a bigger quantization step; it is the opposite. Typical exam questions: draw the JPEG encoder and decoder block diagrams, quantize a given DCT block with a given table, write the zigzag sequence and the (run, value) pairs with EOB, explain DC differential coding, explain blocking and ringing, and compare baseline and progressive modes.

Recap: JPEG is an assembly line: colour convert and subsample, 8x8 blocks, level shift, DCT, quantize, zigzag, DC differences, AC run-lengths, Huffman. Our ramp block's coefficients -32, -145.77 and -15.24 became -2, -13 and -1 with steps 16, 11 and 16; the AC part coded as (0, -13), (4, -1), EOB; and decoding brought every pixel back within 1. Quality settings scale the quantization table. Blocking, ringing and colour bleeding all trace back to specific stations. Next we compare JPEG with GIF, PNG, WebP and friends.
key_points: JPEG pipeline: Y'CbCr and subsampling, 8x8 blocks, level shift -128, DCT, quantization, zigzag, DC differences, AC run-lengths, Huffman.
Only quantization (and chroma subsampling) loses information; quantization uses Fq = round(F / Q).
Example luma table top row: 16, 11, 10, 16, 24, 40, 51, 61; steps grow towards high frequencies.
Worked ramp block: -32/16 = -2, -145.77/11 gives -13, -15.24/16 gives -1; the rest round to 0.
Zigzag puts high-frequency zeros at the end; AC coded as (0,-13), (4,-1), EOB; DC sent as a difference.
Decoded row 97, 104, 113, 121, 127, 135, 144, 151 versus original 96..152: error at most 1.
Quality setting scales the table (IJG: quality 75 gives DC step 8); blocking and ringing come from coarse quantization.
lessons.tip: Practise one full block by hand, from quantization to (run, value) pairs with EOB, until you can do it in ten minutes. Exams love it, and drawing the zigzag path on the grid first prevents most order mistakes.
lessons.task: Draw an 8x8 grid and number the zigzag order from 0 to 63. Then quantize these DCT values with the steps given: DC -80 (step 16), F(0,1) 30 (step 11), F(1,0) -24 (step 12), everything else 0. Write the zigzag list and the (run, value) pairs with EOB.

quiz.q: In the worked block, F(0,1) = -145.77 with step 11. What is the quantized value?
Why does JPEG read quantized coefficients in zigzag order?
options: To make decoding faster on GPUs
Because the DCT outputs them that way
So low frequencies come first and high-frequency zeros bunch at the end for run-length coding
quiz.explain: Zigzag groups the many trailing zeros so a single EOB can replace them.

quiz.q: The AC list is -13, 0, 0, 0, 0, -1, then all zeros. How is it run-length coded?
quiz.explain: Each pair is (number of zeros before, value): no zeros then -13, four zeros then -1, then EOB for the rest.

quiz.q: How does baseline JPEG code the DC coefficient of each block?
options: As the difference from the previous block's DC, then entropy-coded
It is not stored; the decoder guesses it
Together with the AC run-lengths as a (run, value) pair
quiz.explain: DC values of neighbouring blocks are similar, so their differences are small and cheap to code.

quiz.q: Which artefact appears as a visible grid in smooth areas at low JPEG quality?
quiz.explain: Each 8x8 block is quantized independently, so at coarse steps neighbouring blocks no longer match at the edges.

lessons.title: Image Formats Compared: BMP, GIF, PNG, JPEG, WebP and More
lessons.content:
Walk into a hardware shop in Old Dhaka and ask for "a screw". The shopkeeper will ask: for wood or metal, how long, what head? There is no single best screw, only the right screw for the job. Image formats are the same. A photo of your cousin's wedding, a screenshot of a bKash transaction, a university logo and a funny animated sticker each want a different format. Use the wrong one and you get a blurry receipt, a huge file, or a logo with an ugly box around it. In this lesson we line up the main formats, see what each one stores and how it compresses, and build a simple decision rule.

The questions to ask of any format: Is it lossless or lossy? How many colours can it hold: a palette of at most 256, or full true colour? Does it support transparency, and is that on/off (1-bit) or smooth (a full alpha channel)? Does it support animation? Is it raster or vector? And how widely is it supported by browsers, phones and software? Every format below is just a different set of answers to these questions, built from the tools of lessons 07 to 12.

Transparency and alpha, first: An alpha channel stores, for each pixel, how opaque it is, from 0 (fully transparent) to 255 (fully opaque) in 8 bits. Displaying it over a background uses the blend out = alpha x foreground + (1 - alpha) x background. Worked: a pixel with value 200 at alpha 0.5 over a background of 100 shows 0.5 x 200 + 0.5 x 100 = 150. With alpha, a 1920 x 1080 RGBA image costs 4 bytes per pixel raw, 8,294,400 bytes. One-bit transparency is cruder: a pixel is either fully shown or fully hidden, so curved edges look jagged over a coloured background.

BMP, the raw baseline: The Windows bitmap format usually stores pixels uncompressed, row by row, with each row padded to a multiple of 4 bytes. A 1920 x 1080 true-colour BMP is therefore about 6.2 MB, the same as our raw calculation in lesson 03. An optional simple run-length mode exists for palette images, but it is rarely used. BMP is easy to read and write, which makes it handy for teaching and for quick programs, but it is wasteful for storage or the web.
