GIF, palette plus LZW: GIF (Graphics Interchange Format) dates from 1987, with the 1989 version adding animation and transparency. Each frame uses a palette of at most 256 colours, so each pixel is just an index, coded with LZW from lesson 08. One palette entry can be marked transparent, giving 1-bit transparency. GIF also allows several frames with delays, which is why it became the format of short looping animations. Its limits: 256 colours make photos look grainy or banded (encoders use dithering, scattering dots of palette colours to fake in-between shades), and animated GIFs are very large compared with real video.

Palette arithmetic: A palette image stores a small colour table plus small indices. A 640 x 480 image with 256 colours needs 640 x 480 = 307,200 bytes of 8-bit indices, plus a palette of 256 x 3 = 768 bytes. A logo of 500 x 500 pixels with only 4 colours needs just 2 bits per pixel: 500 x 500 x 2 / 8 = 62,500 bytes of indices, against 750,000 bytes as 24-bit true colour, even before LZW or DEFLATE compress the indices further. Few colours, big savings.

Dithering, faking colours you do not have: Suppose a palette has only pure black (0) and pure white (255), and a region should be mid-grey 128. Rounding each pixel to the nearest palette colour turns the whole region one flat colour, losing the grey completely. Dithering instead mixes the available colours in a fine pattern, roughly half black and half white dots, so from a normal viewing distance the eye averages them into grey. Error-diffusion methods such as Floyd-Steinberg push each pixel's rounding error onto its not-yet-processed neighbours, so the average colour over a small area stays right. Dithering makes GIF photos look better, but the dot pattern is noisy, which also hurts LZW compression.

PNG, lossless for everything else: PNG (Portable Network Graphics) appeared in the mid-1990s, partly as a patent-free replacement for GIF. It is always lossless. It supports palette images, grayscale and true colour (8 or 16 bits per channel), and a full alpha channel. Compression is two-stage: each row is filtered with one of five predictors from lesson 09 (None, Sub, Up, Average, Paeth), then the result is compressed with DEFLATE from lesson 08. PNG is ideal for screenshots, diagrams, text, user interface graphics and anything with sharp edges and flat colours. Original PNG has no animation; an extension called APNG adds it and is supported by modern browsers.

JPEG, the photo workhorse: From lesson 12: lossy, DCT-based, 8 bits per channel in its common form, excellent for photographs, with a quality knob. It has no transparency at all. It is bad at sharp text and line art, where ringing appears, and every re-save adds generation loss. Its giant advantage is that literally every device, browser and program reads it.

WebP, one format for many jobs: WebP was introduced by Google around 2010. Its lossy mode is based on the intra-frame coding of the VP8 video codec: it predicts each block from its neighbours and transforms the residual, rather than coding blocks independently like JPEG. Its lossless mode uses different tricks, including prediction and a colour cache. WebP supports full alpha in both modes and also animation. Google's own studies reported lossy WebP files roughly a quarter to a third smaller than JPEG at similar measured quality; results vary by image. All major browsers now support it, and WhatsApp stickers, for example, are WebP images.

AVIF and HEIC, video codecs inside images: A newer idea is to take the intra-frame (still picture) coding of a modern video codec and wrap it as an image format. AVIF uses AV1 from the Alliance for Open Media; HEIC, inside the HEIF container, uses H.265/HEVC and became the default photo format on iPhones from 2017. Both usually beat JPEG at the same visual quality and support features like higher bit depth and alpha, at the cost of slower encoding and, for HEIC, patchier support on non-Apple systems. JPEG XL is another modern standard designed as a JPEG successor, with the trick of losslessly re-compressing existing JPEG files; its browser support has been uneven, so treat it as one to watch.

Interlacing and bit depth: Both GIF and PNG can store an image interlaced, so a browser can show a coarse full picture early and refine it, much like progressive JPEG. GIF uses four passes over the rows; PNG uses a seven-pass scheme called Adam7 that also spreads pixels across columns. Interlacing usually makes the file a little larger, so it is a trade between early preview and size. Bit depth also differs: JPEG in its common form is 8 bits per channel, PNG can go to 16, and AVIF and HEIC support 10 and 12 bits, which matters for smooth gradients and high dynamic range photos where 8 bits can show visible banding.

SVG, not pixels at all: SVG (Scalable Vector Graphics) is an XML text format that describes shapes, paths, text and colours, as in the vector graphics of the Computer Graphics course. It scales to any size without blur, is often tiny for logos and icons, can be styled with CSS and animated, and compresses well with gzip because it is text. It is a poor fit for photographs, which have no simple shape description. Because SVG can contain scripts, websites that accept user-uploaded SVGs must sanitise them.

Metadata and privacy: Camera JPEGs (and HEIC files) usually carry Exif metadata: camera model, exposure settings, date and time, orientation, and, if location is enabled, GPS coordinates. A photo of your house posted on a site that keeps Exif can reveal where you live. Many social platforms strip location data on upload, but not every site or messaging path does, so the safe habit is to check or remove it yourself. Metadata also helps legitimately: photographers and newsrooms use it to organise and verify images.

Choosing the right format, a simple rule: Photograph for the web: JPEG at a sensible quality, or WebP/AVIF if your platform supports them. Screenshot, chart, diagram, scanned text or anything with sharp edges: PNG (or lossless WebP). Logo or icon: SVG if possible, otherwise PNG with alpha. Short animation or sticker: animated WebP, or real video (MP4) for anything longer than a few seconds; avoid big GIFs. Archive master you will edit again: a lossless format (PNG, TIFF or the camera's RAW). Need maximum compatibility, such as an old government portal: JPEG or PNG.

Real-life example 1, a bKash receipt screenshot: You take a screenshot of a payment confirmation to send to a shop owner. Saved as PNG, the text stays razor sharp, and because the screen has large flat areas, DEFLATE compresses it well. If an app converts it to a low-quality JPEG, the small digits of the transaction ID get ringing and blur, and an 8 can start to look like a 3. For text, lossless wins, even though a photo of the same pixel size would be smaller as JPEG.

Real-life example 2, an e-commerce shop on Facebook and the web: A small business in Chattogram selling handmade nakshi kantha posts product photos. Large JPEG or WebP photos keep the page light for customers on mobile data. The shop's logo goes on the website as SVG so it looks crisp on every screen, and a PNG or WebP version with a transparent background is used where SVG is not accepted. A "Sale" badge with a soft shadow needs a full alpha channel, so GIF's on/off transparency would leave jagged edges.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Saving screenshots as JPEG, saving photos as PNG (lossless but often several times larger), using huge GIFs for video clips, and expecting JPEG to keep a transparent background are the usual blunders. Students also confuse lossless with uncompressed: PNG is lossless yet compressed. Typical exam questions: compare GIF, PNG and JPEG on colours, compression, transparency and animation; explain why PNG replaced GIF; compute raw and palette sizes; explain alpha blending; and recommend a format for a given scenario with reasons.

Recap: BMP is raw; GIF is a 256-colour palette with LZW, 1-bit transparency and animation; PNG is lossless with filters plus DEFLATE and full alpha; JPEG is lossy DCT for photos without alpha; WebP covers lossy, lossless, alpha and animation; AVIF and HEIC borrow video codecs for stills; SVG is vector. Palettes save space (4 colours need 2 bits per pixel), alpha blending is alpha x fg + (1 - alpha) x bg, dithering fakes missing colours with dot patterns, interlacing trades a little size for an early preview, and Exif can leak location. Pick formats by content: photos lossy, text and graphics lossless, logos vector. Next we leave images for sound and learn how MP3 and AAC fool the ear.
key_points: Ask of every format: lossless or lossy, palette or true colour, transparency type, animation, raster or vector, support.
Alpha blend: out = alpha x fg + (1 - alpha) x bg; 200 at alpha 0.5 over 100 gives 150; RGBA 1080p raw is 8,294,400 bytes.
BMP is usually raw; GIF uses a 256-colour palette, LZW, 1-bit transparency and animation.
Palette saving: a 4-colour 500x500 logo needs 62,500 bytes of indices versus 750,000 bytes in 24-bit.
PNG is lossless (filters plus DEFLATE) with full alpha, best for screenshots, text and graphics.
JPEG is lossy DCT for photos with no alpha; WebP covers lossy, lossless, alpha and animation; AVIF/HEIC reuse AV1/HEVC.
SVG is vector XML for logos and icons; Exif metadata can reveal camera details and GPS location.
lessons.tip: Make a one-page comparison table with formats as rows and the six questions as columns. Fill it from memory, then check it against this lesson. That single table answers most exam questions on formats.
lessons.task: Take one screenshot with text and one camera photo on your phone or PC. Save each as both PNG and JPEG (any free editor or an online converter you trust), compare the file sizes, and zoom in on the text. Then check the photo's details or properties to see what Exif metadata, including location, it carries.

quiz.q: Which format is the best fit for a screenshot full of small text?
quiz.explain: PNG is lossless, so text stays sharp, and DEFLATE compresses flat screen areas well.

quiz.q: What does GIF's transparency support?
options: Only on/off transparency through one transparent palette entry
quiz.explain: GIF marks one palette index as transparent: each pixel is fully shown or fully hidden.

quiz.q: How many bytes of indices does a 500 x 500 logo with only 4 colours need, before compression?
quiz.explain: 4 colours need 2 bits per pixel: 500 x 500 x 2 / 8 = 62,500 bytes.

quiz.q: A pixel of value 200 with alpha 0.5 is drawn over a background of 100. What is shown?
Which statement about WebP is correct?
options: It supports lossy and lossless modes, alpha and animation
It is only readable on Apple devices
quiz.explain: WebP offers lossy (VP8-style) and lossless modes, both with alpha, plus animation.

lessons.title: Psychoacoustics and Audio Compression: How MP3 and AAC Hide the Missing Bits
lessons.content:
Picture a wedding in Dhaka. The band is playing at full blast, the drums are booming, and your cousin whispers something in your ear. You see her lips move, but you hear nothing. Her whisper still reached your ear as a real pressure wave; your brain simply could not notice it under the loud music. That everyday moment is the secret behind MP3, AAC and almost every music file on your phone. If the listener cannot hear a sound anyway, why spend bits storing it? This lesson explains the science of what we can and cannot hear, called psychoacoustics, and how audio coders use it to shrink music by around ten times while most people hear no difference.

Where we are: In lesson 05 we computed that CD-quality audio (44,100 samples per second, 16 bits, 2 channels) needs 1,411,200 bits per second, so a 3-minute song is 31,752,000 bytes. In lessons 06 to 09 we met lossless tricks such as Huffman and LZW, but on real music those only save a modest amount because audio samples look noisy. In lesson 10 we learned the lossy idea: throw away what matters least. Here we answer the key question for audio: what exactly matters least to a human ear?

What psychoacoustics is: Psychoacoustics is the study of how humans perceive sound, as opposed to how sound physically is. A microphone measures pressure faithfully. The ear and brain do not. They are very sensitive to some frequencies and nearly deaf to others, a loud sound hides quieter sounds near it, and loud events even hide sounds that happen a moment before or after them. An audio coder that models these effects is called a perceptual coder.

The absolute threshold of hearing: The first fact is that the ear needs a minimum loudness before it hears anything, and this minimum depends on frequency. We hear roughly from 20 Hz to 20 kHz (the upper limit falls with age). We are most sensitive somewhere around 2 to 5 kHz, which is where speech consonants and a baby's cry live. At very low frequencies like 30 Hz, or very high ones like 16 kHz, a tone must be much louder before we notice it. If you plot this minimum level against frequency you get a U-shaped curve called the threshold in quiet. Anything below that curve can be deleted completely, because nobody can hear it even in a silent room.

Frequency masking: The second, and most powerful, fact is masking. A loud tone raises the threshold for other sounds near its frequency. Imagine a strong 1 kHz tone. A quiet tone at 1.1 kHz that would normally be audible becomes inaudible while the loud one is playing. The raised threshold around the loud tone is called the masking threshold, and it is shaped like a tent: highest at the masker's frequency and sloping down on both sides. It slopes down more slowly on the high side, so loud low sounds mask higher sounds more easily than the other way round. This is called the upward spread of masking.

Critical bands: Why does masking work only near the masker? Inside the inner ear, the cochlea acts like a bank of overlapping band-pass filters. Each region of it responds to a range of frequencies called a critical band. Sounds inside the same critical band compete strongly; sounds in far-apart bands barely affect each other. Critical bands are narrow at low frequencies (roughly 100 Hz wide below about 500 Hz) and grow wider at higher frequencies, roughly a fifth of the centre frequency. The hearing range splits into about 24 such bands, and a scale that counts them is called the Bark scale.

Temporal masking: Masking also happens in time. After a loud sound stops, the ear stays less sensitive for a short while, typically tens of milliseconds and up to roughly a hundred milliseconds or more for a strong sound; this is post-masking. Surprisingly, a loud sound can also hide a quiet sound that came slightly before it, by a few milliseconds; this is pre-masking. It happens because the brain takes time to process the quiet sound, and the loud one overtakes it. Coders use this around sudden attacks like a drum hit.

Turning masking into bits: Here is the key link to quantization from the DSP course. When we quantize a signal coarsely, we add quantization noise; each extra bit lowers the noise by about 6 dB. A perceptual coder does not try to make the noise tiny everywhere. It only keeps the noise in each frequency band below the masking threshold of that band. If the threshold is high (a loud instrument nearby), the band can be quantized with few bits, and the extra noise stays hidden. If a band has a low threshold, it needs more bits. Bands where everything is below the threshold get zero bits.

Signal-to-mask ratio: For each band the coder computes the signal-to-mask ratio, SMR, the band's signal level minus the masking threshold in dB. Suppose a band's signal is at 60 dB and the masking threshold there is 42 dB, so SMR = 18 dB. Using the 6 dB per bit rule of thumb, about 3 bits per sample in that band keep the quantization noise roughly 18 dB below the signal, which puts it near or below the mask. A band with SMR of 0 dB or less needs no bits at all. Real coders refine this a lot, but that is the core arithmetic.

The perceptual coder block diagram: Almost every perceptual audio coder has four boxes. First, a filter bank splits the audio into many frequency bands, or a transform such as the MDCT (modified discrete cosine transform, a cousin of the DCT from lesson 11) turns each short block of samples into frequency coefficients. Second, in parallel, a psychoacoustic model analyses the same audio, often with an FFT, and computes the masking threshold for each band. Third, bit allocation and quantization decide how coarsely to quantize each band so the noise stays under the mask while meeting the target bit rate. Fourth, the quantized values and side information are entropy coded and packed into a bitstream. The decoder is much simpler: it unpacks, rescales and runs the inverse transform. It does not need the psychoacoustic model at all.

MP3: MP3 is the popular name of MPEG-1 Audio Layer III (also extended in MPEG-2). It uses a hybrid filter bank: a 32-band polyphase filter bank followed by an MDCT on each band, which gives finer frequency resolution. It works on frames of 1,152 samples, which at 44.1 kHz is about 26.1 ms of sound. After quantization it uses Huffman coding, our friend from lesson 07. MP3 also has a bit reservoir, letting an easy frame donate unused bits to a later hard frame, and joint stereo, which codes the left and right channels as a sum (mid) and difference (side) when they are similar, because the difference often needs very few bits.

Worked bit rate comparison: A common MP3 setting is 128 kbps. The CD stream is 1,411.2 kbps, so the compression ratio is 1,411.2 / 128 = about 11.0 to 1. Our 3-minute song shrinks from 31,752,000 bytes to 128,000 x 180 / 8 = 2,880,000 bytes, roughly 2.9 MB. At 128 kbps and 44.1 kHz each 1,152-sample frame takes about 418 bytes. For many listeners on phone earphones, a well-encoded 128 kbps file sounds close to the CD; trained listeners on good equipment can often tell, which is why 192 or 256 kbps is popular for music libraries.

AAC: Advanced Audio Coding was designed as the successor to MP3 and is part of the MPEG-2 and MPEG-4 standards. It uses a pure MDCT with switchable block lengths (long blocks for steady tones, short blocks for sharp attacks to avoid pre-echo), more flexible tools and better entropy coding. In listening tests it generally gives better quality than MP3 at the same bit rate. It is the usual audio track inside MP4 videos, so most streaming and video apps use it. Low-bit-rate versions such as HE-AAC add a trick called spectral band replication: the coder sends the low frequencies carefully and only a small description of the high frequencies, which the decoder rebuilds.

Pre-echo, the typical artefact: Because a transform codes a whole block at once, quantization noise spreads across the whole block in time. If a block contains silence followed by a sudden castanet click, the noise can appear just before the click, as a smeared hiss called pre-echo. Pre-masking hides only a few milliseconds, so coders switch to short blocks around attacks. Other artefacts at very low bit rates are a watery, swirly sound (sometimes called birdies) and missing high frequencies.

Speech codecs and Opus: Voice calls have different needs: low delay and very low bit rates. Classic telephone audio uses G.711 at 64 kbps (8,000 samples per second, 8 bits each, with mu-law or A-law companding). Mobile networks use speech codecs such as AMR, which models the human vocal tract instead of general sound and works at around 4.75 to 12.2 kbps in its narrowband form, and newer codecs such as EVS for voice over LTE. Opus, an open IETF standard, combines a speech-oriented mode and a music-oriented mode, works at low delay, and is used in WebRTC and many internet calling apps. At 64 kbps a 3-minute stream is 1,440,000 bytes, half of our 128 kbps MP3.

Lossless audio: Sometimes you must not lose anything, for archiving recordings or professional editing. FLAC (Free Lossless Audio Codec) predicts each sample from previous ones and stores only the small prediction error with efficient codes, the predictive coding idea from lesson 09. Typical music shrinks to something like half to two thirds of the original size, depending on the music; it never matches the ten-to-one of lossy coders, because noise-like parts of music are hard to predict. ALAC (Apple Lossless) works similarly.

Real-life example 1, a Bangla song on a budget phone: Suppose you want to keep 500 songs of 4 minutes each on a phone with limited storage. As uncompressed CD audio each song is 1,411,200 x 240 / 8 = 42,336,000 bytes, so 500 songs need about 21 GB. At 128 kbps each song is 3,840,000 bytes and 500 songs need about 1.9 GB. That difference is why MP3 made portable music possible, and why streaming apps can play music over a mobile data connection in rural Bangladesh.

Real-life example 2, a voice message on a messaging app: When you send a voice note to your family abroad, the app records your voice, then encodes it with a speech-friendly codec at a low bit rate. Background silence and tiny sounds under the threshold are coded with almost no bits. A one-minute note might be only a few hundred kilobytes instead of several megabytes, so it goes through even on a weak 3G signal. Your mother still recognises your voice instantly, because the parts that carry identity and meaning are kept.

Common mistakes: First, thinking MP3 deletes high frequencies only. It removes or coarsens whatever falls under the masking threshold, at any frequency, and it may low-pass at low bit rates only as an extra measure. Second, thinking re-encoding to a higher bit rate restores quality. Converting a 128 kbps MP3 to 320 kbps just makes a bigger file with the same losses; this is generation loss from lesson 10. Third, confusing lossless (FLAC) with high bit rate lossy (320 kbps MP3); they are fundamentally different. Fourth, forgetting that the psychoacoustic model lives only in the encoder, so different encoders produce different quality at the same bit rate.

What exams ask: Define frequency and temporal masking with a sketch of the masking tent. Draw the perceptual coder block diagram and explain each box. Explain critical bands and the Bark scale. Compute compression ratios such as 1,411.2 to 128 kbps. Explain SMR and bit allocation, and why the decoder is simpler than the encoder. Compare MP3, AAC and a speech codec, and name pre-echo and its cure.

Recap: The ear is not a microphone. It has a frequency-dependent threshold, it masks quiet sounds near loud ones in frequency and in time, and it groups frequencies into critical bands. A perceptual coder splits sound into bands, estimates the masking threshold, and quantizes each band just coarsely enough that the noise hides under the mask, then entropy codes the result. That is how MP3 and AAC reach roughly 11 to 1 at 128 kbps, while speech codecs go even lower, and FLAC keeps everything at a smaller ratio. Next lesson we leave sound and start on video, the biggest medium of all.
key_points: Psychoacoustics studies how we perceive sound; perceptual coders delete or coarsen what the ear cannot notice.
Threshold in quiet: hearing roughly 20 Hz-20 kHz, most sensitive around 2-5 kHz; sounds below the curve can be dropped.
Frequency masking: a loud sound raises the threshold for nearby frequencies, more on the high side (upward spread).
Critical bands (about 24, Bark scale) are narrow at low frequencies and wider at high ones; temporal masking acts before (ms) and after (tens of ms) loud sounds.
Coder = filter bank/MDCT + psychoacoustic model + bit allocation by signal-to-mask ratio + entropy coding; the decoder needs no model.
MP3: hybrid filter bank, 1,152-sample frames, Huffman, bit reservoir, joint stereo; AAC: pure MDCT, block switching, generally better at the same rate.
128 kbps vs 1,411.2 kbps is about 11:1; a 3-minute song drops from 31,752,000 to 2,880,000 bytes.
Speech codecs (G.711 64 kbps, AMR, EVS) and Opus target low delay; FLAC is lossless and typically about half to two thirds of the size.
lessons.tip: Always draw the masking tent when explaining audio compression. One picture of a loud tone with a sloping threshold and a hidden quiet tone explains frequency masking, SMR and bit allocation all at once.
lessons.task: Open any music app or file manager and find one song's size and length. Compute its average bit rate as size x 8 / seconds. Then compute what the same song would weigh as CD audio (1,411,200 bps) and write the compression ratio. Repeat for a voice note from a messaging app.

quiz.q: What is frequency masking?
options: A loud sound making quieter sounds at nearby frequencies inaudible
quiz.explain: A loud masker raises the hearing threshold around its own frequency, so nearby quieter sounds are not heard.

quiz.q: Which box of a perceptual audio coder is NOT needed in the decoder?
quiz.explain: The encoder uses the psychoacoustic model to decide bit allocation; the decoder just follows the stored decisions.

quiz.q: CD audio is 1,411.2 kbps. Coded at 128 kbps, the compression ratio is about:
A band has signal level 60 dB and masking threshold 42 dB. Using about 6 dB per bit, roughly how many bits per sample does it need?
quiz.explain: SMR = 60 - 42 = 18 dB, and 18 / 6 = 3 bits keeps the noise near or under the mask.

quiz.q: What is pre-echo?
options: An echo added on purpose for stereo
Quantization noise smeared before a sudden attack inside a transform block
The delay of a satellite call
quiz.explain: Noise spreads across the whole transform block, so it can be heard just before a sharp attack; short blocks fix it.

lessons.title: Video Basics: Frames, Frame Rates, Interlacing and the Raw Bit Rate Problem
lessons.content:
Take a small notebook and draw a stick figure on the corner of every page, moving its arm a little each time. Now flip the pages quickly with your thumb. The figure waves. Nothing on any single page moves, yet your brain sees motion. That flipbook is exactly what video is: a fast sequence of still images. Everything in this lesson, from frame rates to interlacing to resolutions, is just the details of how many pages, how big each page is, and how fast we flip. At the end we will also see why storing all those pages raw is impossible in practice, which sets up the next three lessons on video compression.

What video is: A digital video is a sequence of digital images called frames, shown one after another at a fixed rate, usually with one or more synchronised audio tracks. Each frame is an image exactly like those in lesson 03: a grid of pixels with some bit depth, usually stored in Y'CbCr with chroma subsampling as in lesson 04. So all our image knowledge carries over. The new dimension is time, and with time comes a new kind of redundancy: neighbouring frames are usually almost identical.

Why a sequence looks like motion: When images change fast enough, the visual system blends them into smooth movement. This is often loosely called persistence of vision; vision scientists describe it in terms of apparent motion and how the brain integrates what it sees over time, but the practical rule is simple: below roughly 10 to 12 images per second we see separate pictures, and above that we start to see motion, which becomes smoother as the rate rises. Flicker is a separate issue: a display that flashes too few times per second looks like it is flickering even when the motion looks fine, which is why cinema projectors traditionally flashed each frame two or three times.

Frame rate: Frame rate is measured in frames per second, fps. Common values are 24 fps for cinema, 25 fps in countries with 50 Hz electricity and PAL television history (including Bangladesh), and 30 fps (strictly 29.97 for the old NTSC colour system) in countries with 60 Hz electricity. Sports, games and phone slow-motion use 50, 60 or higher. A higher frame rate gives smoother motion and less blur in fast action, but every extra frame is another full image to store and send. Going from 30 to 60 fps doubles the raw data.

Frame time: The time each frame stays on screen is 1 / fps. At 25 fps each frame lasts 40 ms; at 30 fps about 33.3 ms; at 60 fps about 16.7 ms. This number matters for games and video calls: if your phone needs more than 33 ms to decode or draw a frame of a 30 fps video, frames will be dropped and the video stutters.

Progressive scan: In progressive video every frame contains all the lines of the picture, drawn top to bottom. The p in 720p and 1080p means progressive. Computer screens, phones and almost all internet video are progressive.

Interlaced scan: Old analogue television had a bandwidth problem. Sending 50 full pictures per second was too costly, but sending only 25 would flicker. The clever answer was interlacing: split each frame into two fields, one with the odd lines and one with the even lines, and send them alternately. PAL sent 50 fields per second, which made 25 full frames. The eye saw 50 updates per second, so flicker was low, while the bandwidth was that of 25 frames. The i in 1080i means interlaced.

The cost of interlacing: The two fields are captured at different moments, 20 ms apart in PAL. For a still scene that does not matter. For fast motion, say a cricket ball, the odd lines show the ball in one place and the even lines show it slightly further along. On a progressive screen that gives a comb-like zig-zag on moving edges, called combing. Modern players run a deinterlacing filter to rebuild full frames, either by blending fields, by doubling lines, or by smarter motion-adaptive methods. Interlacing also makes compression harder, which is one reason internet video is progressive.

Resolution: Resolution is frame width x height in pixels. Standard definition (SD) in PAL regions is 720 x 576, and in NTSC regions 720 x 480. HD is 1280 x 720 (720p). Full HD is 1920 x 1080 (1080p). 4K UHD, used by TVs and streaming, is 3840 x 2160, four times as many pixels as 1080p; cinema 4K is slightly wider at 4096 x 2160. 8K UHD is 7680 x 4320. Online platforms also use small sizes such as 640 x 360 (360p) and 854 x 480 (480p) for mobile and slow connections, which will matter a lot in our capstone.

Aspect ratio: Aspect ratio is width divided by height. Old TV was 4:3, about 1.33. HD and later are 16:9, about 1.78; you can check that 1920 / 1080 = 1.777..., exactly 16/9. Cinema often uses wider ratios. Phone videos shot vertically are 9:16. When the video and the screen ratios differ, the player either adds black bars (letterboxing above and below, pillarboxing at the sides), crops, or stretches, and stretching makes people look fat or thin, so good players avoid it.

Bit depth and colour in video: Most consumer video uses 8 bits per sample in Y'CbCr with 4:2:0 subsampling, giving 12 bits per pixel on average (lesson 04). High dynamic range (HDR) video usually uses 10 bits per sample, so that bright highlights and dark shadows get enough steps without visible banding. Professional editing often keeps 4:2:2 or 4:4:4 to allow clean colour correction and green-screen keying.

Worked raw bit rate, 1080p30: Let us compute what a minute of uncompressed Full HD video costs. Pixels per frame = 1920 x 1080 = 2,073,600. With 4:2:0 at 8 bits we have 12 bits per pixel, so one frame is 2,073,600 x 12 = 24,883,200 bits = 3,110,400 bytes, about 3.1 MB. At 30 frames per second that is 24,883,200 x 30 = 746,496,000 bits per second, about 746 Mbps, or 93,312,000 bytes every second. One hour is 746,496,000 x 3,600 / 8 = about 336 GB.

Worked raw bit rates, other formats: The same formula, bit rate = width x height x bits per pixel x fps, gives: 720p30 in 4:2:0 is 1280 x 720 x 12 x 30 = 331,776,000 bps, about 332 Mbps. 360p30 is 640 x 360 x 12 x 30 = 82,944,000 bps, about 83 Mbps. PAL SD at 25 fps is 720 x 576 x 12 x 25 = 124,416,000 bps, about 56 GB per hour. 4K UHD at 30 fps is 3840 x 2160 x 12 x 30 = 2,985,984,000 bps, about 3 Gbps, and at 60 fps about 6 Gbps. If we did not subsample chroma and used full 24-bit RGB, 1080p30 would be 1,492,992,000 bps, double the 4:2:0 figure.

Why compression is mandatory: A typical good-quality 1080p stream on the internet runs at a few megabits per second. Taking 5 Mbps as an example, the compression ratio is 746,496,000 / 5,000,000 = about 149 to 1. For a 4K stream at around 15 Mbps it is about 199 to 1. Compare that with roughly 11 to 1 for MP3 audio. No lossless method gets anywhere near this; video compression depends on both lossy coding of each picture (lesson 12's ideas) and, above all, on exploiting the similarity between frames, which is the subject of lessons 16 and 17.

Analogue television history in one paragraph: Before digital broadcasting, the main colour TV systems were NTSC (North America, Japan, parts of South America), PAL (much of Europe, Asia including Bangladesh, India and Pakistan, Africa and Australia) and SECAM (France, the former Soviet Union and some others). PAL in its common form used 625 lines and 50 fields per second, matching the 50 Hz mains. That history is why digital SD in PAL regions is 720 x 576 at 25 fps, and why Bangladeshi TV channels and cameras sold here often default to 25 or 50 fps.

Shutter and motion blur: A camera does not capture an instant; each frame is exposed for a short time. A fast-moving rickshaw wheel smears across the frame during that time, giving motion blur. A little blur makes 24 or 25 fps look natural. Very short exposures make each frame sharp but motion looks jerky. This is why a video shot in bright sunlight with a phone sometimes looks oddly choppy: the phone picked a very short exposure.

Real-life example 1, a phone video of a family event: Your phone records a 2-minute clip at 1080p30. Raw, that would be 746,496,000 x 120 / 8 bytes, about 11.2 GB. The file in your gallery is maybe a couple of hundred megabytes, because the phone's hardware encoder compressed it on the fly (lesson 18 explains which codecs). If you switch the camera to 4K60, the raw rate is eight times larger and the compressed file also grows a lot, which is why storage fills up fast.

Real-life example 2, BPL cricket on TV and phone: A cricket broadcast is captured at high frame rates for slow-motion replays, often 50 fps or more in a 50 Hz country. Your TV may receive it as 1080i or 1080p, and the same match streamed to a phone may be delivered at 360p or 480p when the network is weak. The fast ball and bat movements are exactly the hard case for interlacing and for compression, which is why poor streams show smeared, blocky frames whenever the camera pans across the field.

Common mistakes: First, thinking 1080i and 1080p carry the same information per second; at the same field or frame rate, interlaced sends half the lines each time. Second, forgetting chroma subsampling in raw size calculations: 1080p raw at 30 fps is about 746 Mbps in 4:2:0, but 1,493 Mbps in 4:4:4. Third, mixing bits and bytes: always divide by 8 when going to bytes. Fourth, believing 4K means exactly 4,000 pixels wide; consumer 4K UHD is 3,840. Fifth, confusing frame rate with refresh rate: the display may refresh at 60 or 120 Hz while showing a 25 fps video by repeating frames.

What exams ask: Define frame rate, field, interlaced and progressive scan, and draw how odd and even fields combine. Compute raw bit rate and storage for a given resolution, frame rate and sampling format. List standard resolutions and aspect ratios. Explain why PAL used 25 frames and 50 fields per second. Explain why video must be compressed and estimate the ratio for a given streaming rate.

Recap: Video is a flipbook of frames shown at a fixed frame rate, with 24, 25, 30, 50 and 60 fps the common choices. Progressive frames hold all lines; interlaced video sends odd and even fields alternately, saving bandwidth but causing combing on motion. Resolution and aspect ratio describe frame size and shape, from 720 x 576 SD to 3840 x 2160 4K. Raw video is enormous: 1080p30 in 4:2:0 is 746,496,000 bps, about 336 GB per hour, so a 5 Mbps stream needs about 149 to 1 compression. Next lesson shows how codecs use the fact that frame after frame looks almost the same.
key_points: Video is a sequence of frames (images) shown at a fixed frame rate, usually with audio tracks.
Common frame rates: 24 (cinema), 25 (PAL regions like Bangladesh), 30/29.97 (NTSC regions), 50/60 for sport and games; frame time = 1/fps.
Progressive frames contain all lines; interlaced video sends odd and even fields alternately (PAL 50 fields = 25 frames), causing combing on motion.
Raw bit rate = width x height x bits per pixel x fps; 1080p30 4:2:0 8-bit = 746,496,000 bps, about 336 GB per hour.
4K30 raw is about 3 Gbps; 4:4:4 doubles the 4:2:0 figure.
A 5 Mbps 1080p stream implies about 149:1 compression, far beyond lossless methods, so inter-frame coding is essential.
lessons.tip: Memorise one anchor: 1080p30 4:2:0 raw is about 746 Mbps. Any other format can be scaled from it in your head: double for 60 fps, four times for 4K, about a third for 720p.
lessons.task: Record a 10-second video on your phone at its default setting. Check the file size and compute the average bit rate (size x 8 / 10). Then compute the raw 4:2:0 bit rate for the same resolution and frame rate and write the compression ratio your phone achieved.

quiz.q: What does the i in 1080i mean?
options: Interlaced: each frame is sent as two fields of odd and even lines
quiz.explain: 1080i is interlaced; 1080p is progressive with all lines in every frame.

quiz.q: Raw 1080p at 30 fps with 4:2:0 and 8 bits per sample is about:
How long does each frame last at 25 fps?
quiz.explain: Frame time = 1 / 25 s = 0.04 s = 40 ms.

quiz.q: Consumer 4K UHD resolution is:
quiz.explain: 4K UHD is 3840 x 2160, four times 1080p; 4096 x 2160 is cinema 4K.

quiz.q: Why did PAL television use 50 fields per second instead of 50 full frames?
options: To keep flicker low while using the bandwidth of only 25 frames
Because cameras could not record faster
Because the eye cannot see more than 25 images per second
quiz.explain: Two fields per frame give 50 updates per second for low flicker at half the bandwidth of 50 full frames.

lessons.title: Video Compression and Frame Types: I, P and B Frames, GOPs and Decode Order
lessons.content:
Think of a teacher dictating a long passage on the phone to a student in another district. On the first day she reads the whole page. On the second day the page is the same except for two words, so she says only: same as yesterday, but change line 4, word 3 to rice, and line 9, word 1 to river. The student writes everything correctly with a tiny phone call. Video compression works exactly like that. Most frames are almost the same as the frame before, so instead of sending every frame in full, the encoder sends one full picture now and then and, for the rest, only the differences. This lesson explains the frame types that make this possible and the surprising order in which they travel.

Two kinds of redundancy: In lesson 15 we found that raw 1080p30 needs about 746 Mbps, while streams use a few Mbps. Part of the saving is spatial redundancy: inside one frame, neighbouring pixels are similar, so we can use the JPEG-style tools from lessons 11 and 12 (block transform, quantization, entropy coding). The bigger part is temporal redundancy: consecutive frames, 33 or 40 ms apart, show almost the same scene. A newsreader on BTV moves her lips and eyes, but the studio, desk and background stay identical. Coding a frame by reference to other frames is called inter-frame coding, or inter coding; coding it on its own is intra coding.

Intra coding: An intra-coded frame uses only information from inside itself. It is basically a still image compressed much like JPEG. Modern codecs add intra prediction: a block is predicted from already decoded pixels to its left and above, say by copying the row above downwards, and only the error is coded. Intra coding is robust, because it depends on nothing else, but it is expensive in bits.

I-frames: An I-frame (intra frame) is coded entirely with intra coding. A decoder can start decoding at an I-frame without any earlier data, so I-frames are the entry points of a stream. They are also called keyframes in many tools. Their cost is size: an I-frame is typically several times larger than the frames around it.

P-frames: A P-frame (predicted frame) is coded by predicting each block from an earlier reference frame, usually the previous I- or P-frame. For each block the encoder finds the best matching area in the reference (that search is lesson 17), records a motion vector saying where it came from, subtracts the prediction from the real block, and codes only the small difference, called the residual. If the background did not move, the residual is close to zero and costs almost nothing. P-frames are typically much smaller than I-frames.

B-frames: A B-frame (bi-directionally predicted frame) may predict each block from a past reference, from a future reference, or from an average of both. Why look at the future? Imagine a door opening. Behind the door appears a wall that was hidden in all earlier frames, so the past cannot predict it, but the next reference frame already shows it. Averaging two predictions also cancels some noise. B-frames are usually the smallest frames. In older standards such as MPEG-2, B-frames were never used as references for other frames; newer standards such as H.264 and later allow B-frames to serve as references too, in what are called hierarchical structures.

The residual: Whatever the prediction, the encoder codes the residual exactly like an image block: transform (an integer DCT-like transform in modern codecs), quantize, entropy code. The decoder does the reverse and adds the decoded residual to the same prediction to rebuild the block. Because the encoder must produce the same prediction as the decoder, it actually runs a decoder inside itself and predicts from the decoded (slightly lossy) reference frames, not the original frames; otherwise small errors would pile up, a problem called drift.

Macroblocks: Predictions and residuals are handled per block. In MPEG-2 and H.264 the basic unit is the macroblock: 16 x 16 luma pixels plus the matching chroma blocks, which in 4:2:0 are two 8 x 8 blocks (Cb and Cr). A 1920 x 1080 frame is coded as 120 x 68 macroblocks (the height is padded to 1088). Each macroblock in a P- or B-frame can choose its own mode: intra, predicted from the past, from the future, both, or even skipped entirely, which means copy the prediction with no residual. Later codecs replace the fixed macroblock with flexible, larger block trees (lesson 18).

The group of pictures: Frames are organised into a repeating pattern called a group of pictures, GOP. A classic MPEG-2 GOP is I B B P B B P B B P B B, then the next I. Two numbers describe it: N, the distance between I-frames (here 12), and M, the distance between anchor frames I or P (here 3). With 25 fps and N = 12 there is an I-frame roughly every half second. Streaming services commonly use a keyframe every couple of seconds, so that segments can start with one (lesson 21).

Worked size example: Let us use illustrative sizes, not real measurements: I-frame 100 KB, P-frame 30 KB, B-frame 10 KB. The 12-frame GOP above has 1 I, 3 P and 8 B frames, so it costs 100 + 3 x 30 + 8 x 10 = 270 KB, an average of 22.5 KB per frame. If every frame were an I-frame, the average would be 100 KB, about 4.4 times more. At 30 fps the GOP version needs 22.5 x 30 x 8 = 5,400 kilobits per second, about 5.4 Mbps, which is in the typical range for 1080p.

Display order vs decode order: Here is the surprising part. A B-frame needs the future reference before it can be decoded. Take display order I1 B2 B3 P4 B5 B6 P7. B2 and B3 need both I1 and P4, so P4 must arrive first. The encoder therefore sends in decode order: I1 P4 B2 B3 P7 B5 B6. The decoder decodes P4 early, keeps it in memory, decodes B2 and B3, shows them, and then shows P4. That is why every frame carries two timestamps in the container: a decode timestamp and a presentation timestamp (lesson 19).

The price of B-frames: Reordering means the encoder must wait for future frames before coding the B-frames, and the decoder must hold extra frames in memory. That adds delay, a few frame times. For a movie that does not matter. For a video call it does, so real-time conferencing encoders often use only I- and P-frames, or a low-delay structure with no future references. B-frames also make encoding slower, since more prediction options must be tested.

Random access and seeking: When you drag the slider in a video player to minute 12, the player cannot start decoding at an arbitrary P- or B-frame, because their references are missing. It must find the nearest I-frame before that point and decode forward from there. A long GOP saves bits but makes seeking slower and coarser; a short GOP makes seeking snappy but costs bits. Some codecs also define special keyframes that fully reset the decoder's references, such as the IDR frame in H.264, so that nothing after them can refer to anything before them.

Open and closed GOPs: In a closed GOP, no frame refers to anything outside its own GOP, so each GOP can be decoded alone, which is useful for editing and for streaming segments. In an open GOP, the B-frames at the start of a GOP may refer to the last P-frame of the previous GOP; it saves a little bit rate but complicates cutting and switching.

Error propagation: Prediction is a chain. If a packet is lost and part of a P-frame is wrong, every later frame that predicts from it inherits the error, and the damage drifts and smears as motion vectors carry it around. That is the familiar green or grey blocky trail in a broken stream. The chain is cut only at the next I-frame (or by intra-coded blocks inserted gradually, called intra refresh). This is another reason to insert I-frames regularly, and why conferencing systems ask the sender for a new keyframe after heavy loss.

Scene changes: At a cut from one scene to another, the previous frame is useless as a reference. A good encoder detects the cut and inserts an I-frame there, even off the regular GOP pattern; otherwise it would waste bits coding a whole new picture as a giant residual. This is called scene-cut detection.

Rate control: Frame sizes vary wildly, so the encoder needs a policy for how many bits to spend. With constant bit rate (CBR) it adjusts the quantization step frame by frame to keep the output near a fixed rate, which suits broadcast and some live links. With variable bit rate (VBR) it lets hard scenes take more bits and easy scenes fewer, giving more even quality for the same average size. Many encoders also offer a constant-quality mode in which you choose a quality level and the size simply follows from the content.

Real-life example 1, a news broadcast: A Bangla news programme has a newsreader in a fixed studio for minutes at a time. P- and B-frames are tiny there, because only the face moves and the ticker text scrolls. When the programme cuts to field footage of a flood in Sylhet, with water, rain and a moving camera, the encoder needs many more bits, and if the bit rate is capped you may notice the picture getting blockier exactly during those clips.

Real-life example 2, scrubbing a lecture video: An online class recorded as slides with a voice-over is the ideal case for inter coding: for many seconds the slide does not change at all, so P-frames are almost entirely skipped blocks and the file is very small. Some screen-recording tools let you set a long keyframe interval to make such files even smaller, but then seeking through the lecture becomes slow, because the player must decode from a distant keyframe. A common compromise is a keyframe every few seconds.

Common mistakes: First, thinking P-frames store only the pixels that changed; they store motion vectors and a transformed, quantized residual for every block, though many blocks can be skipped. Second, assuming B-frames come after their future reference in display order; they are displayed before it but decoded after it. Third, believing more I-frames always improve quality; at a fixed bit rate, more I-frames leave fewer bits for everything else. Fourth, forgetting that the encoder predicts from decoded frames, not originals.

What exams ask: Define I-, P- and B-frames and compare their sizes and dependencies. Given a GOP pattern, write the decode order and identify which frames depend on which. Define N and M for a GOP. Explain why B-frames add delay and why video calls avoid them. Explain random access and error propagation and how I-frames limit them. Compute average frame size or bit rate for a GOP with given frame sizes.

Recap: Video compression exploits spatial redundancy inside frames and temporal redundancy between them. I-frames are self-contained keyframes; P-frames predict from the past; B-frames predict from past and future and are usually the smallest. Each predicted block sends a motion vector and a coded residual, organised in macroblocks or larger blocks. GOPs repeat a pattern like I B B P B B P; B-frames force a decode order different from display order and add delay. I-frames enable seeking, stop error propagation and are placed at scene cuts. Next lesson: how the encoder actually finds those motion vectors.
key_points: Spatial redundancy is inside a frame; temporal redundancy is between frames and gives the biggest savings.
I-frames are intra coded and self-contained (keyframes); P-frames predict from earlier references; B-frames from past and/or future.
Predicted blocks send a motion vector plus a transformed, quantized residual; the encoder predicts from decoded frames to avoid drift.
Macroblock = 16x16 luma + two 8x8 chroma blocks in 4:2:0; a 1080p frame is 120 x 68 macroblocks.
GOP pattern I B B P B B P..., with N = I-frame distance and M = anchor distance; illustrative sizes give 22.5 KB average vs 100 KB all-I.
Display I1 B2 B3 P4 becomes decode order I1 P4 B2 B3; B-frames add delay, so real-time calls usually avoid them.
I-frames enable seeking and stop error propagation; encoders add them at scene cuts.
lessons.tip: Whenever you see a GOP question, write two rows: display order on top, decode order below, and draw arrows from each B-frame to its two references. The arrows make the reordering obvious.
lessons.task: Write the display order I1 B2 B3 P4 B5 B6 P7 B8 B9 I10 on paper and convert it to decode order. Then, using sizes I = 120 KB, P = 40 KB, B = 15 KB, compute the average frame size and the bit rate at 25 fps.

quiz.q: Which frame type can be decoded without any other frame?
quiz.explain: I-frames are intra coded and self-contained.

quiz.q: Display order I1 B2 B3 P4. In which order are they decoded?
quiz.explain: B2 and B3 need P4 as their future reference, so P4 is decoded right after I1.

quiz.q: Why do real-time video calls usually avoid B-frames?
options: Waiting for a future reference adds delay
B-frames are not allowed in H.264
quiz.explain: A B-frame needs a later frame first, so the encoder must wait, adding latency.

quiz.q: With sizes I = 100 KB, P = 30 KB, B = 10 KB, what is the average frame size of the GOP I B B P B B P B B P B B?
quiz.explain: 1 x 100 + 3 x 30 + 8 x 10 = 270 KB over 12 frames = 22.5 KB.

quiz.q: After a lost packet corrupts a P-frame, the error typically stops spreading at:
options: The end of the audio track
quiz.explain: Later frames predict from the damaged one until an intra-coded frame or refresh resets the chain.

lessons.title: Motion Estimation and Block Matching: Finding Where Each Block Came From
lessons.content:
Imagine you are looking at two photos of a busy Gulistan street taken one second apart, and a friend asks: where did that red bus in the second photo come from? You do not scan pixel by pixel across the whole city. You look near where the bus was in the first photo, try a few nearby spots, and pick the one that looks the same. That small search is exactly what a video encoder does, millions of times per second. It is called motion estimation, and the most common way to do it is block matching. This lesson works through the idea with real arithmetic, counts how expensive it is, and shows the shortcuts encoders use.

Where this fits: In lesson 16 we said a P- or B-frame block is predicted from an area in a reference frame, and the encoder sends a motion vector plus a residual. We did not say how the encoder finds that area. Motion estimation is the search that finds the motion vector. Motion compensation is the use of that vector: take the reference area it points to, use it as the prediction, and code the difference. The encoder does both; the decoder only does motion compensation, because the vector is handed to it. So, as with audio coding, the expensive thinking lives in the encoder.

What a motion vector is: A motion vector (dx, dy) says how far to shift from the block's own position to reach its best match in the reference frame. If a block at column 64, row 32 of the current frame is best matched by the area at column 61, row 30 of the previous frame, the vector is (-3, -2): its content was 3 pixels to the left and 2 pixels up in the previous frame, so the object moved 3 right and 2 down. Note the sign convention: the vector points from the current block back into the reference. A vector of (0, 0) means nothing moved.

The block matching idea: Split the current frame into blocks, classically 16 x 16 luma pixels. For each block, try placing it at a set of candidate positions in the reference frame, measure how different the two blocks are, and keep the position with the smallest difference. The set of candidates is the search window: all shifts from -p to +p in both directions. With p = 7 that is shifts -7..+7 horizontally and vertically, so 15 x 15 = 225 candidate positions. In general (2p + 1)^2.

Matching criteria: The usual measure is the sum of absolute differences, SAD: for each pixel subtract the reference pixel from the current one, take the absolute value, and add everything up. SAD = sum over i, j of |C(i, j) - R(i + dy, j + dx)|. A perfect match gives SAD = 0. Alternatives are the mean absolute difference (SAD divided by the number of pixels) and the mean squared error, which squares differences and punishes big mistakes more. SAD is popular because it needs only subtraction, absolute value and addition, and CPUs even have special vector instructions that compute SAD for many pixels at once.

Worked example, the setup: Let us shrink everything so it fits on paper. The reference frame is 4 x 4 pixels (brightness values): row 0 is 10 10 10 10, row 1 is 10 10 50 50, row 2 is 10 10 50 50, row 3 is 10 10 10 10. So there is a bright 2 x 2 square in the middle right. In the current frame we have a 2 x 2 block located at row 1, column 1, with values: top row 10 10, bottom row 50 50. We search a window of p = 1, so the block's top-left corner may sit at rows 0 to 2 and columns 0 to 2 in the reference, which is 3 x 3 = 9 candidates.

Worked example, computing SADs: Candidate at reference row 0, column 1: the reference block is top 10 10, bottom 10 50. Differences: |10 - 10| + |10 - 10| + |50 - 10| + |50 - 50| = 0 + 0 + 40 + 0 = 40. Candidate at row 0, column 2: reference block top 10 10, bottom 50 50, exactly equal, SAD = 0. Doing all nine gives: row 0: 80, 40, 0; row 1: 80, 80, 80; row 2: 80, 120, 160. The minimum is 0 at row 0, column 2.

Worked example, the vector: The block sits at row 1, column 1 in the current frame and its best match is at row 0, column 2 in the reference. So dy = 0 - 1 = -1 and dx = 2 - 1 = +1: the motion vector is (dx, dy) = (+1, -1). The content came from one column to the right and one row up, meaning the edge of the bright square moved one pixel left and one pixel down. The residual is all zeros, so the encoder sends just the vector and a flag saying there is no residual. That is the dream case: a block coded with a handful of bits.

Counting the cost of full search: Full search, also called exhaustive search, tries every candidate. For a 16 x 16 block and p = 7 that is 225 positions x 256 pixel differences = 57,600 absolute differences per block. A 1080p frame has 120 x 68 = 8,160 macroblocks, so one frame needs 8,160 x 57,600 = 470,016,000 differences, and at 30 fps about 14.1 billion per second. And p = 7 is a small window; fast motion in sport can need far larger ones, with cost growing roughly with p squared. This is why motion estimation is usually the most expensive part of a video encoder.

Fast search: three-step search: Fast algorithms test only a few candidates and assume the SAD surface gets smaller as you approach the best match. The classic three-step search for p = 7 starts with a step size of 4. Step 1: test the centre and the 8 points at distance 4 around it (9 points), pick the best. Step 2: halve the step to 2 and test the 8 neighbours around the new best (8 new points). Step 3: step 1, test 8 more. Total 9 + 8 + 8 = 25 positions instead of 225, nine times fewer.

Other fast searches and their risk: Related ideas include the 2D logarithmic search, which tests a cross-shaped pattern and halves the step when the centre is best, and diamond search, which walks a small diamond pattern towards lower SAD and finishes with a tiny diamond. Real encoders often start from a predicted vector (taken from neighbouring blocks or the previous frame) rather than from (0, 0), which makes the search both faster and more accurate. The risk of every fast search is getting trapped in a local minimum: a position that looks best nearby but is not the true best, for example in repetitive textures like a brick wall or a striped shirt.

Sub-pixel motion: Real objects do not move in whole-pixel steps. If a car moves 2.5 pixels between frames, the best whole-pixel match is still off by half a pixel and leaves a residual. Codecs therefore allow half-pixel and quarter-pixel vectors. The encoder interpolates the reference between pixels; for example, halfway between a pixel of 10 and a pixel of 50 a simple average gives 30 (real codecs use longer interpolation filters). H.264 and its successors use quarter-pixel precision for luma. Searches usually find the best whole-pixel vector first, then refine around it at half and quarter positions.

Variable block sizes: One 16 x 16 block might contain both a moving person and the still background. Codecs like H.264 let the encoder split a macroblock into smaller partitions, down to 4 x 4, each with its own vector; later codecs allow even larger blocks for flat areas and non-square shapes. Small blocks follow complex motion better but need more vectors to send; the encoder chooses the split that minimises total cost, a process called rate-distortion optimisation: cost = distortion + lambda x bits.

Coding the motion vectors: Neighbouring blocks usually move together, so their vectors are similar. Instead of sending each vector raw, codecs predict it from neighbours and send only the difference. In H.264 the prediction is typically the component-wise median of the left, top and top-right neighbours. Worked: neighbours have vectors (2, 1), (3, 1) and (2, 0). The median of x values 2, 3, 2 is 2, and of y values 1, 1, 0 is 1, so the prediction is (2, 1). If the actual vector is (3, 1), only the difference (1, 0) is entropy coded, a few bits.

Multiple references and what motion cannot explain: Codecs since H.264 may choose among several earlier frames as reference, helpful when something is briefly hidden and reappears. Still, block motion is a model of translation only. Zooms, rotations, changes of lighting, smoke, water and newly uncovered background do not fit it well, which is where B-frames, intra blocks and larger residuals take over. Some codecs add tools for more complex motion, but the translational block match is still the workhorse.

Real-life example 1, a cricket camera pan: When the camera pans to follow a ball hit towards the boundary, almost every block in the frame moves by roughly the same vector, say 12 pixels left. Vector prediction makes those nearly free, and the residuals are small, so a pan is cheaper than it looks. But the crowd, with thousands of tiny moving details, has no good match at low bit rates; that is why the stands turn into a blurry mush on weak streams while the pitch stays clear.

Real-life example 2, a video call from a moving bus: On a video call from a Dhaka bus, the background through the window moves fast and unevenly, while your face moves slowly. The phone's encoder has to work within a tight time and battery budget, so it uses a small fast search. Background blocks may find poor matches and need many residual bits; the encoder raises quantization to stay within the network's rate, and the background becomes blocky while your face, which matches well, stays acceptable.

Common mistakes: First, mixing up motion estimation (the search, encoder only) with motion compensation (using the vector, both sides). Second, getting the vector sign wrong: always write vector = reference position minus current position and state your convention. Third, counting search positions as 2p + 1 instead of (2p + 1)^2. Fourth, assuming a fast search always finds the same result as full search; it may not. Fifth, forgetting that vectors themselves cost bits, which is why small blocks are not always better.

What exams ask: Define motion estimation, motion compensation and motion vectors. Compute SAD for given blocks and find the best vector in a small window. Count operations for full search (positions x pixels per block x blocks per frame x fps). Describe the three-step search, count its positions and compare with full search. Explain sub-pixel motion and vector prediction, often with a median example.

Recap: Motion estimation finds, for each block, the shift into the reference frame that matches best; motion compensation uses that shift to predict the block, leaving a small residual. Block matching with SAD over a window of +-p has (2p + 1)^2 candidates; for 16 x 16 blocks and p = 7 that is 225 positions and 57,600 differences per block, about 14.1 billion per second for 1080p30. Fast searches like three-step (25 positions) trade a little accuracy for big speed. Quarter-pixel vectors, variable block sizes and vector prediction squeeze out more. Next lesson: how all these tools are packaged into standards from MPEG-1 to AV1.
key_points: Motion estimation (encoder only) searches for each block's best match; motion compensation (both sides) uses the vector to predict.
Motion vector = position of the match in the reference minus the block's own position; (0, 0) means no motion.
SAD = sum of |current - reference|; cheap and widely used; MSE punishes large errors more.
A +-p window has (2p+1)^2 candidates: p = 7 gives 225 positions and 57,600 differences per 16x16 block.
Full search at 1080p30: 8,160 blocks x 57,600 x 30, about 14.1 billion differences per second.
Three-step search tests 9 + 8 + 8 = 25 positions but can get stuck in local minima.
Quarter-pixel vectors, variable block sizes (down to 4x4 in H.264) and median vector prediction reduce residual and vector bits.
lessons.tip: When you compute SADs by hand, draw the reference frame on squared paper and cut a small paper window the size of the block. Sliding it over the grid makes the candidates impossible to miss.
lessons.task: On squared paper, draw a 6 x 6 reference frame with a small 2 x 2 dark square, and a current 2 x 2 block containing that square shifted by one pixel. Compute SAD for all candidates within p = 1, find the motion vector, and count how many candidates p = 2 would need.

quiz.q: How many candidate positions does full search test with a window of p = 7?
What does motion compensation mean?
options: Using the motion vector to fetch the reference area as the block's prediction
Searching the window for the best match
quiz.explain: Estimation finds the vector; compensation uses it to build the prediction, in both encoder and decoder.

quiz.q: Current block 10 10 / 50 50 and reference block 10 10 / 10 50. What is the SAD?
quiz.explain: Only one pixel differs: |50 - 10| = 40.

quiz.q: How many positions does the three-step search test for p = 7?
quiz.explain: 9 in the first step, then 8 and 8 more: 25 in total.

quiz.q: Neighbouring vectors are (2, 1), (3, 1) and (2, 0). What is the median prediction?
quiz.explain: Median of x (2, 3, 2) is 2 and of y (1, 1, 0) is 1, so (2, 1).

lessons.title: Video Codec Standards: From MPEG-1 to H.264, HEVC, AV1 and Beyond
lessons.content:
Think about the Bangla alphabet and spelling rules. Thousands of writers write in completely different styles, yet every reader in the country can read every book, because everyone agrees on the same letters and rules. A video codec standard is that shared spelling rulebook for compressed video. Any phone, TV or browser that follows the rulebook can play a video made by any encoder that follows it. In lessons 16 and 17 we learned the tools: I/P/B frames, motion compensation, residual transforms. This lesson walks through the family of standards that package those tools, what improved from one generation to the next, and the practical trade-offs of compression, speed, licensing and device support.

What a codec is: A codec (coder-decoder) is a method for compressing and decompressing media. Strictly, a standard defines two things: the bitstream syntax (how the bits are arranged) and the decoding process (exactly how a decoder turns those bits into pictures). It deliberately does not define the encoder. Any encoder that produces a valid bitstream is allowed, which is why two encoders of the same standard can give very different quality at the same bit rate, and why encoders keep improving for years after a standard is frozen. Popular open-source encoders include x264 for H.264, x265 for HEVC, and libaom and SVT-AV1 for AV1.

Who makes the standards: Two big groups dominate. ITU-T, the telecom standards body, has the Video Coding Experts Group, which names its standards H.26x. ISO/IEC has the Moving Picture Experts Group, MPEG. Several key standards were made jointly and so have two names: H.262 is MPEG-2 Video, H.264 is MPEG-4 Part 10 AVC, H.265 is HEVC, H.266 is VVC. A third force is the Alliance for Open Media (AOMedia), formed by technology and streaming companies, which created AV1 with the goal of royalty-free use. Google's earlier VP8 and VP9 belong to the same open lineage.

The common skeleton: Every standard from MPEG-1 to the newest uses the same hybrid structure: block-based prediction (intra from neighbours, or inter with motion compensation), a transform of the residual, quantization, and entropy coding, with a decoder loop inside the encoder. What changes between generations is how flexibly each step can adapt to the content, and each gain costs more computation, mostly in the encoder.

MPEG-1: Standardised in the early 1990s, MPEG-1 targeted about 1.5 Mbps, the data rate of a CD-ROM, at roughly VHS quality (352 x 288 in PAL regions). It introduced the I/P/B frame structure with 16 x 16 macroblocks, an 8 x 8 DCT and half-pixel motion. It powered Video CDs, which were hugely popular in South Asia, including Bangladesh, in the late 1990s and 2000s. Its audio part gave us MP3.

MPEG-2 (H.262): Arriving in the mid-1990s, MPEG-2 extended MPEG-1 to higher resolutions and bit rates and added proper support for interlaced video, which television needed. It became the codec of DVDs and of the first generation of digital television broadcasting worldwide, satellite and cable included. It introduced profiles and levels: profiles say which tools a decoder must support, levels limit resolution and bit rate, so a manufacturer knows exactly what its chip must handle.

MPEG-4 Part 2: Around 1999, MPEG-4 Part 2 (MPEG-4 Visual) improved efficiency for internet and mobile use and was the basis of popular DivX and Xvid encoders, the files people shared on CDs and hard disks in the 2000s. It also contained ambitious object-based coding ideas that saw little real use.

H.264/AVC: Finalised in 2003, H.264 is the most widely supported video codec in history. Compared with MPEG-2 it is commonly described as needing roughly half the bit rate for similar quality. Its key tools: variable block partitions from 16 x 16 down to 4 x 4 (lesson 17), quarter-pixel motion, multiple reference frames, intra prediction with nine directional modes for 4 x 4 blocks, a small integer transform that approximates the DCT exactly in integer arithmetic (so encoder and decoder never drift), an in-loop deblocking filter, and two entropy coders: CAVLC and the more efficient CABAC (arithmetic coding from lesson 09). It is used on Blu-ray, in streaming, video calls, CCTV and phone cameras. Its common profiles are Baseline (simple, low delay), Main and High.

The in-loop deblocking filter: Block-based coding causes visible edges at block boundaries at low bit rates. A post-filter in the player could smooth them, but H.264 put the filter inside the coding loop: the filtered frame is what gets stored as the reference. That improves both the picture you see and the predictions for later frames, so it saves bits as well as looking better. Later codecs added more in-loop filters.

H.265/HEVC: Finalised in 2013, High Efficiency Video Coding was designed to reach the same perceptual quality as H.264 at about half the bit rate, a target mainly approached at high resolutions. It replaced the macroblock with the coding tree unit, up to 64 x 64, recursively split by a quadtree into smaller coding units, so a flat sky can be one huge block while a face is split finely. It has 35 intra prediction modes, transforms from 4 x 4 up to 32 x 32, CABAC as its only entropy coder, and an extra in-loop filter called sample adaptive offset. It is used for 4K broadcasting, Ultra HD Blu-ray and many phone cameras. The price is a much slower encoder and more complex decoder.

VP9: Released by Google in 2013, VP9 targets efficiency in the same class as HEVC and is used heavily on YouTube and in web browsers. It is open and royalty-free by intent. It uses superblocks of 64 x 64 split recursively, similar in spirit to HEVC.

AV1: Released by AOMedia in 2018, AV1 combines ideas from VP9 and other projects. It is generally reported to compress better than VP9 and HEVC at similar quality, especially at low bit rates, which is exactly what matters for weak mobile networks. It uses superblocks up to 128 x 128, many intra and inter prediction tools, and several in-loop filters. Its encoders were very slow at first and have become much faster, and many newer phones, TVs, laptops and browsers can decode it, often in hardware. Being royalty-free by design was a main reason streaming companies backed it.

H.266/VVC: Finalised in 2020, Versatile Video Coding targets about half the bit rate of HEVC for similar quality. It uses coding tree units up to 128 x 128 with more flexible splits including binary and ternary, 67 intra modes, and many new tools. Adoption is still growing; it is mentioned here so you recognise the name.

What improves each generation: Looking across the family, four trends repeat. Bigger and more flexible blocks: 16 x 16 macroblocks, then 64 x 64 trees, then 128 x 128. Richer prediction: more intra directions, finer motion, more references, better motion vector prediction. Better entropy coding: from fixed Huffman-style tables to context-adaptive arithmetic coding. More in-loop filtering: deblocking, then sample offsets and more. Each step squeezes the same quality into fewer bits.

The trade-off triangle: Better compression is not free. Encoding gets slower because the encoder tests many more options; a newer codec at its slowest settings can be many times slower than H.264. Decoding gets heavier, which matters for battery and cheap phones. So engineers juggle three things: bit rate, quality and complexity. For live sports they may use fast presets; for a movie encoded once and watched millions of times, spending hours of encoding per title pays off.

Measuring better: How do researchers claim one codec saves 30 or 50 percent? They encode the same set of test clips at several bit rates with each codec, measure quality at each point (PSNR from lesson 10, or a perceptual metric such as VMAF, or real viewers' scores), and draw quality versus bit rate curves. The average horizontal gap between two curves, the extra bit rate one codec needs for the same quality, is summarised as the Bjontegaard delta rate (BD-rate). A negative BD-rate means savings. Because the result depends on the clips, resolutions and encoder settings, different studies report different numbers, which is why we quote design targets and trends rather than single figures.

Video codecs inside image formats: A still picture is just an I-frame. So modern image formats borrow intra coding from video codecs: HEIC/HEIF commonly stores HEVC intra-coded images, and AVIF stores AV1 intra frames (lesson 13). This is why newer image formats beat JPEG: they inherit prediction modes, flexible blocks and in-loop filters that video research produced.

Licensing and device support, in general terms: H.264 and HEVC are covered by many patents, licensed through patent pools; the details and fees have changed over time and differ by use, so we will not quote figures here. AV1 and VP9 were designed to be royalty-free. For a developer, the deciding question is often simpler: what can the user's device decode in hardware? Hardware decoders use far less battery than software ones. H.264 hardware decoding is practically universal; HEVC and AV1 support depends on the device age and model. That is why platforms usually store the same video in more than one codec and send each device what it can play.

Real-life example 1, a video platform serving Bangladesh: A platform with users on budget Android phones might keep every video in H.264 as a safe baseline, plus VP9 or AV1 versions for devices that support them. A user in Rangpur on a weak 4G signal with a newer phone gets AV1 at a low bit rate with acceptable quality; a user with an older phone gets H.264 at a slightly higher bit rate for similar quality. Both are watching the same lecture.

Real-life example 2, your phone camera setting: Many phones offer a setting like most compatible versus high efficiency. Most compatible records in H.264, which plays everywhere. High efficiency records in HEVC, which roughly halves storage for similar quality but may not play on an old laptop or upload cleanly to every site. Now you know exactly what that switch means.

Common mistakes: First, saying a standard defines the encoder; it defines the bitstream and the decoder. Second, quoting the 50 percent savings as a guaranteed fact for every video; it is a design target, and real gains vary with content, resolution and encoder settings. Third, confusing a codec with a container: an MP4 file can hold H.264, HEVC or AV1 (lesson 19). Fourth, assuming the newest codec is always the right choice; device support and encoding cost may decide otherwise.

What exams ask: Name the standards bodies and give the two names of joint standards. List the main tools of H.264 and explain the in-loop deblocking filter. Compare H.264 and HEVC (block structure, intra modes, transform sizes, efficiency target). Explain profiles and levels. Discuss the trade-off between compression efficiency and complexity, and why royalty-free codecs like AV1 were created.

Recap: All mainstream video codecs share one hybrid design: predict, transform the residual, quantize, entropy code, with an internal decoder loop. Standards fix the bitstream and decoder, leaving encoders free to improve. MPEG-1 (Video CD), MPEG-2 (DVD and digital TV), MPEG-4 Part 2, H.264 (everywhere), HEVC and VP9, AV1 and VVC each added bigger flexible blocks, richer prediction, better entropy coding and more in-loop filtering, roughly halving bit rate every generation at the cost of complexity. Next lesson: once video and audio are compressed, how they are packaged together into files and streams.
key_points: A standard defines the bitstream syntax and decoding process, not the encoder; encoders keep improving.
Bodies: ITU-T VCEG (H.26x), ISO/IEC MPEG, joint names (H.262/MPEG-2, H.264/AVC, H.265/HEVC, H.266/VVC); AOMedia made AV1.
All share the hybrid design: prediction, residual transform, quantization, entropy coding, decoder loop.
MPEG-1 for Video CD (~1.5 Mbps), MPEG-2 for DVD and digital TV with interlace support, profiles and levels.
H.264: partitions down to 4x4, quarter-pixel, multiple references, integer transform, in-loop deblocking, CAVLC/CABAC.
HEVC: coding tree units up to 64x64, 35 intra modes, transforms to 32x32, SAO, about half H.264's bit rate as a design target.
VP9 and AV1 aim to be royalty-free; AV1 uses blocks up to 128x128; VVC targets about half HEVC's rate.
Better compression costs encoder and decoder complexity; device hardware support often decides the codec.
lessons.tip: Learn the generations as a timeline with one keyword each: MPEG-1 Video CD, MPEG-2 DVD and TV, H.264 everywhere, HEVC 4K, AV1 royalty-free, VVC newest. Hang the details on those hooks.
lessons.task: On your phone, find the camera's video format setting (often under formats or video settings) and note the two options. If you can, record the same 10-second scene with both and compare file sizes. Then look up which codec a video you downloaded uses, using any media info app or a file properties screen.

quiz.q: What does a video coding standard actually specify?
options: The bitstream syntax and the decoding process
quiz.explain: Standards fix how bits are arranged and decoded; encoders are free to choose how to produce them.

quiz.q: H.264 is also known as:
quiz.explain: H.264 was produced jointly by ITU-T and MPEG and is MPEG-4 Part 10, Advanced Video Coding.

quiz.q: Why is H.264's deblocking filter placed inside the coding loop?
options: So filtered frames are used as references, improving later predictions too
Because the player cannot run filters
quiz.explain: In-loop filtering improves both displayed quality and the reference frames, saving bits.

quiz.q: What is the largest coding tree unit size in HEVC?
quiz.explain: HEVC replaced 16 x 16 macroblocks with coding tree units up to 64 x 64.

quiz.q: Which codec was created by AOMedia with royalty-free use as a goal?
quiz.explain: AV1 was released by the Alliance for Open Media in 2018, designed to be royalty-free.

lessons.title: Containers vs Codecs: MP4, MKV, WebM, MPEG-TS and How Streams Are Packaged
lessons.content:
Think of a tiffin carrier, the stacked steel lunch box many office workers in Dhaka carry. One box holds rice, one holds dal, one holds fish curry, and a clip holds them together with a handle. The food is cooked in different ways; the carrier just keeps the boxes together, labelled, and in the right order. A media file works the same way. The video is cooked by a video codec, the audio by an audio codec, the subtitles are plain text, and a container holds them all together with labels and timing. Mixing up the carrier and the food is one of the most common confusions in multimedia, and this lesson clears it up.

The two words: A codec is a method of compressing and decompressing one kind of media: H.264, HEVC and AV1 for video (lesson 18), AAC, MP3 and Opus for audio (lesson 14).
