A container (also called a wrapper or file format) is a structure that stores one or more already-compressed streams, plus the information needed to play them together: which streams exist, which codec each uses, timestamps, durations, an index for seeking, and metadata such as title and language. The file extension, like .mp4 or .mkv, names the container, not the codec.

Why containers exist: A raw H.264 bitstream alone has no audio, no reliable duration, no fast way to seek, and no idea of which language a subtitle is in. Someone must interleave audio and video so they can be read together, record when each frame should be shown, and keep an index so the player can jump to minute 30 without reading everything before it. That is the container's job. Combining streams into a container is called muxing (multiplexing); pulling them apart for decoding is demuxing.

Tracks: Inside a container each stream is a track. A movie file might have one video track, two audio tracks (Bangla and English dubbing), three subtitle tracks and a chapter list. The player demuxes the file, picks one video and one audio track (by default or by your choice), and sends each to its decoder. Each track's header records its codec, so the player knows which decoder to load.

Interleaving: Containers usually interleave the tracks in small chunks: a bit of video, the matching bit of audio, the next bit of video, and so on. If all the video were stored first and all the audio afterwards, a player streaming the file would need the whole video before it could play any sound. Interleaving lets playback start after downloading just the beginning.

Timestamps: Every frame or audio chunk carries timing. The presentation timestamp (PTS) says when it should be shown or heard. The decode timestamp (DTS) says when it must be decoded. Without B-frames they are equal. With B-frames they differ, because of the reordering from lesson 16: display order I1 B2 B3 P4 is stored as I1 P4 B2 B3, so P4 has an early DTS but a later PTS. Timestamps count in ticks of a timescale; MPEG transport streams, for example, use a 90 kHz clock, so at 25 fps each frame advances the PTS by 90,000 / 25 = 3,600 ticks.

Lip sync: Audio and video are decoded separately and kept together by their timestamps against a shared clock, usually the audio clock, because people notice audio glitches more than an occasional repeated or dropped video frame. If timestamps are wrong, or a device adds delay to one path (a TV's picture processing or a Bluetooth headset's audio delay), lips and voice drift apart. Studies used for broadcast guidance found that people notice sound arriving early sooner than sound arriving late, which matches everyday life: light reaches us before sound, so a slight audio lag feels natural. Players often provide an audio delay setting to correct it.

MP4: The most common container today. MP4 is MPEG-4 Part 14, built on the ISO base media file format, which grew out of Apple's QuickTime. It is organised into boxes (also called atoms): ftyp says which brand of file it is, moov holds the metadata and sample tables (where each frame is, its size and timestamps), and mdat holds the actual compressed data. It typically carries H.264, HEVC or AV1 video and AAC audio. M4A is the same container with audio only.

Fast start and fragmented MP4: A camera writes mdat while recording and only writes moov at the end, when it knows all the sizes. If such a file is put on a website, the player must fetch the end of the file before it can start, which slows progressive download. Moving moov to the front, called fast start, fixes that. For streaming (lesson 21), MP4 is used in fragmented form: a short header, then many small fragments each with its own mini index (moof) and data (mdat), so a player can start with any segment.

MKV and WebM: Matroska (.mkv) is an open, very flexible container that can hold almost any codec, many audio and subtitle tracks, chapters and attachments such as fonts. That makes it popular for movies with multiple languages. WebM is a restricted version of Matroska designed for the web: video in VP8, VP9 or AV1 and audio in Vorbis or Opus. Browsers that support WebM know exactly what to expect inside.

MOV and AVI: MOV is Apple's QuickTime format, common from iPhones and editing software; MP4 is its standardised cousin. AVI is an old Microsoft container from the early 1990s based on the RIFF structure. It still plays almost everywhere, but it handles modern features such as B-frames, variable frame rate and many tracks awkwardly, so it is rarely the right choice for new files.

MPEG transport stream: MPEG-TS (.ts) was designed for broadcast, where errors happen and a receiver may tune in at any moment. It chops everything into fixed 188-byte packets, each with a 4-byte header containing a packet identifier that tells which stream it belongs to. Fixed small packets make it robust: a lost packet damages only a little, and a decoder can lock on quickly. The 4-byte header alone is 4 / 188, at least about 2.1 percent overhead, more than MP4. Digital TV broadcasting uses TS, and HLS streaming traditionally used .ts segments, though fragmented MP4 is now common there too.

Even simple files are containers: A .wav file is a RIFF container usually holding uncompressed PCM. An .mp3 file is mostly a sequence of MP3 frames with an optional ID3 tag for title and artist. Ogg is an open container often used with Vorbis or Opus. So even audio has the same split between what is inside and how it is wrapped.

Metadata matters too: Containers also carry metadata that changes how a file behaves. Phones often record video in the sensor's natural orientation and simply store a rotation flag saying display this rotated by 90 degrees; a player that ignores the flag shows your portrait video lying sideways. Other metadata includes creation date, GPS location, language codes for each audio and subtitle track, chapter titles and cover art. Remember the privacy point from lesson 13: a shared video may reveal where it was shot unless that metadata is removed.

Subtitles: Subtitles can be soft or burned in. Soft subtitles are a separate text track (formats like SRT, or WebVTT on the web) that you can switch on and off, change language, or resize. Burned-in subtitles are drawn into the video pixels and cannot be removed. Bangla soft subtitles need a player and font that do proper Unicode shaping (lesson 02); otherwise conjuncts and vowel signs may render wrongly, which is one reason some channels burn in Bangla subtitles.

The famous puzzle, plays but no sound: You copy a movie.mkv to a TV and the picture plays, but there is no sound. The container is fine, and the TV can decode the video codec, but the audio track uses a codec the TV does not support, for example a surround format it lacks a licence or decoder for. The fix is not to rename the file, but to convert the audio track to a supported codec such as AAC while copying the video untouched. The reverse puzzle, sound but black picture, usually means an unsupported video codec, for example HEVC on an older laptop.

Remuxing vs transcoding: Changing the container without touching the compressed data is remuxing. It is fast, takes seconds, and loses no quality, but it works only if the new container supports the codecs. Re-encoding with a different codec or bit rate is transcoding: slow, and since it decodes and re-compresses, it adds generation loss. In the popular open-source tool ffmpeg the idea looks like this: ffmpeg -i in.mkv -c copy out.mp4 remuxes; ffmpeg -i in.mkv -c:v copy -c:a aac out.mp4 keeps the video and converts only the audio; and the companion tool ffprobe in.mp4 lists every stream with its codec, resolution and duration.

Codecs inside labels: Containers and web pages identify codecs with short codes. In MP4 these are four-character codes such as avc1 for H.264, hvc1 or hev1 for HEVC, av01 for AV1, and mp4a for AAC audio. A web page can ask the browser whether it can play a format by giving the container type with a codecs parameter, for example video/mp4 with codecs avc1 and mp4a; that is how streaming players decide which version to fetch.

Real-life example 1, a wedding video from the videographer: The videographer hands you a USB stick with a large .mov file. Your relatives' phones struggle with it. Running ffprobe shows HEVC video and uncompressed PCM audio. Remuxing to MP4 with the video copied and the audio converted to AAC shrinks the file somewhat and makes it play on more phones, with no visible quality loss, because the video was never re-encoded. If an old phone still cannot play HEVC, then and only then you transcode the video to H.264.

Real-life example 2, live TV on a phone: A Bangladeshi TV channel broadcasts in MPEG-TS over satellite. For its mobile app, the same encoded streams are repackaged into short fragmented MP4 or TS segments with an HLS playlist (lesson 21). The video codec may not change at all; only the packaging changes from a broadcast container to a web streaming container.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: The classic mistakes are saying an MP4 is a codec, renaming .mkv to .mp4 and expecting it to work, assuming the file extension tells you the codec, and transcoding when a remux would do. Exams ask you to define codec and container with examples, explain muxing and demuxing, explain PTS and DTS with a B-frame example, compare MP4, MKV and MPEG-TS, and explain lip sync and why audio is usually the master clock.

Recap: A codec compresses one kind of media; a container packages one or more compressed tracks with timestamps, an index and metadata. Muxing combines, demuxing separates. PTS says when to present, DTS when to decode, and they differ with B-frames. MP4 (boxes ftyp, moov, mdat, fast start, fragmented for streaming), MKV/WebM (flexible, open) and MPEG-TS (188-byte packets for broadcast) are the main containers. Remuxing is fast and lossless; transcoding is slow and lossy. Next lesson: sending these streams across a real network, with all its delays and losses.
key_points: Codec = how one media type is compressed (H.264, AV1, AAC, Opus); container = how compressed tracks are packaged (MP4, MKV, WebM, TS).
The file extension names the container, not the codec.
Muxing combines and interleaves tracks; demuxing separates them for the decoders.
PTS = when to present, DTS = when to decode; they differ when B-frames are reordered; TS uses a 90 kHz clock (3,600 ticks per frame at 25 fps).
MP4 boxes: ftyp, moov (metadata and index), mdat (data); fast start moves moov to the front; fragmented MP4 is used for streaming.
MKV is open and flexible; WebM restricts it to VP8/VP9/AV1 and Vorbis/Opus; MPEG-TS uses robust 188-byte packets for broadcast.
Remuxing changes only the wrapper and is lossless; transcoding re-encodes and adds generation loss.
lessons.tip: Whenever a file misbehaves, first ask two separate questions: what is the container, and what codec is each track? Most playback problems are answered by the second question.
lessons.task: Pick three video files on your phone or computer (for example a camera clip, a downloaded video and a messaging app video). Using a media info app or the file properties, write down for each: container, video codec, audio codec, resolution, frame rate and bit rate. Note which ones share a container but differ in codec.

quiz.q: Which of these is a container, not a codec?
quiz.explain: MKV (Matroska) is a container; the others are codecs.

quiz.q: With B-frames, what is the difference between PTS and DTS?
options: PTS is when to present a frame, DTS is when to decode it, and they can differ
quiz.explain: Reordering for B-frames means some frames are decoded earlier than they are shown.

quiz.q: A movie plays with picture but no sound on a TV. The most likely cause is:
options: The audio track uses a codec the TV cannot decode
quiz.explain: Picture works, so the container and video codec are fine; the audio codec is unsupported.

quiz.q: Why does MPEG-TS use small fixed 188-byte packets?
options: To make files smaller than MP4
For robustness and quick lock-on in broadcast, where errors happen
quiz.explain: Small fixed packets limit damage from errors and let receivers join mid-stream.

quiz.q: What does remuxing do?
options: Re-encodes the video at a lower bit rate
Moves compressed tracks to a new container without re-encoding
quiz.explain: Remuxing copies the compressed data into a new wrapper, fast and lossless.

lessons.title: Multimedia Networking and Streaming: Buffers, Jitter, Loss, RTP and RTSP
lessons.content:
Imagine your uncle in Chattogram sends you a basket of mangoes every day by courier, one basket leaving at exactly 9 am. The baskets do not arrive at exactly the same time: one day the bus is quick, another day it is stuck at a jam near Feni, and once two baskets arrive together. If you promise to serve one basket at every evening meal, you would be wise to keep one or two spare baskets in the kitchen first, so a late delivery never leaves the table empty. That spare stock is a buffer, and the varying arrival time is jitter. Streaming audio and video over the internet faces exactly this problem, many times per second. This lesson explains how media apps survive a network that delivers packets late, out of order, or not at all.

Why media is special on a network: Ordinary data, like a web page or a file download, cares about correctness and total time; a few seconds of extra delay is annoying but harmless. Continuous media is time-based (lesson 01): each audio sample and video frame must be played at its moment. Data that arrives after its play time is as useless as data that never arrived. On the other hand, media tolerates small losses: a missing 20 ms of audio or a slightly damaged frame is often barely noticed. So multimedia networking trades the strict reliability of file transfer for timeliness. Computer Networks (deep-cse-4-3) gave us TCP, UDP, HTTP and CDNs; here we use them for media.

Three classes of multimedia applications: First, streaming stored media: a recorded video or song on a server, like a lecture on YouTube. Playback can start before the download finishes, the user can pause and seek, and a delay of a few seconds at the start is acceptable. Second, streaming live media: a live cricket match or a news channel. It is like stored streaming, but content is created as it is sent, so the buffer cannot run far ahead, and viewers usually accept a delay of several seconds or more behind real time. Third, conversational (interactive) media: voice and video calls. Here delay is the enemy; beyond a few hundred milliseconds of one-way delay, conversation becomes awkward (lesson 22).

Download, progressive download, streaming: With plain download, you fetch the whole file and then play it. With progressive download, the player fetches the file over HTTP from the start and begins playing once enough is buffered, while the rest keeps downloading; seeking far ahead may have to wait. True streaming delivers media in pieces as needed, lets the player jump anywhere, and can adapt quality to the network (lesson 21). Most modern internet video uses HTTP-based adaptive streaming, which blends the last two.

The playout buffer: The player does not play data the instant it arrives. It collects some data first, the initial buffering you see as a spinning circle, and then plays from the buffer while the network keeps refilling it. If the network is temporarily slower than the video's bit rate, the buffer drains; if it empties, playback stalls, which is called rebuffering. A bigger buffer protects against network hiccups but makes you wait longer at the start.

Worked buffer example: A 10-minute lecture is encoded at 2 Mbps, but your connection steadily gives only 1.5 Mbps. How long must you wait before pressing play so that it never stalls? The whole video is 2 Mbps x 600 s = 1,200 megabits. Downloading it takes 1,200 / 1.5 = 800 s. Playing takes 600 s. To finish playback no earlier than the download finishes, you must start at 800 - 600 = 200 s. In general, if the bit rate r is larger than the network rate R, the wait is D x (r / R - 1) for a video of duration D: 600 x (2 / 1.5 - 1) = 200 s. If R is larger than r, a short buffer is enough. Waiting over three minutes is unacceptable to most users, which is exactly why adaptive streaming lowers the quality instead.

Jitter: Packets sent at regular intervals do not arrive at regular intervals. Each one waits in different router queues, so its end-to-end delay varies. The variation of delay is called jitter. A voice app sends one packet every 20 ms; if packets arrive 15 ms, then 30 ms, then 10 ms apart, playing them on arrival would make speech choppy and uneven.

The jitter buffer, worked: The receiver delays playback by a fixed playout delay and plays each packet at its send time plus that delay. Suppose packets are sent at 0, 20, 40, 60 and 80 ms and their network delays are 40, 55, 45, 80 and 50 ms, so they arrive at 40, 75, 85, 140 and 130 ms (packet 5 overtakes packet 4). With a playout delay of 70 ms, packets must play at 70, 90, 110, 130 and 150 ms. Packets 1, 2, 3 and 5 are in time, but packet 4 arrives at 140, after its slot at 130, so it is treated as lost. With a playout delay of 90 ms every packet is in time, but every word you hear is 20 ms later. That is the fundamental trade-off: a longer playout delay means fewer late losses but more latency. Adaptive jitter buffers estimate the jitter continuously and adjust the delay, usually in silent gaps between talk spurts so no one notices.

Sequence numbers and timestamps: To do this, the receiver must know each packet's order and its intended play time, even when packets arrive out of order. That is why media packets carry a sequence number (to detect loss and reorder) and a timestamp (to schedule playout). These two fields are the heart of RTP, described below.

Packet loss: Media over UDP is not retransmitted by the transport layer, and on the internet a small fraction of packets is lost to congestion, especially on mobile and Wi-Fi links. There are three main defences: concealment at the receiver, forward error correction (FEC) at the sender, and interleaving. Retransmission is possible only if there is time for it, which is true for buffered streaming but rarely for calls.

Loss concealment: The receiver hides the loss. For audio it can repeat the previous packet, or better, interpolate a plausible waveform from the packets before and after; modern speech codecs do this well for single lost packets. For video it can copy the corresponding area from the previous frame or use neighbouring motion vectors to guess the missing block. Concealment costs no bandwidth, but it fails for long bursts of loss.

Forward error correction, worked: The sender adds redundant data so the receiver can rebuild a lost packet without asking. A simple scheme sends one parity packet after every n data packets, where each byte of the parity is the XOR of the corresponding bytes of the n packets. With n = 4, take one byte position with values 5, 9, 12 and 3. Parity = 5 XOR 9 XOR 12 XOR 3 = 3. If the packet carrying 9 is lost, the receiver XORs the survivors with the parity: 5 XOR 12 XOR 3 XOR 3 = 9, recovered. The cost is one extra packet per four, 25 percent more bandwidth, and it can only repair one loss per group. Another FEC trick is to piggyback a low bit rate copy of each audio chunk onto the next packet, so a lost chunk can be replaced by its lower-quality twin.

Interleaving: Instead of putting consecutive 5 ms audio chunks in the same packet, the sender mixes them: packet 1 carries chunks 1, 5, 9, 13, packet 2 carries 2, 6, 10, 14, and so on. If one packet is lost, the listener loses several tiny scattered gaps rather than one long hole, and tiny gaps are easy to conceal. The price is extra delay, since the sender must collect several chunks before sending.

TCP or UDP: Buffered streaming of stored and most live video usually runs over HTTP, and therefore over TCP (or QUIC, which runs over UDP and gives reliable streams). Reliability is fine here, because the buffer gives time for retransmissions, HTTP passes through firewalls easily, and ordinary web caches and CDNs can deliver it. Conversational media usually runs over UDP, because waiting for a retransmission would add more delay than the lost packet is worth; the application handles loss itself.

RTP: The Real-time Transport Protocol is the standard packet format for real-time media, usually carried over UDP. Its fixed header is 12 bytes and includes a payload type (which codec), a sequence number, a timestamp in units of the media clock, and a source identifier (SSRC) so streams from different senders can be told apart. For 8 kHz telephone audio, 20 ms of sound is 160 samples, so the timestamp advances by 160 per packet. RTP itself guarantees nothing about delay or delivery; it just gives the receiver the information to reorder, detect loss and schedule playout.

Worked header overhead: A G.711 voice call sends 20 ms of audio per packet: 64,000 bps x 0.02 s = 1,280 bits = 160 bytes of payload. Add RTP (12 bytes), UDP (8 bytes) and IPv4 (20 bytes), 40 bytes of headers, and each packet is 200 bytes. At 50 packets per second that is 200 x 8 x 50 = 80,000 bps: an 80 kbps stream for 64 kbps of voice, a quarter extra. Using larger packets lowers overhead but adds delay, another classic trade-off.

RTCP and RTSP: RTP has a companion, the RTP Control Protocol (RTCP). Participants periodically send reports with packet counts, the fraction lost and the measured jitter, so senders can adapt their bit rate; RTCP traffic is kept to a small share of the session bandwidth, commonly around 5 percent. The Real Time Streaming Protocol (RTSP) is different again: it is like a network remote control. A client sends commands such as DESCRIBE, SETUP, PLAY, PAUSE and TEARDOWN to a media server, while the media itself usually flows over RTP. Many IP security cameras still offer an RTSP address for viewing their live feed.

Real-life example 1, a CCTV camera in a shop: A shopkeeper in Mirpur installs an IP camera. The recorder box connects to the camera's RTSP address, sends SETUP and PLAY, and receives H.264 video in RTP packets. On the local network, loss and jitter are tiny, so a small buffer works. When the owner views the feed from home on a phone app, the stream is often relayed and repackaged for the internet, where the app adds a bigger buffer, so the picture lags real time by a few seconds.

Real-life example 2, a voice call on a crowded network: On a call during evening peak hours, the app's jitter buffer stretches its playout delay as jitter grows, and its codec conceals occasional losses. If losses become heavy, you hear robotic or garbled speech, the sign of concealment running out. Video calls in the same conditions freeze briefly and then jump, as the receiver waits for a fresh keyframe (lesson 16).

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Mistakes include thinking a bigger buffer fixes a link that is permanently too slow (it only delays the stall), confusing delay with jitter, assuming RTP provides QoS guarantees, and thinking RTSP carries the media. Exams ask you to classify applications, compute initial buffering for given rates, compute playout times with a jitter buffer, explain FEC with XOR and interleaving, list RTP header fields and their purpose, and compare TCP and UDP for media.

Recap: Media must arrive on time more than perfectly. Stored, live and conversational applications have very different delay budgets. A playout buffer absorbs rate dips and jitter; the 2 Mbps over 1.5 Mbps example needs 200 s of waiting, which is why we adapt instead. A jitter buffer plays each packet at send time plus a playout delay, trading lateness losses against latency. Loss is handled by concealment, XOR FEC (25 percent overhead for n = 4) and interleaving. RTP adds sequence numbers and timestamps, RTCP reports quality, and RTSP acts as a remote control. Next lesson: how HLS and DASH adapt quality to your connection.
key_points: Media data that arrives after its play time is useless; small losses are tolerable, so timeliness beats perfect reliability.
Three classes: streaming stored, streaming live, conversational (most delay-sensitive).
Initial buffering when bit rate r exceeds link rate R: wait = D x (r/R - 1); 10 min at 2 Mbps over 1.5 Mbps needs 200 s.
Jitter is variation in delay; a jitter buffer plays packets at send time + playout delay, trading late losses for latency.
Loss defences: concealment, FEC (XOR parity: 1 per 4 packets = 25% overhead, fixes one loss), interleaving.
Buffered streaming uses HTTP over TCP/QUIC; conversational media usually uses UDP with RTP.
RTP header (12 bytes): payload type, sequence number, timestamp, SSRC; G.711 at 20 ms becomes 80 kbps with headers.
RTCP reports loss and jitter; RTSP is a remote control (SETUP, PLAY, PAUSE, TEARDOWN) used by many IP cameras.
lessons.tip: For jitter buffer questions, make a three-column table: send time, arrival time, scheduled play time. Any row where arrival is later than the play time is a lost packet. The table never lets you miss one.
lessons.task: During a video call or while streaming on mobile data, note the moments when the picture freezes or the sound turns robotic. Then compute: if a 15-minute video is encoded at 1.2 Mbps and your connection gives 0.8 Mbps, how many seconds of initial buffering would avoid any stall? What bit rate would need no waiting?

quiz.q: A 10-minute video at 2 Mbps over a steady 1.5 Mbps link. Minimum initial wait to avoid stalls?
quiz.explain: Download 1,200 Mb / 1.5 = 800 s, minus 600 s of playback = 200 s.

quiz.q: What is jitter?
options: The bit rate of the video
quiz.explain: Jitter is how much the end-to-end delay changes from packet to packet.

quiz.q: Packets sent at 60 ms arrive at 140 ms. With a playout delay of 70 ms, the packet is:
options: Too late and treated as lost
quiz.explain: Its play time is 60 + 70 = 130 ms, before it arrives at 140 ms.

quiz.q: One XOR parity packet is sent per 4 data packets. What is the bandwidth overhead?
quiz.explain: One extra packet for every four is a 25 percent increase, and it can repair one loss per group.

quiz.q: Which RTP header field lets the receiver detect lost and reordered packets?
quiz.explain: Sequence numbers increase by one per packet, so gaps and reordering are visible.

lessons.title: Adaptive Bitrate Streaming: HLS and DASH
lessons.content:
Imagine you are watching a cricket match on your phone while riding a bus from Mirpur to Motijheel. Near the big roads your 4G signal is strong, then the bus goes under a flyover or into a crowded area and the signal drops. If the video had one fixed quality, it would either look blurry the whole time or freeze every few minutes. Instead, a good streaming app quietly makes the picture a bit softer when the network is weak and sharper again when it recovers. The match keeps playing. That quiet switching is called adaptive bitrate streaming, usually shortened to ABR, and it is how most video on the internet is delivered today.

What problem ABR solves: In the previous lesson we saw that a player must receive data at least as fast as it plays it, or the buffer runs dry and the video stalls. The trouble is that a viewer's throughput is not one number. It changes from second to second, and it is very different for a fibre user in Gulshan and a 3G user in a village in Kurigram. A server that sends one bit rate to everybody must choose: too high and many people stall, too low and everybody gets a poor picture. ABR removes that choice by preparing several versions and letting each viewer's player pick, again and again, the best one its connection can carry right now.

Streaming over plain HTTP: Older streaming systems used special servers and protocols such as RTSP with RTP over UDP. Modern ABR systems instead use ordinary HTTP, the same protocol that fetches web pages. The video is cut into small files and the player downloads them one by one with normal GET requests. This sounds less clever, but it has huge advantages. Ordinary web servers can host the files, HTTP passes easily through firewalls and NAT, and above all, the files can be cached by CDNs and proxy caches exactly like images and scripts. TCP underneath gives reliable delivery, and the buffer hides TCP's retransmission delays.

Segments: The encoder first produces the video at several quality levels. Each version is then cut into segments, short pieces that each hold a few seconds of video, commonly somewhere around 2 to 6 seconds. Every segment usually starts with an I-frame, so the player can begin decoding at any segment boundary. Crucially, the segment boundaries are aligned across all versions: segment 37 of the low-quality version covers exactly the same moments of the match as segment 37 of the high-quality version. That alignment is what makes switching seamless. The player can play segment 36 in high quality and segment 37 in low quality, and the viewer only notices the picture getting softer, never a jump in time.

The bitrate ladder: The set of versions is called the bitrate ladder, and each version is a rung. A simple ladder for a lecture or a drama might be: 240p at 400 kbps, 360p at 800 kbps, 720p at 1,500 kbps and 1080p at 3,000 kbps, plus an audio track. The exact numbers depend on the codec and the content. A talking-head lecture with a still background compresses far better than a fast football match, so some services tune the ladder for each title instead of using one ladder for everything. The bottom rung matters a lot in Bangladesh, because it decides whether someone on a weak mobile connection can watch at all.

A segment worked out: Take the 800 kbps rung with 4-second segments. One segment holds 800,000 bits per second times 4 seconds = 3,200,000 bits, which is 400,000 bytes, about 400 KB. If the phone's throughput is 1 Mbps, that segment takes 3.2 seconds to download, less than the 4 seconds it plays for, so the buffer grows. If throughput falls to 600 kbps, it takes about 5.3 seconds, more than 4, so the buffer shrinks by over a second per segment. That simple comparison, download time versus play time, is the heart of every ABR decision.

The manifest: How does the player know which rungs exist and where the segment files are? It first downloads a small text file called the manifest. The manifest lists the available versions with their bit rates, resolutions and codecs, and tells the player how to find each segment. The player reads the manifest once at the start (and again and again for live streams, because new segments keep appearing), then fetches segments directly.

HLS: HTTP Live Streaming, HLS, was introduced by Apple and is now supported very widely, on phones, browsers, smart TVs and set-top boxes. Its manifests are playlists with the extension .m3u8. A master (multivariant) playlist lists the variants, each with a line such as BANDWIDTH=800000,RESOLUTION=640x360, followed by the address of that variant's media playlist. Each media playlist lists the segments in order, each preceded by a tag like #EXTINF:4.0 giving its duration. Segments were traditionally MPEG transport stream files, and fragmented MP4 is now also used.

MPEG-DASH: Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP, DASH, is an international standard from the MPEG group. Its manifest is an XML file called the MPD, Media Presentation Description. Inside, Periods divide the timeline, Adaptation Sets group interchangeable versions (for example all the video versions, or all the audio languages), and each Representation is one rung with its own bit rate. DASH itself does not care which codec is used, so the same idea works for H.264, HEVC, VP9 or AV1. In practice many services prepare both HLS and DASH manifests that point to the same set of fragmented MP4 segments, an approach associated with the CMAF format, so they do not have to store the video twice.

Who decides, server or player: In ABR the intelligence lives in the player, not the server. The server is just a file host. This is a big design choice. It means millions of viewers can be served from caches without the server tracking anyone, and each player can make decisions using what it alone knows: its own measured download speed, its own buffer level and even its screen size. There is no point sending 1080p to a small phone screen in a power-saving mode, and a well-written player knows that.

Throughput-based switching: The simplest rule is to measure how fast recent segments downloaded and pick the highest rung safely below that. Suppose the last few segments arrived at an average of 1.2 Mbps. Throughput estimates are noisy, so players apply a safety margin, for example use only 80 percent: 1.2 x 0.8 = 0.96 Mbps. With the ladder 400, 800, 1,500 and 3,000 kbps, the highest rung under 960 kbps is 800 kbps, so the next segment is fetched at 360p. If speed later averages 2.5 Mbps, 80 percent is 2.0 Mbps and the player steps up to 1,500 kbps.

Buffer-based switching: Throughput estimates can be fooled by a single lucky or unlucky segment. Another family of methods looks mainly at the buffer. If the buffer holds only a few seconds, choose a low rung to fill it quickly. If it holds 30 seconds, it is safe to try a higher rung, because even a slow download has a cushion. Real players usually combine both signals and also avoid switching too often, since rapid up-down jumps in quality annoy viewers more than a steady slightly lower picture.

Startup and rebuffering: Two events dominate how viewers feel about a stream. Startup delay is the time from pressing play to seeing the first frame. Rebuffering, or stalling, is when playback freezes with a spinning circle. Studies of viewer behaviour consistently show stalls are very disliked, so players usually start at a modest rung to begin quickly, then climb. Choosing a short segment duration helps react faster but adds more requests and overhead; a long segment is efficient but makes switching sluggish. Engineers balance these.

Data use worked: For viewers on mobile data packs, the rung decides how quickly the pack runs out. Data per hour = bit rate x 3,600 seconds / 8. At 1 Mbps that is 1,000,000 x 3,600 / 8 = 450,000,000 bytes, which is 450 MB per hour. At 400 kbps it is 180 MB per hour, at 1,500 kbps 675 MB and at 3,000 kbps 1,350 MB, about 1.35 GB. A student with a 1 GB pack can watch a bit over two hours at 1 Mbps, or more than five hours at 400 kbps. This is why many apps offer a data saver setting that caps the ladder.

CDNs in the picture: Because segments are ordinary files, they can be copied to CDN servers near viewers. When a popular drama is released, the first viewer in Dhaka causes the nearby CDN node to fetch a segment from the origin; the next thousands of viewers get it from that node. Some international services also place caching servers inside local ISPs or at exchange points so that popular content does not need to cross the expensive international link every time. ABR and CDNs work hand in hand: CDNs make HTTP delivery cheap, and HTTP delivery makes CDNs usable for video.

Live streaming with ABR: For a live match, the encoder produces new segments every few seconds and keeps updating the manifest. The player refreshes the manifest to learn about new segments. Because a segment must be completely produced, uploaded and listed before players fetch it, and players keep a few segments in their buffer, classic HTTP live streams often lag the real event by many seconds, sometimes tens of seconds. Low-latency versions of HLS and DASH reduce this by delivering parts of a segment before the whole segment is finished. Truly interactive uses such as video calls still use RTP-style real-time delivery instead, as we will see next lesson.

Real-life example 1, a Bangladeshi OTT app: A local streaming platform uploads a new drama episode. Its encoding pipeline creates perhaps five video rungs and one or two audio tracks, cuts them into aligned 4-second segments, and writes both an m3u8 playlist and an MPD. The files go to the origin storage and are pulled into CDN caches. A viewer on home Wi-Fi in Chattogram starts at 360p, and within ten seconds the player sees fast downloads and climbs to 1080p. Another viewer on a crowded mobile network in Sylhet stays on 360p and occasionally drops to 240p, but rarely stalls. Same files, different experiences, no special work on the server.

Real-life example 2, an online class recording: A university posts recorded lectures. The teacher's slides and voice matter most; tiny details of the teacher's face do not. The team creates a ladder with a very low video rung plus a good audio track, and an audio-only option. Because the player can drop to the bottom rung while keeping clear audio, students in areas with patchy coverage can still follow the lecture. This is a direct application of ABR thinking: decide what matters most to the user and make sure the lowest rung still delivers it.

Common mistakes: Students often say ABR changes the bit rate in the middle of a segment; it switches only at segment boundaries. Another confusion is to think HLS and DASH are codecs; they are delivery formats, and the codec inside the segments is a separate choice. A third mistake is to think the server measures the network and picks the quality; in standard HLS and DASH the client decides. Finally, people mix up kbps and KB/s: 800 kbps is 100 KB per second, a factor of eight.

What exams ask: Define adaptive bitrate streaming and explain why HTTP is used. Draw the flow: encoder, ladder, segmenter, manifest, origin, CDN, player. Compare HLS and DASH (manifest format, origin, codec neutrality). Given a ladder and a measured throughput with a safety factor, pick the rung. Compute the size of one segment and the data use per hour of a rung. Explain the trade-off of short versus long segments and why live HTTP streams lag.

Recap: ABR prepares the same video at several bit rates, cuts every version into aligned segments, and describes them in a manifest. The player fetches segments over HTTP and chooses the rung for each segment using its throughput and buffer. HLS uses m3u8 playlists, DASH uses an XML MPD, and both work well with CDNs. Simple formulas, segment size = bit rate x duration / 8 and data per hour = bit rate x 3,600 / 8, let you reason about stalls and data packs.
key_points: ABR prepares several versions (a bitrate ladder) and lets the player choose the best rung for its current network.
Every version is cut into short segments with aligned boundaries, so switching happens cleanly between segments.
Delivery uses plain HTTP, which passes firewalls and lets CDNs cache segments like ordinary files.
HLS uses .m3u8 playlists (master plus media playlists); MPEG-DASH uses an XML MPD with Adaptation Sets and Representations.
The client, not the server, decides the rung, using measured throughput (with a safety margin) and buffer level.
Segment size = bit rate x duration / 8: 800 kbps x 4 s = 400 KB.
Data per hour = bit rate x 3,600 / 8: 1 Mbps = 450 MB, 400 kbps = 180 MB, 3 Mbps = 1.35 GB.
Classic live HTTP streams lag by several seconds or more; low-latency HLS/DASH reduce this.
lessons.tip: Whenever you see a streaming question, convert everything to the same unit first (bits per second and seconds), then compare download time with play time. Almost every ABR exam problem reduces to that one comparison.
lessons.task: Open YouTube on your phone, play a video and open "Stats for nerds" (or check the quality menu with Auto selected). Switch between Wi-Fi and mobile data and note how the resolution changes. Then calculate how many MB one hour would use at each quality you saw, assuming roughly 400 kbps for 360p and 1,500 kbps for 720p.

quiz.q: Why do ABR systems cut every version into segments with aligned boundaries?
options: So each segment can use a different codec
So the server can track every viewer
So segments can be sent over UDP
So the player can switch versions between segments without a jump in time
quiz.explain: Aligned boundaries mean segment k covers the same moments in every rung, so the player can switch rung at any boundary seamlessly.

quiz.q: A player measures 1.2 Mbps and uses an 80% safety margin. Ladder: 400, 800, 1,500, 3,000 kbps. Which rung does it pick?
quiz.explain: 1.2 x 0.8 = 0.96 Mbps; the highest rung below 960 kbps is 800 kbps.

quiz.q: What is the manifest format of MPEG-DASH?
options: An XML file called the MPD
quiz.explain: DASH describes periods, adaptation sets and representations in an XML Media Presentation Description.

quiz.q: How much data does one hour at 1 Mbps use?
In standard HLS/DASH, who decides which quality to download next?
quiz.explain: The server only hosts files; the player measures its throughput and buffer and chooses the rung.

lessons.title: QoS and Video Conferencing
lessons.content:
Think of a family video call on Eid: your cousin in Dubai, your aunt in Rajshahi and you in Dhaka. Watching a recorded drama, you do not mind if it starts two seconds late. In a call, two seconds of delay is a disaster: everybody talks over each other, then everybody waits, then everybody says "hello? can you hear me?" at once. Live conversation is the most demanding kind of multimedia, because the network must not only carry enough bits, it must carry them quickly and steadily. This lesson is about the measures of that quality, called Quality of Service, and about how video conferencing systems are built to survive real networks.

What QoS means: Quality of Service, QoS, is the set of measurable properties a network gives to a flow of packets, and the mechanisms that try to guarantee or improve them. Users experience quality as "the call was clear" or "it kept freezing"; that subjective feeling is often called Quality of Experience, QoE. QoS is the engineering side underneath: numbers we can measure and control. Good QoS usually leads to good QoE, but a smart application can also hide bad QoS, for example by concealing lost packets.

The four QoS parameters: The first is bandwidth or throughput, how many bits per second the flow gets. The second is delay or latency, how long a packet takes from sender to receiver. The third is jitter, the variation in that delay from packet to packet. The fourth is packet loss, the fraction of packets that never arrive or arrive too late to use. Different applications care about different parameters. File download cares about throughput and loss, but not much about delay. Stored video streaming needs throughput but can tolerate delay and jitter thanks to its buffer. A voice or video call needs moderate throughput but is very sensitive to delay and jitter, and fairly sensitive to loss.

How much delay is acceptable: For conversation, the delay that matters is mouth-to-ear, one way. The ITU-T recommendation G.114 gives planning guidance: up to about 150 milliseconds one way is acceptable for most conversations, delays up to roughly 400 ms can be tolerated in some cases with users noticing, and above that conversation becomes awkward and is generally not acceptable for planning. Note that satellite links in geostationary orbit already add about a quarter of a second each way just from the distance, which is why old satellite phone calls felt so clumsy.

A delay budget worked: Engineers split the 150 ms into a budget. Suppose capture and encoding take 30 ms, the network (propagation plus queuing) takes 60 ms, the receiver's jitter buffer holds 40 ms, and decoding plus playback take 20 ms. Total: 30 + 60 + 40 + 20 = 150 ms, right at the comfortable limit. If the call goes over a congested path that adds 80 ms of queuing, we are at 230 ms and people start interrupting each other. You can see why conferencing systems use small jitter buffers and fast codecs: every component must be lean.

Jitter, recapped: Packets of a call leave the sender every 20 ms, say, but arrive with gaps like 18, 25, 19, 40 ms because queues in routers change. The receiver holds packets in a jitter buffer and plays them at the steady original rate. A deeper buffer absorbs more jitter but adds delay; a shallow buffer keeps delay low but more packets arrive "too late" and count as lost. Many real systems use an adaptive jitter buffer that grows when the network is jittery and shrinks when it is calm.

Loss and how calls cope: Calls usually run over UDP with RTP, so lost packets are not retransmitted by the transport; a retransmitted voice packet would arrive too late anyway. Instead, receivers use packet loss concealment, for example repeating or smoothly stretching the previous audio, and video decoders freeze or patch the damaged area until the next good frame. Senders may add forward error correction, extra redundant data so some losses can be repaired without asking. When loss is heavy, the receiver can ask the sender for a fresh keyframe so the picture recovers quickly.

Best effort and its limits: The basic Internet is best effort: every packet is treated the same, with no promise about delay or loss. When a link is congested, a voice packet waits in the same queue as a big file download. For most of the Internet's history this was handled by over-provisioning (buying more capacity) plus clever applications. But inside company networks, ISP cores and mobile networks, engineers do use QoS mechanisms, which come in two classic architectures.

IntServ: Integrated Services aims for per-flow guarantees. Before sending, an application uses a signalling protocol, RSVP, to ask every router along the path to reserve resources for its flow. Each router must remember state for every flow. That gives strong guarantees, but it does not scale to the core of the Internet, where millions of flows pass through each router. IntServ is mostly studied as an idea today.

DiffServ: Differentiated Services takes a simpler route. Packets are marked at the edge of the network with a small code in the IP header, the DSCP (Differentiated Services Code Point), 6 bits in the old Type of Service byte. Core routers do not track flows; they just look at the mark and apply a per-hop behaviour, such as Expedited Forwarding for voice (low delay, low jitter) or Assured Forwarding classes for important data. Because routers handle a few classes rather than millions of flows, DiffServ scales well and is widely used inside managed networks.

Scheduling and shaping recap: The per-hop behaviours are implemented with schedulers you met in Computer Networks: priority queues (voice queue served first), weighted fair queuing (each class gets a share), and policing or shaping using a token bucket. A token bucket with rate r and size b lets a flow send at most b + r t bits in any t seconds. With r = 2 Mbps and b = 1 Mb, the flow can send at most 1 + 2 x 1 = 3 Mb in any one second: bursts are allowed, but only up to the bucket size.

What conferencing systems must do: A video call has to capture camera and microphone, encode them, send them to several people, receive their streams, decode, mix or arrange them on screen, and play everything in sync, all within the delay budget. The hard design question is: how do streams travel between participants? There are three classic architectures.

Mesh (peer to peer): Every participant sends their stream directly to every other participant. With n people, each person uploads n - 1 copies and the call has n(n - 1) streams in total. With 3 people that is 6 streams; with 5 people it is 20 streams, and each person uploads 4 copies. If one copy is 1 Mbps, each person needs 4 Mbps of upload, which many home and mobile connections in Bangladesh cannot give. With 10 people it is 90 streams. Mesh is simple and needs no server for media, so it is fine for two or three people, but it collapses quickly.

SFU (Selective Forwarding Unit): Every participant uploads one stream to a server, and the server forwards copies to the others without decoding them. With 5 people, the SFU receives 5 streams and sends out 20, but each participant uploads only 1 and downloads 4. Server CPU is low because it just forwards packets, and it can choose which streams to forward to whom, for example only the active speaker in high quality. Most modern conferencing services are built around SFUs.

MCU (Multipoint Control Unit): The server decodes every incoming stream, mixes the audio and composes the video into one grid picture, re-encodes it and sends each participant a single stream. Clients have the easiest job, one upload and one download, which suits weak devices. But the server does heavy work, adds delay for decoding and re-encoding, and everybody gets the same layout. MCUs were common in older room systems; SFUs are more common now.

Simulcast and SVC: In an SFU call, receivers differ: one is on fibre, another on a weak phone. With simulcast, each sender encodes its camera at, say, two or three qualities at once and uploads all of them; the SFU forwards to each receiver the copy that fits that receiver. With scalable video coding, SVC, the sender produces one layered stream, a base layer plus enhancement layers, and the SFU drops layers for weaker receivers. Both bring the ABR idea of the last lesson into real-time calls.

WebRTC and signalling: WebRTC is the browser and app technology that makes real-time calls possible without plug-ins. It provides camera and microphone access, codecs (Opus for audio is standard; common video codecs include VP8 and H.264), encrypted transport with SRTP, congestion control, and NAT traversal with ICE, STUN and TURN, because most users sit behind NAT. WebRTC deliberately does not define signalling, the step where peers exchange who they are and which codecs they support (described with SDP). Apps can use their own signalling over WebSocket, or SIP, the text-based call-setup protocol used widely in VoIP telephony, with requests like INVITE.

Audio processing matters most: People forgive a blurry picture but not bad sound. Conferencing clients run acoustic echo cancellation, so the far side does not hear its own voice coming back from your speaker; noise suppression to remove fans and traffic; and automatic gain control to even out loud and quiet speakers. Many apps even lower video quality first to protect audio when the network struggles.

Real-life example 1, an online class during a power cut: A teacher in Khulna runs a class for 40 students on a conferencing app. The service uses an SFU. The teacher uploads one camera stream using simulcast and one screen-share stream; students with weak 3G receive the low simulcast layer, while those on broadband receive the higher one. Most students keep their cameras off, which saves both their upload and the SFU's forwarding. When the teacher's network briefly drops packets, Opus's concealment smooths the audio and the video freezes for a moment until a new keyframe arrives.

Real-life example 2, a telemedicine consultation: A doctor at a city hospital talks to a patient at an upazila health complex. Two people means a direct peer-to-peer WebRTC call is enough, with a TURN relay as a backup if NAT blocks the direct path. The hospital network marks call packets with a DiffServ class so that large file backups in the hospital do not delay them. The delay budget is kept under about 150 ms within the country, so the conversation feels natural.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Do not confuse jitter with delay: a link can have a large but steady delay and no jitter. Do not say mesh scales; it grows as n(n - 1). Remember SFU forwards without decoding, MCU decodes and mixes. Exams ask you to list QoS parameters and which applications need what, compare IntServ and DiffServ, compute stream counts and upload needs for mesh versus SFU, build a delay budget against G.114 guidance, and explain simulcast versus SVC.

Recap: QoS is measured by bandwidth, delay, jitter and loss. Conversation needs low one-way delay, around 150 ms or less, so every stage has a small budget. IntServ reserves per flow and does not scale; DiffServ marks packets into classes and does. Conferencing uses mesh for tiny calls, SFUs for most group calls and MCUs where clients are weak, with simulcast or SVC to fit different receivers, and WebRTC to bring it all to browsers.
key_points: QoS parameters: bandwidth, delay, jitter and packet loss; QoE is how the user actually feels about quality.
ITU-T G.114 guidance: about 150 ms one-way delay or less keeps conversation natural; much beyond 400 ms is generally unacceptable.
Delay budget example: 30 encode + 60 network + 40 jitter buffer + 20 decode = 150 ms.
IntServ (RSVP, per-flow state) gives guarantees but does not scale; DiffServ marks packets with DSCP and routers treat classes.
Mesh needs n(n - 1) streams: 5 people = 20 streams, 4 uploads each.
SFU forwards streams without decoding (1 up, n - 1 down per user); MCU decodes, mixes and re-encodes into one stream.
Simulcast (several encodings) and SVC (layers) let an SFU give each receiver a fitting quality.
WebRTC provides media, SRTP encryption, congestion control and ICE/STUN/TURN; signalling is left to the app (often WebSocket or SIP).
lessons.tip: For any conferencing question, draw the participants as dots and the server as a box, then literally count arrows. Stream counts and upload needs fall out of the picture.
lessons.task: Make a group video call with three or four friends on any app. Note how the quality changes when one person moves to a weak signal, and whether audio or video suffers first. Then compute how many streams a mesh call with your group would need and how much upload each person would need at 1 Mbps per stream.

quiz.q: Which QoS parameter measures the variation in packet delay?
quiz.explain: Jitter is the variation of delay from packet to packet; latency is the delay itself.

quiz.q: How many streams does a full mesh call with 5 participants need?
quiz.explain: n(n - 1) = 5 x 4 = 20 streams; each person uploads 4.

quiz.q: What does an SFU do with incoming video streams?
options: Forwards them to other participants without decoding
Decodes and mixes them into one picture
Stores them and sends them later
quiz.explain: A Selective Forwarding Unit only forwards (and selects) packets; mixing is what an MCU does.

quiz.q: Why does DiffServ scale better than IntServ?
options: It uses UDP instead of TCP
It reserves bandwidth per flow with RSVP
Routers treat a few marked classes instead of keeping per-flow state
quiz.explain: DiffServ marks packets with DSCP at the edge; core routers apply per-hop behaviour per class, not per flow.

quiz.q: Following G.114 guidance, which one-way delay keeps a conversation comfortable for most users?
options: Any delay, if jitter is zero
quiz.explain: G.114 suggests up to about 150 ms one way is acceptable for most conversational applications.

lessons.title: Multimedia Databases and Content-Based Retrieval
lessons.content:
Suppose your phone has 12,000 photos and you want the one of the green paddy field you took in Sreemangal last winter. You do not remember the date, and you never typed a caption. Searching "paddy" in a normal database finds nothing, because there is no text to match. Yet your gallery app may find it anyway, by looking at the pictures themselves. That is the big idea of this lesson: storing images, audio and video in a way that lets us search by what they contain, not only by the words someone typed about them.

Why ordinary tables are not enough: A classic relational database is excellent at exact questions on structured fields: "students with CGPA above 3.5", "orders from Sylhet in March". Multimedia breaks this model in three ways. First, the objects are huge: one photo can be several megabytes, one lecture video several hundred. Second, they have no natural fields to compare; two photos of the same field are never equal byte for byte. Third, users ask fuzzy questions: "pictures like this one", "the song that goes like this". A multimedia database system must therefore store large objects efficiently, describe them with features, and answer similarity queries ranked from most to least similar.

Storing the objects, BLOB or path: There are two common ways to keep media. One is to put the bytes inside the database as a BLOB, a binary large object. This keeps everything in one place, with transactions and backups covering the media too. The other is to store the media as files, today often in an object storage service, and keep only the path or key plus metadata in the database. This is much more common for large collections because file and object stores are cheaper, can be served directly by web servers and CDNs, and keep the database small and fast. Either way, the database also holds the descriptions we search on.

Metadata and text-based retrieval: The first and simplest way to search media is by its metadata. Some metadata is automatic: file type, size, resolution, duration, codec, and for photos the EXIF data such as capture time, camera model and sometimes GPS location. Some is added by people: title, tags, captions, the speaker's name, the subject of a lecture. Text-based retrieval then uses ordinary text search. It is fast and works well when good tags exist, as on YouTube, where titles and descriptions carry much of the search. Its weaknesses are that tagging by hand is slow and costly, different people use different words, and most personal media is never tagged at all.

Content-based retrieval: Content-based retrieval, CBIR for images, searches using features computed from the media itself. The pipeline has two phases. Offline, when an object is added, the system extracts a feature vector, a list of numbers that summarise its colour, texture, shape or sound, and stores it in an index. Online, the user gives a query, often an example image (query by example), a rough sketch, or a hummed tune; the system extracts the same kind of features from the query, measures the distance to stored vectors, and returns the closest items in ranked order.

Colour histogram features: The simplest image feature is a colour histogram: count how many pixels fall into each colour bin, then divide by the total number of pixels so the bins sum to 1. With 4 levels per channel there are 4 x 4 x 4 = 64 bins; with 8 levels, 512 bins. A histogram ignores where colours are, so it is unaffected by small shifts and rotation, and normalising makes it independent of image size. The price is that very different pictures can share a histogram: a red flag on green grass and a green flag on red earth may look alike to it.

Histogram intersection worked: To keep numbers small, use just 4 bins: green, sky blue, brown and red. The query photo of the paddy field has Q = [0.5, 0.3, 0.2, 0]. Stored image A, another field shot with a red-roofed hut, has A = [0.4, 0.2, 0.1, 0.3]. Stored image B, a sunset over a red brick building, has B = [0.1, 0.1, 0.2, 0.6]. Histogram intersection adds the smaller value in each bin: for Q and A, min(0.5, 0.4) + min(0.3, 0.2) + min(0.2, 0.1) + min(0, 0.3) = 0.4 + 0.2 + 0.1 + 0 = 0.7. For Q and B: 0.1 + 0.1 + 0.2 + 0 = 0.4. A higher intersection means more similar, with 1 meaning identical histograms, so A is ranked first.

Distances as an alternative: We could instead use Euclidean distance, the square root of the sum of squared differences. Q to A: differences 0.1, 0.1, 0.1 and 0.3, squares sum to 0.12, distance about 0.346. Q to B: about 0.748. Smaller distance means more similar, so again A wins. Different measures can rank items differently in harder cases, which is why systems tune the measure to the feature.

Texture and shape: Colour alone cannot tell a brick wall from a red carpet. Texture features describe patterns of brightness change: coarse or fine, smooth or rough, directional or not. Classic methods compute statistics from co-occurrence matrices of neighbouring grey levels, or measure energy in filters tuned to different directions and scales. Shape features first separate an object from its background, then describe its outline with measures like area, perimeter, compactness or moments, ideally unchanged by moving, scaling or rotating the object. The MPEG-7 standard defined a common vocabulary of such descriptors for colour, texture, shape, motion and audio.

The semantic gap: Low-level features measure pixels, but people search for meanings: "my grandmother", "a wedding", "a goal by Shakib". The distance between what features capture and what users mean is called the semantic gap. A white wall and a white sari can share colour and smoothness. Systems narrow the gap with relevance feedback, where the user marks results as good or bad and the system adjusts, and increasingly with learned features: neural networks trained on many labelled images produce feature vectors, often called embeddings, in which pictures with similar meaning lie close together. Some models are trained on images with captions so that text and images share one vector space, letting a typed phrase search untagged photos. The retrieval idea, nearest vectors win, stays the same.

Nearest-neighbour search: Given a query vector, the system returns the k nearest neighbours, the k stored vectors with the smallest distance. A simple linear scan compares the query with every stored vector; with a few thousand photos on a phone that is fine. With a hundred million images it is far too slow. Classic index trees such as k-d trees and R-trees prune large parts of the space, but they lose their advantage as the number of dimensions grows into the hundreds, a problem known as the curse of dimensionality. Large systems therefore use approximate nearest-neighbour methods, which accept occasionally missing the true best match in exchange for huge speed-ups. Dedicated vector databases are built around such indexes.

Audio retrieval and fingerprinting: Audio can be searched by metadata (title, artist), by content features such as tempo, pitch or timbre, or by fingerprint. The published idea behind song recognition apps like Shazam is to compute a spectrogram of a few seconds of the recording, pick out strong peaks in time and frequency, and turn pairs of peaks into compact hashes. The database holds hashes for millions of songs. A noisy clip recorded in a tea stall still shares many peak pairs with the original, and when many hashes match with a consistent time offset, the song is identified. Query by humming instead compares pitch contours, the up-down shape of a melody.

Video retrieval: Video adds time. A video is first split into shots, continuous runs from one camera; a shot boundary often shows as a large jump in the colour histogram between consecutive frames. From each shot, one or a few keyframes are picked and indexed like images. Speech in the soundtrack can be turned into text by speech recognition and searched with ordinary text search, and on-screen text can be read with OCR. This combination lets a lecture archive answer "find where the teacher explains Huffman coding" by matching words in the transcript and slides.

Measuring retrieval quality: How good is a search? Two classic measures come from information retrieval. Precision is the fraction of returned items that are relevant; recall is the fraction of all relevant items that were returned. Suppose the database holds 8 photos of the paddy field, and a search returns 10 photos of which 6 are paddy field shots. Precision = 6 / 10 = 0.6; recall = 6 / 8 = 0.75. Returning more items usually raises recall and lowers precision. The F1 score combines them: 2 x 0.6 x 0.75 / (0.6 + 0.75) = about 0.667.

Real-life example 1, a photo gallery on your phone: Modern gallery apps run models on the phone or in the cloud to compute embeddings for every photo, detect faces and group them, and read text in screenshots. When you type "mountain" or "receipt", the app compares the text query with photo embeddings, ranks them by similarity, and combines that with metadata such as date and location. Your Sreemangal paddy field shows up even though you never tagged it.

Real-life example 2, a news archive in Dhaka: A television newsroom has thousands of hours of footage. It stores videos in object storage and keeps a database with metadata: date, reporter, location, Bangla and English transcripts from speech recognition, and keyframes from shot detection. An editor looking for flood footage from Sunamganj searches by text and date, then browses keyframes and can ask for "more shots like this one" using visual similarity. Because transcripts are stored in Unicode, Bangla search works properly.

Common mistakes: Students sometimes think content-based retrieval understands meaning; classic features only measure low-level properties, hence the semantic gap. Another mistake is mixing similarity and distance: a higher intersection means more similar, but a higher distance means less similar. Some forget to normalise histograms, so a big photo looks "more red" than a small one just because it has more pixels. And precision and recall are often swapped; remember precision looks at what you returned, recall looks at what you should have returned.

What exams ask: Explain why conventional databases are unsuitable for multimedia. Compare text-based and content-based retrieval. Draw the CBIR architecture (feature extraction, index, query, similarity, ranking, feedback). Compute histogram intersection or Euclidean distance for small histograms. Define the semantic gap and the curse of dimensionality. Compute precision and recall from a result list. Describe shot detection or audio fingerprinting in a few steps.

Recap: Multimedia databases store large objects as BLOBs or, more often, as files with metadata in the database. Retrieval can use metadata and text, or content features such as colour histograms, texture, shape and learned embeddings. Similarity is measured by intersection or distance and served by nearest-neighbour indexes, often approximate. Audio uses fingerprints and video uses shots, keyframes and transcripts. Precision and recall tell you how well it all works.
key_points: Multimedia objects are large, have no exact fields to compare, and need similarity queries ranked by closeness.
Media is stored as BLOBs or, more often, as files/objects with the path and metadata in the database.
Text-based retrieval uses metadata and tags; content-based retrieval compares feature vectors computed from the media.
A normalised colour histogram ignores position; 8 levels per channel gives 512 bins.
Histogram intersection worked: Q = [0.5,0.3,0.2,0] vs A = [0.4,0.2,0.1,0.3] gives 0.7; vs B gives 0.4, so A ranks first.
The semantic gap separates low-level features from meaning; relevance feedback and learned embeddings narrow it.
High-dimensional search suffers the curse of dimensionality, so large systems use approximate nearest-neighbour indexes.
Precision = relevant returned / returned; recall = relevant returned / all relevant (6/10 = 0.6, 6/8 = 0.75).
lessons.tip: Keep two directions straight: similarity scores go up when things match, distances go down. Write "higher is better" or "lower is better" next to every measure you use in an answer.
lessons.task: Pick three photos from your phone: two of similar scenes and one very different. On paper, estimate a 4-bin histogram for each (green, blue, brown/grey, red/other, fractions summing to 1), then compute the histogram intersection of the first photo with the other two. Does the ranking match what your eyes say?

quiz.q: What is the main reason content-based retrieval is needed?
options: Most media has no useful tags, and users want "find things like this"
quiz.explain: Untagged media and similarity queries cannot be served by matching typed text alone.

quiz.q: Histogram intersection of Q = [0.5, 0.3, 0.2, 0] and A = [0.4, 0.2, 0.1, 0.3] is:
quiz.explain: Sum of bin-wise minimums: 0.4 + 0.2 + 0.1 + 0 = 0.7.

quiz.q: What is the "semantic gap"?
options: The time between upload and indexing
The difference between low-level features and the meaning users search for
The gap between precision and recall
quiz.explain: Features measure colour, texture and shape, but users search for concepts like "wedding" or "grandmother".

quiz.q: A search returns 10 items, 6 relevant; the database holds 8 relevant items. What is the recall?
quiz.explain: Recall = relevant returned / all relevant = 6 / 8 = 0.75. Precision would be 6 / 10 = 0.6.

quiz.q: How is a shot boundary in a video commonly detected?
options: By a large jump in the colour histogram between consecutive frames
quiz.explain: Within a shot consecutive frames look alike; a cut causes a sudden large histogram difference.

lessons.title: Authoring Tools and AR/VR Media
lessons.content:
A wedding video maker in Old Dhaka does not just press record. Before the day, she plans which moments to capture. On the day, she films from several angles. Afterwards, she sits at a computer, lays clips on a timeline, adds music, titles and transitions, then exports versions for YouTube, Facebook and a USB drive for the family. That whole craft, planning, assembling and publishing media into one experience, is called multimedia authoring. This lesson covers how authoring is organised, the main styles of authoring tools, and then the newest kinds of media we author for: 360-degree video, virtual reality and augmented reality.

What authoring means: Authoring is the process of combining media elements, text, images, audio, video and animation, into a structured and often interactive product, and defining how they behave: when each appears, how long it stays, what happens when the user clicks or taps. An authoring tool is software that lets people do this without writing every detail in a programming language. The product might be an e-learning module, a museum kiosk, an interactive story, a promotional video or a website.

The production process: Most multimedia projects move through three stages. Pre-production is planning: deciding the audience and goal, writing a script, drawing a storyboard (a sequence of sketches showing each scene or screen) and, for interactive work, a flowchart or navigation map showing how screens link. Production is creating and gathering the assets: recording audio, shooting video, drawing graphics, writing text, and checking permissions for anything borrowed. Post-production is assembling, editing, testing with real users and finally publishing in the right formats. Skipping pre-production is the classic beginner mistake; changing a storyboard costs minutes, changing a finished video costs days.

Paradigm 1, timeline-based: In timeline tools, time runs from left to right, and each media element sits on a track as a bar showing when it starts and ends. Video editors work this way, and so did classic animation and multimedia tools such as Macromedia Director and Flash, whose idea lives on in animation tools today. Timelines are perfect for linear or mostly linear products: a documentary, an animated explainer, a slideshow with narration. Interaction is possible, for example jumping to a marker when a button is clicked, but complex branching quickly becomes hard to follow.

Paradigm 2, card or page-based: Here the product is a stack of cards or pages, and each page holds media plus buttons that link to other pages. Apple's HyperCard was the famous early example, and presentation software and many e-book and e-learning tools follow the same model. It suits content you navigate rather than watch: a quiz, a catalogue, a reference guide. The structure is easy to understand, though precise timing of media inside a page is weaker than in a timeline.

Paradigm 3, icon or flow-based: Here the author builds a flowchart of icons: display this, wait for input, decide based on the answer, play a sound, loop back. Authorware was the well-known example. Flow-based authoring is strong for training programs with branching logic, such as "if the learner answers wrongly twice, show a hint video". Many modern visual scripting systems, including the node graphs in game engines, use the same idea; game engines themselves are covered in the Game Development course.

Scripting and the web as the authoring target: Most serious authoring tools also offer a scripting language for logic the visual interface cannot express. Today the most common target platform is the web. HTML5 gives native elements for media: video and audio elements that play files directly in the browser, a canvas element for drawing graphics and animation with JavaScript, and a track element that attaches subtitle or caption files in the WebVTT format. A tiny example: a video element with a source file lecture.mp4 and a track pointing to captions-bn.vtt with language "bn" gives a lecture with Bangla captions that works on phones and laptops without any plug-in. Many e-learning tools export to HTML5 for exactly this reason.

Designing for people: Good authoring follows a few principles. Keep navigation consistent, so buttons stay in the same place on every screen. Do not overload: a slide full of text plus narration reading different text splits attention. Give users control: pause, replay, skip. Keep file sizes appropriate for the audience's network, which in Bangladesh often means mobile data. And test with real users early, because what is obvious to the author is often confusing to a first-time viewer.

Accessibility: Multimedia must work for people with disabilities. Captions or subtitles help deaf and hard-of-hearing users, and also anyone watching on a noisy bus. Transcripts let people search and read. Images need alternative text, a short description read aloud by screen readers. Video can carry audio description for blind users. Colour should not be the only way to show meaning, and text needs enough contrast. International guidelines such as WCAG describe these practices. Building them in from the start is far easier than adding them later.

From flat screens to immersive media: All media so far was shown in a rectangle. Immersive media tries to surround the viewer. Three related ideas are often confused. 360-degree video records every direction around the camera, and the viewer looks around by turning a phone or a headset. Virtual reality, VR, replaces the user's view entirely with a computer-generated or recorded world shown in a headset. Augmented reality, AR, keeps the real world visible and adds digital objects on top of it, through a phone camera or see-through glasses.

360-degree video and the equirectangular projection: A 360 camera usually has two or more wide lenses whose images are stitched into one sphere of view. To store a sphere in an ordinary video file, it is flattened, most commonly with the equirectangular projection, the same idea as a world map in which longitude becomes x and latitude becomes y. The full view covers 360 degrees across and 180 degrees up-down, so the frame has a 2:1 shape, for example 3840 x 1920. Areas near the poles are stretched, just as Greenland looks huge on a flat map, which wastes pixels; alternative layouts such as cube maps reduce this waste.

Why 360 video looks soft, worked: Suppose a 360 video is 3840 pixels wide, covering 360 degrees. A viewer whose headset or screen shows a 90-degree field of view sees only 90/360 of the width: 3840 x 90 / 360 = 960 pixels across. So a "4K" 360 video looks roughly like a 960-pixel-wide normal video in the viewer's window, which is why it looks soft. To get about 1920 pixels across the visible window, you need a 7680-pixel-wide frame, which is why 360 content needs very high resolutions and bit rates.

Stereoscopic VR: Our two eyes see slightly different views, and the brain merges them into depth. Stereoscopic VR shows a separate image to each eye. For video, two views are recorded and often packed into one frame, top-bottom or side by side. That doubles the pixels: a stereo 3840 x 1920 view needs 3840 x 1920 x 2 = 14,745,600 pixels per frame, before compression. Headsets also add lenses so a screen a few centimetres from the eye looks distant and wide.

Comfort: frame rate and latency: VR has a special problem: if the image does not follow your head quickly and smoothly, the mismatch between what your eyes see and what your inner ear feels can cause discomfort and motion sickness. Headsets therefore refresh fast, typically somewhere between about 72 and 120 frames per second. At 90 frames per second, each frame has a time budget of 1000 / 90, about 11.1 ms, for tracking, rendering and display. The motion-to-photon latency, from moving your head to seeing the updated image, is often said to need to stay around 20 ms or less for comfort. This is a far stricter demand than ordinary video.

Degrees of freedom: A 360 video lets you turn your head (yaw, pitch, roll) but not move through the scene: three degrees of freedom, 3DoF. Full VR with computer-generated 3D worlds also tracks position, so you can lean, crouch and walk: six degrees of freedom, 6DoF. 6DoF needs the world as 3D models, not just a recorded sphere, because the view must be rendered fresh from wherever your head goes.

3D assets and spatial audio: 3D media is described by meshes, materials and textures (see Computer Graphics). For sharing and the web, a widely used format is glTF from the Khronos Group, designed to be compact and fast to load, sometimes called the JPEG of 3D. Older formats such as OBJ and FBX are also common, and Apple platforms use USDZ for AR objects. Sound matters too: spatial audio places sounds in 3D so a voice seems to come from the left when its source is on your left, and 360 video often uses ambisonics, a way of recording the full sound field that can be rotated as the viewer turns.

How AR works: AR must know where the camera is and what surfaces exist. Early AR used printed markers, patterns the camera could recognise. Modern phone AR, through platforms such as ARCore and ARKit, uses markerless tracking: it combines the camera image with motion sensors to track the phone's position, detects floors and tables, and estimates lighting, so a virtual object can sit on a real table and stay put as you walk around it. The media challenge is to render the overlay in real time and match its lighting and scale to the real scene.

Real-life example 1, a virtual museum tour: Imagine the Liberation War Museum or a heritage site like Sompur Mahavihara offering an online 360 tour. A team shoots 360 photos at many points, stitches them, saves them as equirectangular images, and authors a web page where visitors look around and tap hotspots to jump to the next point, play narration in Bangla or English, or open close-up photos of artefacts. This is card-based authoring wrapped around 360 media, and it reaches students across the country on ordinary phones.

Real-life example 2, AR in a textbook or shop: A science book could print a marker next to a diagram of the heart. Pointing a phone at it shows a beating 3D heart model in glTF that students can rotate. A furniture shop uses AR so a customer in Chattogram can see a sofa model at true size in their living room before buying. Both depend on small, well-compressed 3D assets, because the users are on mobile data.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Do not mix up VR (replaces the view) and AR (adds to the real view); 360 video is a form of immersive media that is usually 3DoF. Remember the equirectangular frame is 2:1 and wastes pixels near the poles.
