Exams ask you to compare timeline, card and flow paradigms with examples, describe the stages of multimedia production and the role of a storyboard, explain why 360 video needs high resolution (with the 90-degree calculation), explain why VR needs high frame rates and low latency, and contrast 3DoF with 6DoF.

Recap: Authoring combines media into structured, often interactive products, through pre-production, production and post-production. Tools follow timeline, card/page or icon/flow paradigms, with scripting and HTML5 as the common target, and accessibility must be built in. Immersive media extends this: 360 video stores a sphere in a 2:1 equirectangular frame, VR demands stereo images, high frame rates and low latency, and AR overlays 3D assets on a tracked real scene.
key_points: Multimedia production runs through pre-production (script, storyboard, flowchart), production (assets) and post-production (assembly, testing, publishing).
Authoring paradigms: timeline-based (linear media), card/page-based (navigable content), icon/flow-based (branching logic).
HTML5 video, audio, canvas and track (WebVTT captions) make the web the most common authoring target.
Accessibility (captions, transcripts, alt text, contrast) should be designed in from the start.
360 video is usually stored equirectangular in a 2:1 frame; a 90-degree view of a 3840-wide frame shows only 960 pixels across.
Stereo VR needs one image per eye, doubling pixels; headsets refresh at roughly 72-120 fps (90 fps = about 11.1 ms per frame).
3DoF allows turning only; 6DoF also tracks position and needs 3D models rather than a recorded sphere.
AR overlays virtual objects on the real view using markers or markerless tracking; glTF is a common compact 3D format.
lessons.tip: Before any multimedia project, even a class presentation, spend ten minutes on a paper storyboard. It is the cheapest place to fix mistakes, and examiners love a neat storyboard in project answers.
lessons.task: Take any 360 photo app or the panorama mode on your phone and capture a full view of your room or a nearby place. Then calculate: if the panorama is 4000 pixels wide for 360 degrees, how many pixels wide is a 90-degree slice? Finally, sketch a three-screen storyboard for a tiny interactive tour of that place.

quiz.q: Which authoring paradigm is best suited to a linear animated explainer video?
quiz.explain: Timeline tools place media on tracks over time, ideal for linear, precisely timed products.

quiz.q: A 360 video is 3840 pixels wide. How many pixels across does a 90-degree view show?
quiz.explain: 3840 x 90 / 360 = 960 pixels, which is why 360 video looks soft.

quiz.q: What is the usual aspect ratio of an equirectangular 360 frame?
quiz.explain: It covers 360 degrees across and 180 degrees vertically, giving a 2:1 frame such as 3840 x 1920.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between AR and VR?
options: AR needs a headset, VR needs a phone
AR adds digital objects to the real view; VR replaces the view entirely
quiz.explain: Augmented reality overlays content on the real world; virtual reality replaces what you see.

quiz.q: Why do VR headsets need high frame rates and low motion-to-photon latency?
options: To keep the image in step with head movement and avoid discomfort
quiz.explain: Lag between head motion and image causes a mismatch with the inner ear that can lead to motion sickness.

lessons.title: Copyright, DRM and Multimedia Ethics
lessons.content:
A young filmmaker in Rajshahi spends six months and her savings making a short film. Two days after release, a full copy appears on a Facebook page with a million followers, with her name cropped out. Meanwhile, a student in Dhaka puts a popular song under his class project video and is surprised when YouTube blocks it in some countries. Both stories are about the same question: who is allowed to copy, change and share a piece of media, and how is that enforced? Multimedia makes copying perfect and free, so the rules, the technology and the ethics around it matter more than ever.

Why this belongs in a CSE course: As engineers you will build the upload buttons, players, recommendation engines and editing tools. Your design decisions decide whether creators get credit, whether users' privacy leaks through a photo, and whether fake videos spread. You do not need to be a lawyer, but you must understand the basic ideas, the protection technologies and the ethical risks well enough to design responsibly and to know when to ask a lawyer.

Copyright basics: Copyright is a legal right given to the creator of an original work, such as a text, photo, song, recording, film, drawing or software, to control how it is copied and used. Under the international Berne Convention, which most countries follow, copyright arises automatically when the work is created and fixed; no registration is required, although many countries, including Bangladesh, have a copyright office where registration can serve as useful evidence. Copyright protects the expression, not the idea: anyone may make a film about a village flood, but nobody may copy your particular footage.

What the owner controls: The owner typically controls reproduction (making copies), distribution, adaptation (translations, remixes, dubbing), public performance and communication to the public, which includes streaming and uploading. Many systems also recognise moral rights: the right to be named as the author and to object to distorting changes. Copyright lasts a long time, commonly the author's life plus several decades, but the exact term depends on the country and the type of work. When it ends, the work enters the public domain and anyone may use it freely.

Ownership in practice: A single song can involve several separate rights: the composer and lyricist own the musical work, the label or producer often owns the sound recording, and performers may have their own related rights. A film bundles script, music, footage and performances. This is why "I bought the CD" or "it is on YouTube" does not mean you may reuse it. Works made by employees as part of their job are often owned by the employer, depending on contract and law.

Exceptions: fair use and fair dealing: Copyright is not absolute. Laws allow some uses without permission. The United States uses a flexible fair use test that weighs four factors: the purpose (for example education or commentary, and whether the use transforms the work), the nature of the work, how much is used, and the effect on the market for the original. Many other countries use fair dealing, a narrower list of allowed purposes such as research, private study, criticism, review and news reporting. Details differ by country, so a short quoted clip in a film review may be allowed, while re-uploading a whole drama "for education" usually is not.

Creative Commons: Many creators want people to share their work, with some conditions. Creative Commons licences give a ready-made way to say so. The building blocks are BY (give attribution), SA (share alike: adaptations must use the same licence), NC (non-commercial use only) and ND (no derivatives: no changes). So CC BY-SA lets anyone reuse and adapt with credit, if they share alike, while CC BY-NC-ND only allows sharing unchanged copies for non-commercial purposes. CC0 lets the creator waive rights as far as the law allows, close to public domain. Wikipedia text and many Wikimedia Commons images use such licences, which is why they are safe to reuse when you follow the conditions.

What DRM is: Digital Rights Management, DRM, is technology that controls how digital content can be used after delivery, for example allowing playback only on a paid account, only on a limited number of devices, only for a rental period, or blocking screen recording. Law alone cannot stop a perfect copy from being made in a second, so streaming services, and the film studios that license content to them, rely on DRM as a technical fence.

How streaming DRM works: The video is encrypted, commonly with AES, before it is placed on the CDN; for DASH and HLS a common encryption scheme lets one set of encrypted segments serve several DRM systems. The encrypted segments can be cached anywhere, because they are useless without keys. When you press play, the player sends a licence request to a licence server, together with proof of your account. The server checks the rules (subscription active? region allowed? device limit?) and returns the decryption key wrapped so that only a trusted component on your device, called a content decryption module, can use it. In browsers this is connected through a standard interface called Encrypted Media Extensions.

The main DRM systems: Three systems dominate streaming: Google's Widevine (Android, Chrome and many smart TVs), Apple's FairPlay (Apple devices and Safari) and Microsoft's PlayReady (Windows and many TVs). A service that wants to reach every device often supports all three. Systems usually define security levels; when decryption happens inside protected hardware, the service may allow full HD or 4K, and when it happens only in software, it may limit resolution. On the cable to the TV, a separate protection called HDCP encrypts the digital video link.

Limits and criticism of DRM: DRM raises the effort for casual copying, but it cannot stop everything. A person can still point a camera at a screen, the so-called analog hole, and determined attackers sometimes break specific implementations. Critics point out that DRM can inconvenience paying customers: content may stop working if a service closes, cannot be moved between platforms, and may block legitimate uses such as accessibility tools or teaching clips. The balance between protecting creators and respecting users is a real ethical debate, not a solved problem.

Watermarking: A watermark is information embedded into the media itself. A visible watermark is a logo in the corner of a TV channel's broadcast or a photographer's preview. An invisible watermark hides data in the signal, for example small changes to DCT coefficients or audio frequencies that people cannot notice. Robust watermarks are designed to survive compression, resizing and re-recording, so they can prove ownership. Fragile watermarks are designed to break on any change, so they can show that an image was tampered with.

Forensic watermarking worked: Streaming services and film screeners can embed a different invisible ID for each viewer, so a leaked copy reveals which account it came from. How many bits are needed? With n bits we can label 2^n users. 24 bits label 2^24 = 16,777,216 users; 32 bits label 2^32 = 4,294,967,296, more than enough for any service. In practice extra bits are added for error correction, because the leaked copy may be compressed and cropped.

Fingerprinting versus watermarking: Fingerprinting does not add anything to the media. Instead, it computes a compact signature from the content itself, like the audio fingerprints of lesson 23, and compares uploads against a database of reference fingerprints. Large video platforms use such systems: rights owners submit reference files, and new uploads that match can be blocked, tracked or monetised for the owner. This is what happened to the student's project video with the popular song. Fingerprinting finds copies; watermarking can also identify which copy leaked.

Deepfakes and manipulated media: Modern machine learning can swap faces in video, clone a voice from a short sample, or generate realistic images of events that never happened. These deepfakes can be harmless fun, but they can also be used for fraud (a cloned voice asking a family member to send money by mobile banking), harassment, especially of women through fake intimate images, and political misinformation. Defences include detection tools, which are imperfect, and provenance: standards such as C2PA content credentials let cameras and editing tools attach signed records of where a piece of media came from and how it was edited. Media literacy, checking the source before sharing, remains essential.

Privacy in media: Photos and videos carry more than you see. EXIF metadata can include the exact GPS location and time of capture, so posting a photo of your home can reveal your address; many platforms strip this on upload, but files shared directly may keep it. Faces in crowd photos can be recognised automatically. Recording people without consent, sharing images of children, or keeping CCTV footage longer than needed all raise privacy and legal issues. Engineers can help by stripping metadata by default, blurring faces where appropriate, and storing only what is needed.

Accessibility and inclusion as ethics: Ethics is not only about what not to do. Providing captions, transcripts, audio descriptions and Bangla as well as English options means more people can use your product, including deaf users, people with low vision and people more comfortable in their mother tongue. Designing for low bandwidth is also an inclusion choice in a country where many users rely on mobile data.

Real-life example 1, a local OTT platform: A Bangladeshi streaming service licenses a new web series. The contract with the producer requires DRM, so the service encrypts the segments, runs licence servers for Widevine and FairPlay, and limits each account to a few devices. It also adds forensic watermarks. When a copy appears on a Telegram channel, the watermark points to one account, which is closed, and takedown notices are sent to the platforms hosting the copy.

Real-life example 2, a student's documentary: A university team makes a documentary on river erosion. They use their own footage, interview people with signed consent forms, take background music from a Creative Commons BY collection and credit the composer in the end titles, and use a short news clip only for commentary, with the source named. They remove GPS data from photos of villagers' homes and add Bangla and English captions. The film can be shared publicly without legal or ethical worries.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Thinking "no copyright notice means free to use" is wrong; protection is automatic. Thinking "credit the creator" makes any use legal is wrong; credit is required by some licences but does not replace permission. Confusing DRM (controls use) with watermarking (marks the content) and fingerprinting (recognises content) is common. Exams ask you to define copyright and its exceptions, explain Creative Commons elements, draw the DRM licence flow, compare watermarking and fingerprinting, and discuss ethical issues such as deepfakes and privacy.

Recap: Copyright gives creators automatic control over copying, adaptation and sharing of their expression, with limited exceptions like fair use or fair dealing, and Creative Commons offers simple sharing licences. DRM encrypts content and releases keys only under licence rules, through systems like Widevine, FairPlay and PlayReady, but it has limits and critics. Watermarks embed marks, fingerprints recognise content, and engineers carry real responsibility for privacy, provenance and accessibility.
key_points: Copyright arises automatically on creation and protects expression, not ideas; registration is optional evidence in many countries.
Owners control copying, distribution, adaptation and communication to the public; terms and exceptions differ by country.
Fair use (flexible four-factor test, US) and fair dealing (listed purposes) allow limited uses without permission.
Creative Commons elements: BY (attribution), SA (share alike), NC (non-commercial), ND (no derivatives); CC0 waives rights.
Streaming DRM: encrypt segments, licence server checks rules, trusted decryption module gets the key; Widevine, FairPlay, PlayReady.
Watermarks embed visible or invisible data (robust or fragile); n bits of forensic ID label 2^n users (32 bits = 4,294,967,296).
Fingerprinting computes signatures from content to find copies without modifying the media.
Ethical risks: deepfakes, EXIF location leaks, consent; provenance (C2PA), stripping metadata and accessibility are engineering responses.
lessons.tip: When you study this lesson, make a three-column table: DRM, watermarking, fingerprinting, with rows "what it does", "changes the media?" and "example". Most exam confusion disappears once that table is clear in your head.
lessons.task: Pick five images or songs you would like to use in a class video. For each, find its licence or copyright status (Wikimedia Commons, Creative Commons search, the artist page). Write what you are allowed to do and what credit line you must add. Then check one photo on your phone: does its details view show GPS location?

quiz.q: When does copyright protection usually begin under the Berne Convention approach?
options: After registration with a copyright office
Automatically when the original work is created and fixed
Only after a copyright notice is added
quiz.explain: Protection is automatic; registration, where it exists, is useful evidence but not required.

quiz.q: What does the NC element of a Creative Commons licence mean?
options: New copies must use the same licence
quiz.explain: NC = non-commercial; ND is no derivatives, SA is share alike, BY is attribution.

quiz.q: In streaming DRM, what does the licence server do?
options: Checks the rules and returns the decryption key for a trusted module
Stores and serves the video segments
Re-encodes the video at lower quality
quiz.explain: Segments are encrypted on the CDN; the licence server checks entitlement and releases keys only to a trusted decryption module.

quiz.q: How many users can a 32-bit forensic watermark ID distinguish?
quiz.explain: 2^32 = 4,294,967,296 distinct IDs (24 bits would give 16,777,216).

quiz.q: Which technique recognises copies of a song without adding anything to the original file?
quiz.explain: Fingerprinting computes signatures from the content itself and matches them against reference fingerprints.

lessons.title: Capstone: A Low-Bandwidth Video Lecture Platform for Bangladesh
lessons.content:
Picture Rumana, a second-year student in a char area of Gaibandha. Her university posts lectures online, but her phone gets a weak mobile signal, her data pack is 2 GB a month, and power cuts are common. A platform that only offers full HD video is useless to her. A platform designed with everything in this course, media representation, compression, streaming, Unicode text and ethics, can give her nearly the same learning as a student in Dhaka. In this capstone we will design that platform step by step, with real numbers, and use it to review the whole course.

Step 1, understand the users and the content: Good multimedia design starts with people, not codecs. Our users mostly have mid-range Android phones, mobile data that ranges from good 4G to weak 3G or worse, limited monthly data packs, and sometimes no network for hours. The content is lectures: a teacher talking, slides or a whiteboard, sometimes a demonstration. The key insight from lesson 1 and lesson 10 is to ask what information matters. In a lecture, the voice and the slides carry almost all the learning; the teacher's face in sharp detail carries very little. That one decision drives everything else.

Step 2, why raw is impossible: Recall raw video sizes. A 720p frame at 30 frames per second in 4:2:0 8-bit needs 1280 x 720 x 12 x 30 = 331,776,000 bits per second, about 332 Mbps. A 400 kbps compressed stream is about 829 times smaller. Without the DCT, quantization, motion compensation and entropy coding we studied, online lectures would simply not exist on mobile networks.

Step 3, the media modes: We will offer four ways to consume each lecture. Audio-only mode: just the voice, for the weakest connections. Slides plus audio mode: the voice plus the slide images, changing when the teacher changes slides. Low video mode: small-resolution video for when seeing the board or demonstration matters. Normal video mode: decent quality for good connections. The player can switch between video rungs automatically with ABR, and the student can choose audio-only or slides mode manually.

Step 4, the audio track: Audio is the backbone, so it must be clear at a low rate. Speech does not need the full 20 kHz band; modern perceptual codecs designed for speech and music, such as Opus or AAC profiles meant for low bit rates, give clear speech well below CD rates. Let us budget 48 kbps for a mono speech track. One hour then uses 48,000 x 3,600 / 8 = 21,600,000 bytes, 21.6 MB, and a 45-minute lecture uses 16.2 MB. Compare that with CD-quality PCM at 1,411.2 kbps from lesson 5: about 29 times smaller, and for speech still very understandable. Recording quality matters more than codec settings: a cheap lapel microphone near the teacher's mouth beats an expensive camera microphone across the room.

Step 5, slides plus audio worked: If a teacher shows about one slide per minute, a 45-minute lecture has about 45 slides. Slides are text and diagrams with flat colours, so from lesson 13 we choose PNG or lossless WebP for them, not JPEG, which would blur text edges. Suppose each compressed slide image is about 100 KB. Then the slides total 45 x 100 KB = 4.5 MB, plus 16.2 MB of audio = 20.7 MB per lecture. Spread over 2,700 seconds, that is about 61 kbps on average, yet text stays perfectly sharp, sharper than any low-rate video could show. Timestamps tell the player when to show each slide, exactly like synchronising tracks in a container (lesson 19).

Step 6, the video ladder: For video modes we build a bitrate ladder (lesson 21), total rates including audio: 240p at 200 kbps, 360p at 400 kbps and 720p at 800 kbps. These are modest because lectures have little motion: most macroblocks in P and B frames are skipped or have tiny residuals, so motion-compensated coding (lessons 16 and 17) works extremely well. Data per hour: 200 kbps is 90 MB, 400 kbps is 180 MB, 800 kbps is 360 MB. A 45-minute lecture is 67.5 MB, 135 MB or 270 MB.

Step 7, what a student's data pack buys: Suppose a course has 30 lectures of 45 minutes, 22.5 hours in total. In audio-only mode the course needs 30 x 16.2 = 486 MB. In slides plus audio mode, 30 x 20.7 = 621 MB. At 240p it needs 2.025 GB, at 360p 4.05 GB and at 720p 8.1 GB. With Rumana's 2 GB monthly pack, slides mode lets her follow the whole course and still have data left for other things, while 720p would be impossible. That is the whole argument for multiple modes, in one table of numbers.

Step 8, choosing codecs: The video codec should be one that every target phone can decode in hardware, because software decoding drains the battery. H.264 is the safest baseline because hardware support for it is nearly universal. Newer codecs such as HEVC or AV1 can give similar quality at a noticeably lower bit rate, but support varies across older devices and there are licensing questions to check, so we can offer them as extra versions for devices that report support, keeping H.264 as the fallback. Encoder settings matter too: a slower preset and a longer GOP suit lectures because there are few scene cuts.

Step 9, packaging and delivery: Each version is cut into aligned segments of about 4 seconds, packaged as fragmented MP4, and described in both an HLS playlist and a DASH MPD (lessons 19 and 21). Segments go to object storage and are served through a CDN, ideally with caches inside Bangladesh, so popular lectures do not cross the international link each time. The player starts at the lowest video rung for a fast start, uses throughput and buffer level to climb, and never goes above 360p on a small screen in data saver mode.

Step 10, offline first: Live streaming alone is not enough for users with patchy coverage. The app lets students download lectures in a chosen mode when they have Wi-Fi or a cheaper night-time data pack, and play them offline later. A slides-mode lecture of 20.7 MB downloads in about 166 seconds even at 1 Mbps. Downloads must resume after interruptions, so the app requests segments one by one and remembers which have arrived; this falls out naturally from the segmented design.

Step 11, captions, text and search: Every lecture gets captions in Bangla and English, stored as WebVTT text tracks (lesson 24). Text is stored in Unicode, UTF-8, never in legacy Bijoy-style encodings, so it displays correctly and search works (lesson 2). The app must use fonts that shape Bangla conjuncts properly, so that ক্ষ and vowel signs render right on older phones. Captions help deaf students, students watching in a noisy household, and anyone whose network drops audio for a moment. Captions plus slide text become a searchable transcript: a student can type "Huffman" and jump straight to the minute where it is explained, a direct use of text-based retrieval from lesson 23.

Step 12, live classes: For live classes, interaction matters, so we use a WebRTC-based conferencing service with an SFU (lesson 22). The teacher's stream is simulcast at two or three qualities so weak receivers get the low layer. Students join with audio and cameras off by default, which saves upload bandwidth. The session is recorded on the server, then processed into the same four on-demand modes, so students who missed it because of a power cut can catch up.

Step 13, cost estimate: Delivery cost is driven by bytes. Suppose 10,000 students each watch 20 hours a month. At an average of 200 kbps that is 10,000 x 20 x 90 MB = 18,000,000 MB, 18 TB per month. If most students use slides or audio modes and the average falls to about 96 kbps, it becomes 10,000 x 20 x 43.2 MB = 8.64 TB, less than half. Storage is small in comparison: storing one hour in audio plus three video rungs needs about (48 + 200 + 400 + 800) kbps x 3,600 / 8, which is 651.6 MB, plus a few MB of slides.

Step 14, protection and ethics: The university owns its lectures, but students should be able to download them for study. We use simple measures: signed, time-limited URLs and app-level encryption for downloads, and perhaps a light per-user watermark, rather than heavy DRM that might block old phones (lesson 25). Any music, images or clips in slides must be licensed or used under the exceptions allowed by law, with credits. We record consent from guest speakers, strip GPS metadata from uploaded photos, and store minimal personal data.

Step 15, measuring quality: We measure what students actually experience: startup time, rebuffering ratio, average bit rate, mode usage and caption usage, broken down by district and network operator. Objective measures like PSNR (lesson 10) can guide encoder settings, but we also run short surveys and watch completion rates. If many users in one area keep stalling at 240p, we add a lower rung or push slides mode harder there.

Step 16, the processing pipeline: When a teacher uploads a recording, an automatic pipeline runs. It first checks the file with a tool like ffprobe to read its codecs, resolution and duration. It extracts and cleans the audio, normalising loudness so every lecture plays at a similar volume. It encodes the audio track and each video rung, cuts and packages segments, writes the HLS and DASH manifests, exports slide images from the teacher's PDF with their timestamps, and generates draft captions with speech recognition for a human to correct. Finally it copies everything to storage, warms the CDN for the first lectures of the week, and indexes the transcript for search. Automating this means a teacher only has to press upload once.

Common mistakes in such designs: Starting with the highest resolution instead of the most important information; using JPEG for slides; forgetting captions and Bangla Unicode; assuming always-on networks; and ignoring cost per GB. Another mistake is quoting codec gains as fixed numbers; real savings depend on content and encoder, so always test with your own lectures.

Course recap: We began by asking what multimedia is and how text, images, audio and video become bits, including Unicode and Bangla shaping. We learned colour spaces and chroma subsampling, PCM audio, and why raw media is huge. Information theory told us how far lossless coding can go, and RLE, Huffman, LZW and arithmetic coding showed how. Lossy coding added the DCT and quantization, and the JPEG pipeline put it all together, while psychoacoustics explained MP3 and AAC. Video added frames, I/P/B pictures and motion estimation, leading to H.264, HEVC and AV1. Containers packaged streams; RTP, HLS and DASH delivered them; QoS and conferencing made them interactive. Finally we searched, authored, protected and used media responsibly.

What next: From here you can go deeper in several directions: image processing and computer vision, speech and audio processing, video engineering and encoding at scale, networked systems and CDNs, AR/VR and graphics, or game development. A good next step is hands-on: install ffmpeg, encode a lecture at several bit rates, package it for HLS, and watch it on your own phone over mobile data. Nothing teaches multimedia like seeing your own numbers come to life.
key_points: Design from the users and the information that matters: in lectures, voice and slides carry most of the learning.
Raw 720p30 4:2:0 is about 332 Mbps; a 400 kbps stream is about 829 times smaller.
Audio-only at 48 kbps uses 21.6 MB per hour, 16.2 MB per 45-minute lecture.
Slides plus audio: 45 slides x 100 KB + 16.2 MB audio = 20.7 MB per lecture, about 61 kbps, with sharp text (PNG/lossless WebP, not JPEG).
Video ladder 200/400/800 kbps = 90/180/360 MB per hour; a 22.5-hour course needs 486 MB (audio) to 8.1 GB (720p).
Use H.264 as the universal baseline with newer codecs as optional extras; deliver with HLS/DASH segments via a CDN, plus offline downloads.
Captions in Bangla and English as Unicode WebVTT enable accessibility and transcript search.
Delivery cost scales with bytes: 10,000 students x 20 h at 200 kbps = 18 TB per month; at 96 kbps, 8.64 TB.
lessons.tip: In any design question, write a small table of modes with bit rate, MB per hour and MB per course. Numbers turn a vague answer into an engineering answer, and examiners notice.
lessons.task: Plan your own version for one real course you are taking: list its number of lectures and length, choose your modes and bit rates, and compute MB per lecture and per course for each mode. Then check what your own monthly data pack would allow, and decide which mode you would actually use.

quiz.q: For slides in the slides-plus-audio mode, which image format choice is best?
quiz.explain: Slides are text and flat colours; lossless PNG/WebP keeps edges sharp and compresses them well, while JPEG blurs text.

quiz.q: How much data does a 45-minute lecture use in 48 kbps audio-only mode?
Why is H.264 chosen as the baseline video codec in this design?
options: It always gives the smallest files
It has no patents or licences at all
Hardware decoding support for it is nearly universal on target phones
It is the only codec HLS supports
quiz.explain: Hardware decode saves battery and works on old phones; newer codecs are offered as optional extras where supported.

quiz.q: 10,000 students each watch 20 hours a month at 200 kbps. Monthly delivery is about:
Why should captions and transcripts be stored as Unicode (UTF-8) text?
options: So Bangla displays correctly and lectures become searchable
quiz.explain: Unicode text renders correctly with proper fonts and supports search, unlike legacy Bijoy-style encodings.
